But the window loads only the local bundle (main.cjs:188-189) and nothing in src/ calls getUserMedia or Notification, so reaching this requires the navigation gap above plus a renderer compromise — a checklist hardening item, not an exploitable path on its own. | Confirmed by grep: neither `setPermissionRequestHandler` nor `setPermissionCheckHandler` appears anywhere in apps/shell, and Electron's default handler does approve media and notification requests without prompting. The gap is real and free to close. But I cannot construct a failure without a prior renderer compromise — the renderer loads only the local bundle (main.cjs:189 `window.loadFile(...dist/index.html)`), has no remote content and, per the grep in finding 4, no navigation path of its own. Pure defense-in-depth, and the impact story leans entirely on finding 4. Low. (Minor citation error: apps/shell/README.md:70, not :76, is the `/api/settings` row that mentions devices.)

findings.title: DevTools reachable in the shipped build via the default menu accelerator
findings.quote: autoHideMenuBar: true,
findings.why_wrong: `autoHideMenuBar` hides the menu bar visually but does not remove the menu or its accelerators, and I confirmed there is no `Menu.setApplicationMenu(null)` and no `devTools: false` in webPreferences anywhere in apps/shell. Electron's default application menu includes View → Toggle Developer Tools bound to Ctrl+Shift+I / F12, which remains live in the packaged build produced by scripts/package.mjs.
findings.impact: Anyone at the keyboard of a shared sim rig — or a driver following a bad forum instruction — opens a JS console inside the app's origin with `window.ssc` in scope. That is the practical delivery vehicle for the `api:command` route injection above, and it also exposes the entire `/api/settings` and `/api/data` surface interactively. It downgrades every 'requires renderer compromise' caveat in this report to 'requires physical or remote-desktop access'.
findings.fix: `Menu.setApplicationMenu(null)` and `devTools: !app.isPackaged` in webPreferences, keeping DevTools for the dev-server path guarded by `process.env.VITE_DEV_SERVER_URL`.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed: main.cjs:163 `autoHideMenuBar: true` hides the bar without removing accelerators, main.cjs:5 does not even import `Menu`, and my grep found no `Menu.setApplicationMenu(null)` and no `devTools: false` anywhere in apps/shell — so Electron's default menu, including View -> Toggle Developer Tools, is live in the packaged build. The impact is smaller than stated: it requires someone at the keyboard, the bearer token is never in the renderer (preload.cjs exposes only IPC wrappers), and anyone at the keyboard can already drive the same commands through the UI. The real delta is scripted access to `window.ssc`. | Verified: `autoHideMenuBar: true` at main.cjs:163 only hides the bar, and grep finds no `Menu.setApplicationMenu(null)` and no `devTools: false` in the webPreferences block (main.cjs:164-169), so Electron's default View > Toggle Developer Tools accelerator is live in the packaged build. Downgrading, because the threat model is thin: opening DevTools requires physical or remote-desktop access to the machine, and anyone with that already has the user's own privileges — they can read the SQLite app home and settings directly without going through the app. It genuinely does make finding 1 reachable by hand, which is why it is worth fixing, but it is not itself a medium-severity vulnerability. Low.

findings.title: Renderer crash and console-error handlers are registered only under the smoke flag
findings.quote:
if (SMOKE) {
    window.webContents.on("console-message", (event) => {
findings.why_wrong: Both `console-message` (line 172) and `render-process-gone` (line 177) sit inside `if (SMOKE)`, i.e. they exist only when `SSC_SHELL_SMOKE === "1"` (main.cjs:14). In the shipped app neither is attached, and there is no `unresponsive` handler and no `webContents.reload()` recovery path anywhere in the file.
findings.impact: A renderer OOM or GPU-process crash mid-race leaves the window painted `#12161d` (the backgroundColor at main.cjs:161) and permanently blank. The main process is still alive and still streaming state into a dead renderer, the Python host keeps running, and the driver gets no dialog, no auto-reload and no crash record — the exact opposite of what `install_crash_handlers` does for the Python side at api/__main__.py:31.
findings.fix: Move both listeners out of the `if (SMOKE)` block. In production, log `render-process-gone` details to the same crash-report path the host uses and call `window.webContents.reload()` once, showing an error banner if the reload also fails.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed verbatim: main.cjs:171 `if (SMOKE) {` encloses both `console-message` (:172) and `render-process-gone` (:177), with SMOKE defined at :14 as `process.env.SSC_SHELL_SMOKE === "1"`. There is no `unresponsive` handler and no `webContents.reload()` anywhere in the file, and the main process keeps pushing state at :96 into a dead renderer (the `isDestroyed` guard there does not detect a crashed render process). For a display the driver reads mid-race, a silently blank window with no recovery and no crash record is a real defect, and it contrasts with `install_crash_handlers(paths.crash_report, role="shell-host")` at api/__main__.py:31. | Confirmed by reading main.cjs:171-181: both `console-message` (172) and `render-process-gone` (177) are inside `if (SMOKE)`, where SMOKE is `process.env.SSC_SHELL_SMOKE === "1"` (main.cjs:14). No `unresponsive` handler and no `webContents.reload()` anywhere in the file. Concrete failure is constructible without an attacker: a renderer OOM or GPU crash mid-session leaves the window painted `backgroundColor: "#12161d"` (main.cjs:161) and permanently blank, the main process keeps streaming state into a dead webContents via the `!window.isDestroyed()` guard at main.cjs:96 (which passes for a live window with a gone renderer), and nothing tells the driver or records it — while the Python side does get `install_crash_handlers(paths.crash_report, role="shell-host")` at api/__main__.py:31. Medium stands.

findings.title: The 'another host is running' case is reported to the user as a malformed handshake, then the app exits silently
findings.quote: const handshake = parseHandshake(first);
findings.why_wrong: When the native Control Center holds the single-instance mutex, api/__main__.py:28 prints a well-formed, actionable line — `print(json.dumps({"error": "another SSC Race Engineer host is running"}), flush=True)` — and returns 2. `parseHandshake` (host.cjs:28-34) only looks for `port` and `token`, never at `error`, so it throws the generic `"Runtime host handshake is malformed"`. That reaches the `.catch` at main.cjs:205, which does `process.stderr.write(...)` followed by `app.exit(1)` — and stderr is not attached to anything in a packaged Windows GUI app. README.md:80-82 claims this refusal is a designed behaviour, but the shell never surfaces it.
findings.impact: The overwhelmingly common user story — native Control Center already open, driver clicks the Start-menu entry for the desktop shell — produces absolutely nothing: no window, no dialog, no message. The user clicks again, gets nothing again, and has no way to learn that the fix is to close the other app. The one diagnostic the host went out of its way to provide is discarded.
findings.fix: Have `parseHandshake` return or throw a typed result when `parsed.error` is a string, and have the `.catch` in main.cjs show `dialog.showErrorBox("SSC Race Engineer", message)` before exiting.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed end to end. api/__main__.py:25-29 prints `{"error": "another SSC Race Engineer host is running"}` and returns 2; host.cjs:28-34 `parseHandshake` only inspects `parsed.port`/`parsed.token` and throws the generic 'Runtime host handshake is malformed', discarding `error`; that lands in main.cjs:205-208, which does `process.stderr.write(...)` then `app.exit(1)` — stderr goes nowhere in a packaged Windows GUI app. apps/shell/README.md:80-82 does present the refusal as designed behaviour ('The host refuses to start while the native Control Center holds the single-instance mutex'). Common user story, zero feedback. | Fully confirmed. api/__main__.py:25-29 `if _acquire_single_instance() is None:` prints `json.dumps({"error": "another SSC Race Engineer host is running"})` and returns 2; `parseHandshake` (host.cjs:28-34) inspects only `parsed.port` and `parsed.token` and throws the generic `"Runtime host handshake is malformed"`, never reading `error`. That reaches main.cjs:205-208 `process.stderr.write(...)` then `app.exit(1)` — and a packaged Windows GUI Electron app has no console attached, so the message goes nowhere. apps/shell/README.md:80-82 does claim the refusal as designed behaviour ('The host refuses to start while the native Control Center holds the single-instance mutex'). The trigger is the most ordinary user action there is: native Control Center open, click the shell's Start-menu entry (created at installer/SSC_Race_Engineer.iss:73-74). Medium stands.

findings.title: No single-instance lock on the Electron app itself
findings.why_wrong: `app.requestSingleInstanceLock()` is not called anywhere in apps/shell — I grepped. The Python host has a Windows named mutex (`Local\\SSC_Race_Engineer_Desktop_v06`, ui/app.py:51) but the shell process does not, so a second shell launch always starts, always spawns a second host, and that host always loses the mutex race.
findings.impact: Launching the shell twice (a second Start-menu click while the first is still starting, or the desktop shortcut plus the startup task at installer/SSC_Race_Engineer.iss:80) reliably burns a full process start and then dies with no message, via the mis-reported handshake path above. The mutex is `Local\` scoped, so it is also per-logon-session: two Windows sessions pointed at the same `SSC_APP_HOME` get two hosts against one SQLite app home with no interlock at all.
findings.fix: Call `if (!app.requestSingleInstanceLock()) app.quit();` at the top of main.cjs and add a `second-instance` handler that focuses the existing window. Consider `Global\\` for the host mutex if a shared app home across sessions is possible.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed: `app.requestSingleInstanceLock` appears nowhere in apps/shell (grepped), while the Python side does hold `Local\\SSC_Race_Engineer_Desktop_v06` (src/ssc_engineer/ui/app.py:45-55, the name string at :54 rather than :51). So a second shell launch always spawns a second host that loses the mutex and dies through the mis-reported handshake path above. The 'two Windows sessions on one SSC_APP_HOME' sub-claim is weak — the app home is per-user under %LOCALAPPDATA% — but the primary failure is real and user-visible. | Confirmed: `requestSingleInstanceLock` appears nowhere in apps/shell, and the Python mutex is `"Local\\SSC_Race_Engineer_Desktop_v06"` at ui/app.py:51-55 with a 5 s retry deadline (line 49), so a second shell always spawns a second host that loses the race and dies via the silent path above. One impact claim is wrong: the startup task at installer/SSC_Race_Engineer.iss:80 writes a Run key pointing at `{app}\{#MyAppExeName}` (.iss:83), i.e. the native app, not the shell — so that specific double-launch story does not occur. The double-click / second-Start-menu-click story does. Largely a duplicate of the consequence in finding 12; medium stands on that basis.

findings.title: CSP is meta-only, allows unsafe-inline styles, and omits form-action
findings.quote: <meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy" content="default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; img-src 'self' data:; font-src 'self' data:; connect-src 'self'; worker-src 'self' blob:; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'" />
findings.why_wrong: Three concrete gaps. (1) It is delivered only as a meta tag; there is no `session.defaultSession.webRequest.onHeadersReceived` injecting a CSP header (grepped — absent), so any document loaded into this webContents that is not this exact file has no policy at all. (2) `style-src 'unsafe-inline'` permits injected `<style>` and `style=` attributes, which is a working CSS-exfiltration and UI-redress primitive; StyleX compiles to static classes at build time and does not require it. (3) `form-action` is absent, and unlike most directives it does not fall back to `default-src`, so a form can post the DOM to any origin — which, with no `will-navigate` handler, is a complete exfiltration path that never touches `fetch`.
findings.impact: The policy reads as strict but leaves the two channels an attacker would actually use — inline CSS and cross-origin form submission — wide open, and evaporates entirely the moment the window navigates. It gives a false assurance that README.md:79-80 repeats to reviewers as 'strict CSP'.
findings.fix: Add `form-action 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'; script-src 'self'` as a real response header via `onHeadersReceived` on the default session, and drop `'unsafe-inline'` from `style-src` (verify the Astryx/StyleX build emits no runtime inline styles; if it needs one, use a nonce).
findings.verifier_notes: The quote at index.html:6 is exact. Gap (1) confirmed: no `onHeadersReceived` anywhere in apps/shell (grepped), so the policy is document-scoped only. Gap (3) confirmed: `form-action` is absent and does not inherit from `default-src`. Gap (2) is confirmed as written in the policy, but the sub-claim that StyleX makes `'unsafe-inline'` unnecessary is unverified — StyleX and the @astryxdesign components can emit `style` attributes for dynamic values and node_modules is not present to check, so removing it may well break rendering. Overall the three verified content gaps stand; exploitation still presupposes a renderer compromise. | The three structural gaps are real as read at index.html:6, and grep confirms no `onHeadersReceived` CSP header anywhere in apps/shell. But the exploitability arguments do not stand on their own and one supporting claim is wrong: `style-src 'unsafe-inline'` is not gratuitous, because vite.config.ts has no CSS-handling overrides and the same index.html is served by the Vite dev server under `VITE_DEV_SERVER_URL` (main.cjs:188), where inline style injection is required — so 'StyleX does not require it' is only true of the production build. The `form-action` gap needs the same prior renderer compromise as finding 4, and there are no forms or links in the renderer at all. apps/shell/README.md:80 does say 'strict CSP', so the documentation mismatch is accurate. Low.

findings.title: Window bounds file is deserialized and spread straight into the BrowserWindow constructor
findings.quote:
window = new BrowserWindow({
    width: 1440,
    height: 900,
    ...saved,
findings.why_wrong: `saved` is `JSON.parse` of `window-bounds.json` from `app.getPath("userData")` (main.cjs:129-131) and every key it contains is spread into the constructor. The validation at main.cjs:133-137 only inspects `x`, `y`, `width` and `height` — and with loose `>=` comparisons that coerce strings — so any other BrowserWindow option in the file is applied verbatim: `kiosk`, `alwaysOnTop`, `transparent`, `frame: false`, `opacity`. The security-relevant keys happen to be safe here only by ordering luck: `webPreferences` is written after the spread at line 164 and so wins.
findings.impact: A tampered or corrupted bounds file in the user-writable profile yields a frameless, always-on-top or transparent window with no way to close it, and the user's only recourse is deleting a file they do not know exists. The safety of the `webPreferences` key rests entirely on object-literal key order, which a future refactor can silently invert into a real privilege escalation.
findings.fix: Destructure explicitly — `const { x, y, width, height, maximized } = readBounds()` — validate each with `Number.isFinite`, and pass only those. Never spread deserialized data into a privileged constructor.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed: main.cjs:155-158 spreads `...saved` into the constructor, where `saved` is `JSON.parse(readFileSync(boundsFile(), "utf8"))` (:131) and the validation at :133-137 only tests `saved.x/y/width/height` against the work area, letting any other BrowserWindow option through. `webPreferences` at :164 is written after the spread and does win, so the observation that the safety rests on object-literal ordering is accurate. Requires write access to the user's profile directory, so the practical impact is the annoyance described, not escalation — low is the right grade. | Confirmed as read: main.cjs:155-158 spreads `...saved` into the constructor, `saved` is `JSON.parse(readFileSync(boundsFile(), "utf8"))` (main.cjs:131), and the check at main.cjs:133-137 only reads `saved.x/.y/.width/.height` with `>=`/`<=` comparisons that coerce strings. Every other key rides through — and `webPreferences` is indeed safe only because it is written after the spread at main.cjs:164. The exploit half is weak (writing `window-bounds.json` in `app.getPath("userData")` again presupposes an attacker running as the user) and the app itself only ever writes bounds plus `maximized` (main.cjs:147), so benign corruption produces junk, not `kiosk: true`. Confirmed as the latent-refactor-hazard the finding itself rates it. Low stands.

findings.title: Installer silently ships without the shell when the Electron build has not run
findings.quote:
#ifexist MyShellDir + "\" + MyShellExe
  #define HasShell
#endif
findings.why_wrong: `HasShell` gates both the `[Files]` entry at line 66-68 and the Start-menu icon at line 73-74. If `apps/shell/out/SSC Race Engineer Shell-win32-x64/SSC Race Engineer Shell.exe` is absent — `pnpm package` skipped, or it failed after `rmSync(path.join(root, "out"), ...)` at scripts/package.mjs:17 wiped the previous output — Inno compiles a perfectly valid installer with no shell and no warning, because `#ifexist` is a silent compile-time test with no `#else #error`.
findings.impact: A release build produced on a machine where the Electron step failed ships to drivers as a complete installer that is quietly missing the entire new desktop shell. Nothing in the build output, the installer, or the installed product says a component is absent, so the defect is found by a user reporting a missing Start-menu entry.
findings.fix: Add `#else` `#error "Shell build missing; run pnpm package in apps/shell"` unless an explicit `-DSkipShell` is passed, and assert the shell exe exists in scripts/windows/BUILD_INSTALLER.bat before invoking ISCC.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed: installer/SSC_Race_Engineer.iss:12-14 is `#ifexist MyShellDir + "\" + MyShellExe` / `#define HasShell`, gating the [Files] entry at :66-69 and the Start-menu icon at :73-75, with no `#else #error`. Worth noting the window is narrower than stated: scripts\windows\BUILD_INSTALLER.bat:29-30 aborts the build if `pnpm package` fails, and :24-25 at least echoes 'pnpm not found: building the installer without the desktop shell' when pnpm is missing. The silent case is running ISCC directly, or after `rmSync(path.join(root, "out"))` at scripts/package.mjs:17 wiped a previous output — real, but a narrow build-process hazard. | Confirmed by reading the .iss in full: lines 12-14 `#ifexist MyShellDir + "\" + MyShellExe` / `#define HasShell` with no `#else #error`, gating the `[Files]` entry at 66-69 and the Start-menu icon at 73-75. The build-order hazard is real: scripts/package.mjs:17 `rmSync(path.join(root, "out"), { recursive: true, force: true })` wipes the previous output before `packager()` runs at 18, so a failure after that point leaves no shell directory at all and Inno compiles a valid, silently incomplete installer. Nothing in the installer or the installed product records that a component is missing. Low stands.

findings.title: Monthly Dependabot cadence for a Chromium-embedding desktop app
findings.quote:
- package-ecosystem: npm
    directory: /apps/shell
    schedule:
      interval: monthly
    open-pull-requests-limit: 3
findings.why_wrong: Electron 44.4.1 (apps/shell/package.json:37, pnpm-lock.yaml:422) embeds Chromium and ships security releases roughly every two weeks, frequently for actively-exploited V8 and renderer bugs. A monthly check with a three-PR cap means a shipped installer can carry a Chromium renderer that is up to a month behind a known in-the-wild exploit. The github-actions ecosystem directly above it is checked weekly, so the cadence is not a repo-wide policy — the most security-sensitive dependency got the slowest schedule. There is also no `pnpm audit` step in windows-ci.yml (grepped).
findings.impact: A Chromium RCE disclosed shortly after a Dependabot run sits unpatched in the release pipeline for weeks, and since nothing in CI fails on a vulnerable dependency, a release can be cut from that state without anyone noticing.
findings.fix: Move `/apps/shell` to `interval: daily` (or weekly at minimum), raise the PR limit, and add a `pnpm audit --audit-level high` step to the Desktop shell job in windows-ci.yml so a known-vulnerable Electron blocks the build rather than merely opening a PR.
findings.verifier_notes: Facts check out: .github/dependabot.yml:20-25 gives /apps/shell `interval: monthly` with `open-pull-requests-limit: 3`, while github-actions at :4-8 is `interval: weekly`, so the cadence difference within one file is real; apps/shell/package.json:37 pins `"electron": "44.4.1"`; and grepping .github/workflows/windows-ci.yml for 'audit' returns nothing — the shell job (:88-98) runs install/typecheck/test/smoke/package with no vulnerability gate. This is a process judgement rather than a code defect, which low correctly reflects. | Facts verified: .github/dependabot.yml:20-25 sets npm /apps/shell to `interval: monthly` with `open-pull-requests-limit: 3`, while github-actions at lines 4-8 is `interval: weekly`, so the inconsistency within the same file is real; electron is pinned at `"electron": "44.4.1"` in apps/shell/package.json:37; and .github/workflows/windows-ci.yml:93-98 runs `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`, typecheck, test, smoke and package with no audit step. This is a process observation rather than a defect with a repro — there is no input and no state that makes it fail — but the user explicitly asked for process problems, and the asymmetry (slowest cadence on the single most security-sensitive dependency) is a fair call. Low, as filed.

findings.title: Updater hands the plaintext OpenAI key and team access code to the downloaded installer's environment
findings.why_wrong: `credentials._store()` (credentials.py:62) and `bootstrap_api_key()` (credentials.py:151) deliberately place the secret into `os.environ["OPENAI_API_KEY"]` / `os.environ["SSC_TEAM_ACCESS_CODE"]` so the voice child can inherit it. `launch_verified_installer` then copies that entire environment and passes it as `env=environment` to `subprocess.Popen([...installer.exe, '/VERYSILENT', ...])`. The only filtering performed is removal of `_PYI_*` PyInstaller variables. The Inno Setup installer — and every `[Run]` entry, custom DLL and post-install script it executes, typically after UAC elevation — therefore receives the user's live OpenAI API key and team access code in its process environment.
findings.impact: User has voice configured (key in Credential Manager, hence in os.environ) and update_policy='automatic'. An update lands, `launch_verified_installer` runs, and `SSC_Race_Engineer_v1.0.5_Setup.exe` starts with OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-proj-... in its environment. Any bug, telemetry step or tampered installer stage in that process can read and exfiltrate a billable OpenAI credential the app went to great lengths to keep out of TOML, logs and exports. On Windows the elevated child's environment is also readable by any process holding PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION on it.
findings.fix: Build a minimal environment for the installer instead of copying the process environment: start from `os.environ.copy()`, then `for name in (OPENAI_ACCOUNT, TEAM_ACCESS_ACCOUNT): environment.pop(name, None)` before the Popen. Apply the same scrub in `update_recovery._clean_pyinstaller_environment` (update_recovery.py:270) and in `ui/controller.write_diagnostic_report`'s `env=os.environ.copy()` (controller.py:615).
findings.verifier_notes: Code-truth confirmed. src/ssc_engineer/updater.py:230-257 `launch_verified_installer` does `environment = os.environ.copy()`, strips only `_PYI_*`, and passes `env=environment` to Popen of the installer. credentials.py:62 `os.environ[account] = value` and credentials.py:151 `os.environ[OPENAI_ACCOUNT] = stored` do put the live secrets there. However the finder's threat model is overstated: the installer is not arbitrary — updater.py:52 calls `verify_release_manifest_signature` and updater.py:160 refuses `if not release.signature_verified`, plus the download is size- and SHA-256-checked against the signed manifest (updater.py:214-218) before launch. The 'tampered installer stage' path therefore requires defeating Ed25519 first, and the child runs as the same user who already owns the Credential Manager entry. Real hygiene defect (the installer needs neither variable), not a critical breach. | Confirmed in code: updater.py:236-258 copies the full os.environ (filtering only _PYI_*) and passes it as env= to Popen of the installer, and credentials.py:62/151 do put OPENAI_API_KEY and SSC_TEAM_ACCESS_CODE into os.environ. So the Inno Setup child genuinely inherits live secrets - a real least-privilege defect fixable by popping the two names. But 'critical' is not supportable: the installer is size- and SHA-256-verified against the gateway manifest before launch (updater.py:214-218), so the 'tampered installer stage' path requires a gateway compromise that already holds the codes; and the key is already in the same-user parent process environment, so no new local reader gains access (reading an elevated child's env needs PROCESS_VM_READ, i.e. admin, who could read the parent too). Real defect, wrong severity.

findings.title: urllib forwards the team access-code bearer across cross-origin redirects
findings.why_wrong: `headers` contains `"Authorization": f"Bearer {self._access_code}"` (line 134). `urllib.request.urlopen` installs `HTTPRedirectHandler` by default and follows 301/302/303/307/308. I read CPython's `HTTPRedirectHandler.redirect_request` in this venv: it strips only `CONTENT_HEADERS = ("content-length", "content-type")` and rebuilds the Request with every other header, including `Authorization`, regardless of whether the redirect target is a different origin. Unlike `requests`, urllib has no same-host guard. No `redirect=error` equivalent is set, and `team_gateway_url` is a user-editable TOML value that `config.py:456` validates only as "some HTTPS origin".
findings.impact: A misconfigured, compromised or attacker-substituted gateway (or anyone who can edit voice.toml to point `team_gateway_url` at their own HTTPS host) returns `302 Location: https://attacker.example/collect` to `/v1/access`. urllib immediately re-issues the request to attacker.example carrying `Authorization: Bearer ssc_live_<256-bit code>`. That code grants team radio, team actions, mobile snapshot, release downloads and — per finding 4 — OpenAI Realtime credential minting on the owner's account.
findings.fix: Install an opener with a redirect handler that refuses cross-origin redirects, or drops `Authorization` when the new URL's scheme+netloc differ from `self._origin`: `class _NoCrossOriginRedirect(urllib.request.HTTPRedirectHandler): def redirect_request(self, req, fp, code, msg, headers, newurl): if urlsplit(newurl)[:2] != urlsplit(req.full_url)[:2]: return None; return super().redirect_request(...)`, then `urllib.request.build_opener(_NoCrossOriginRedirect()).open(request, timeout=...)`. Apply the same to `_websocket_url`'s consumer in team_sync.py.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed exactly. team_gateway.py:134 sets `"Authorization": f"Bearer {self._access_code}"`, team_gateway.py:146-157 builds a plain `urllib.request.Request` and calls `urllib.request.urlopen(request, ...)` with the default opener. I dumped `HTTPRedirectHandler.redirect_request` from this venv (Python 3.11.15): `CONTENT_HEADERS = ("content-length", "content-type")` / `newheaders = {k: v for k, v in req.headers.items() if k.lower() not in CONTENT_HEADERS}` — Authorization survives, with no same-host check. config.py:456-470 indeed only validates scheme/netloc/no-credentials/no-query. Severity trimmed: exploitation needs either a gateway that is already compromised (which already holds the code) or a user who edits team_gateway_url to an attacker HTTPS origin; TLS blocks the network-level variant. | The urllib behaviour is accurate (I read redirect_request: CONTENT_HEADERS = ("content-length","content-type") only, Authorization is rebuilt into the new Request), but there is no exploit. I grepped services/team-gateway/src/index.js for 301/302/Location/Response.redirect - the Worker never emits a redirect on any route, so a 3xx can only come from a host the client is already sending 'Authorization: Bearer <code>' to on the very first request. The two scenarios given (compromised gateway, or a user editing team_gateway_url to an attacker host) both hand over the code directly with no redirect involved, so the redirect adds zero exposure. TLS plus config.py:456-471 (HTTPS-only origin, no credentials/query/fragment, path must be '' or '/') rule out a MITM-injected redirect. No concrete failure can be constructed.

findings.title: Gateway rate limiting fails open on exactly the two routes that spend the owner's OpenAI key
findings.quote:
async function rateLimit(binding, key) {
  if (!binding || typeof binding.limit !== "function") return true;
findings.why_wrong: `rateLimit` returns `true` (allow) whenever the binding is absent or malformed. `realtimeToken` (line 207) and `speech` (line 238) gate on it, and both then call OpenAI with `Authorization: Bearer ${env.OPENAI_API_KEY}` — the owner's full-privilege key. The authors clearly knew this pattern is unsafe: at line 437 the mobile route explicitly fails closed with `if (!env.SESSION_RATE_LIMITER?.limit) return jsonResponse(503, {error: "MOBILE_RATE_LIMIT_UNAVAILABLE"})` and comments "Fail closed without the existing configured limiter". That guard was never applied to the two OpenAI-spending routes.
findings.impact: A deploy from `wrangler.sync-only.jsonc` or any config where the `ratelimits` block is dropped, renamed or its namespace_id collides silently removes `SESSION_RATE_LIMITER` and `TTS_RATE_LIMITER`. `/v1/realtime-token` and `/v1/tts` then accept unbounded requests from any holder of any valid team code, each one billed to the owner's OpenAI account, with no 429 and nothing in the health endpoint to signal it.
findings.fix: Mirror the mobile guard in both handlers: `if (!env.SESSION_RATE_LIMITER?.limit) return jsonResponse(503, { error: "RATE_LIMIT_UNAVAILABLE" });` at the top of `realtimeToken`, and the same for `env.TTS_RATE_LIMITER` in `speech`. Better: change `rateLimit` itself to `return false` on a missing binding and give the routes that may legitimately run unlimited an explicit opt-out.
findings.verifier_notes: The code defect is real: index.js:201-203 `if (!binding || typeof binding.limit !== "function") return true;`, consumed by `realtimeToken` (index.js:208) and `speech` (index.js:239), both of which then call OpenAI with `Authorization: Bearer ${env.OPENAI_API_KEY}` (index.js:212, 252). The contrast with index.js:437 (`if (!env.SESSION_RATE_LIMITER?.limit) return jsonResponse(503, {error: "MOBILE_RATE_LIMIT_UNAVAILABLE"})`) is accurate. BUT the finder's concrete trigger is wrong: I read services/team-gateway/wrangler.sync-only.jsonc:33-54 and it declares all three limiters — COORDINATION_RATE_LIMITER, SESSION_RATE_LIMITER and TTS_RATE_LIMITER — identically to wrangler.jsonc:39-60. No shipped config drops them. The finding reduces to a latent fail-open inconsistent with the project's own stated practice, contingent on a hypothetical future misconfiguration. | The central factual claim of the repro is false. I read both configs: wrangler.jsonc lines 36-60 AND wrangler.sync-only.jsonc lines 33-57 each define all three limiters (COORDINATION_RATE_LIMITER 180/60, SESSION_RATE_LIMITER 12/60, TTS_RATE_LIMITER 30/60). The 'sync-only drops the ratelimits block' premise does not hold, and no committed configuration produces the absent-binding state the finding needs. 'namespace_id collides silently' is asserted without evidence. What remains is a style inconsistency with the mobile route's explicit fail-closed guard (index.js:437), not a reachable defect with real inputs.

findings.title: No role gate on /v1/realtime-token and /v1/tts: a read-only observer can mint OpenAI credentials
findings.why_wrong: Every other privileged route consults the role: `/v1/team/action` goes through `teamRoomRequest` which checks `actionCapability`, and `/v1/mobile/snapshot` filters its payload by `capabilitiesForRole(access.role)`. These two do not — they receive only `access.driver` and never look at `access.role`. The `observer` role's capability set (ROLE_CAPABILITIES, line 56) is purely read-only: `receive_engineer_radio`, `view_system_health`, `view_strategy_state`, `view_connection_quality`. Nothing in it authorises minting an OpenAI Realtime client secret or generating speech, yet an observer code reaches both handlers.
findings.impact: A code issued as `issue_access.py leon:observer` for a guest spectator can POST /v1/realtime-token and receive a live OpenAI Realtime `ek_...` client secret minted from the owner's API key, then use it directly against api.openai.com for the secret's lifetime, and POST /v1/tts up to 30x/min. The least-privilege role model the gateway advertises in its `/v1/access` `capabilities` response is not enforced for the two most expensive routes.
findings.fix: Add capability constants (e.g. `use_voice_credential`, `use_team_tts`) to the privileged roles in ROLE_CAPABILITIES and gate both routes: `const caps = capabilitiesForRole(access.role); if (!caps.includes("use_voice_credential")) return jsonResponse(403, { error: "NOT_PERMITTED" });` before calling `realtimeToken`/`speech`. Mirror the same constants in `team_gateway.ROLE_CAPABILITIES` (team_gateway.py:38) so the desktop agrees.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed, and it is the strongest finding in the set. index.js:482-485: `if (url.pathname === "/v1/realtime-token") { return realtimeToken(request, env, access.driver); }` / `if (url.pathname === "/v1/tts") return speech(request, env, access.driver);` — only `access.driver` is passed, `access.role` is never consulted, and neither handler (index.js:207, 238) takes a role. The observer capability list at index.js:205-210 is read-only (`receive_engineer_radio`, `view_system_health`, `view_strategy_state`, `view_connection_quality`) and contains nothing authorising credential minting or TTS. The contrast is real: `hasCapability` exists at index.js:190 and the mobile route filters via `capabilitiesForRole(access.role)` (index.js:444). Any authenticated code of any role reaches both handlers. | Confirmed by reading the router: index.js:482-486 dispatches to realtimeToken(request, env, access.driver) and speech(request, env, access.driver) with only access.driver, never access.role, while every other privileged route consults the role (mobile snapshot filters via capabilitiesForRole(access.role) at line 444, team actions via teamRoomRequest). ROLE_CAPABILITIES.observer (index.js:56-61) is read-only. issue_access.py:77 stores {"driver","role","room"} objects and supports DRIVER:ROLE, so an observer code is a real, issuable credential. Concrete repro needs nothing exotic: POST /v1/realtime-token with an observer's ssc_live_ code returns an OpenAI ek_ client secret minted from env.OPENAI_API_KEY (index.js:210-231). Genuine authorisation gap on the two routes that spend the owner's money.

findings.title: Team-code handoff file is written world-readable, then locked down afterwards (TOCTOU)
findings.quote:
args.handoff.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    args.handoff.write_text("\n".join(lines) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
    try:
        _restrict_to_current_user(args.handoff)
findings.why_wrong: `lines` (built at 167-177) contains every teammate's plaintext `ssc_live_` code, one per line. `write_text` creates the file with default inherited permissions — on Windows the parent directory's inherited ACL, on POSIX mode 0666 & ~umask. `_restrict_to_current_user` (line 68), which runs `icacls /inheritance:r /grant:r` or `chmod(0o600)`, is only invoked *after* the full content is already on disk and flushed. The ordering is backwards: the file is at its most sensitive precisely during the window when it is least protected. The failure path at 182-184 unlinks the file, which correctly implies the author understood the ACL is load-bearing.
findings.impact: Operator runs `deploy_for_team.py --handoff C:\Users\leon\Desktop\codes.txt`. Between `write_text` returning and `icacls.exe` completing (a subprocess spawn — tens of milliseconds, unbounded if the machine is loaded), the file holds every team access code under the Desktop's inherited ACL. Any other local account, a backup agent, a OneDrive/Dropbox sync client watching that folder, or an indexer can read it. If `icacls` fails the file is deleted, but a sync client that already uploaded it has published the codes to cloud storage.
findings.fix: Create the file empty and restricted before writing any secret: `args.handoff.touch(mode=0o600); _restrict_to_current_user(args.handoff)`, then `args.handoff.write_text(...)`. On Windows, open with `os.open(path, os.O_CREAT|os.O_EXCL|os.O_WRONLY, 0o600)` and apply the ACL to the empty file before the first write.
findings.verifier_notes: Ordering confirmed at deploy_for_team.py:178-184: `args.handoff.write_text("\n".join(lines) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")` then `try: _restrict_to_current_user(args.handoff)`. `lines` (167-177) does contain `*(f"{driver}: {code}" for driver, code in authorized)` — plaintext `ssc_live_` codes. `_restrict_to_current_user` (line 68) is chmod(0o600) on POSIX or an `icacls.exe` subprocess on Windows, and runs only after the content is on disk. Severity trimmed: the exposure window is a single subprocess spawn, the operator chooses the destination, and the failure path unlinks. SECURITY.md:13-14 also puts findings requiring a compromised local account out of scope, which narrows this to sync-client/backup-agent exposure. | Ordering confirmed: deploy_for_team.py:179-184 does write_text(...) with every plaintext ssc_live_ code (lines built at 167-177) and only then calls _restrict_to_current_user, which at line 68-86 spawns icacls.exe (or chmod 0o600 on POSIX). The window between flush and ACL replacement is real and the file is genuinely at its most sensitive during it. Downgrading from high: the exposure requires another principal on the box or a sync client racing a subprocess spawn on the operator's own admin workstation, the failure path unlinks the file, and the codes are revocable by re-issuing. Concrete but narrow.

findings.title: Developer's real Windows profile path and employer are committed in three tracked docs — and fail the project's own privacy validator
findings.quote: - Editable repository: `C:\Users\leonl\OneDrive - TBZ\Desktop\SSC Race Engineer`
findings.why_wrong: `distribution_privacy._WINDOWS_PROFILE_PATH` (distribution_privacy.py:43) exists specifically to keep `X:\Users\<name>\` out of distributed documentation, and `validate_source_archive` raises `DistributionPrivacyError` on any `.md/.txt/.rst` member that matches. I ran `document_has_personal_path` against all three files and it returned True for each: CLAUDE_HANDOFF_2026-09-10.md, -09-14.md and -09-17.md. So these tracked files are, by the project's own definition, disqualifying content. Beyond the Windows account name `leonl`, the path discloses `OneDrive - TBZ` (a named organisation's tenant), and the 09-10 file additionally exposes local Codex attachment GUIDs and a `G:\My Drive\...` path.
findings.impact: Two concrete consequences. (1) Any source archive produced the obvious way (`git archive HEAD`) hits `validate_source_archive` and aborts the release with 'Source archive contains a personal path in documentation' — the release path is blocked, or is silently being bypassed. (2) This is a private repo today, but the whole point of the validator is the moment source is shared; the account name and organisation are already permanently in git history and reach anyone granted repo access.
findings.fix: Rewrite the three docs to use a placeholder root (`<repo>` or `%USERPROFILE%\...`) as the rest of the docs do, add `docs/handoffs/` to the source-archive exclusion set, and extend `_WINDOWS_PROFILE_PATH` to also catch `/home/<user>/` and `/Users/<user>/`. Purging git history is the only complete remedy for the already-committed copies.

findings.title: Voice SQLite redaction pattern does not know about team access codes or bearer tokens
findings.quote: _SECRET_PATTERN = re.compile(r"(?:sk-[A-Za-z0-9_-]{8,}|OPENAI_API_KEY\s*=\s*\S+)")
findings.why_wrong: This is the filter applied by `_safe_message` and `_safe_json` to everything the voice layer writes into SQLite — error strings (line 119), tool-call arguments and results (213-214), tool errors (216), persisted transcripts (247), playback reasons (280, 316) and status messages (356). It covers only OpenAI `sk-` keys and literal `OPENAI_API_KEY=` assignments. The project's *other* redactor, `runtime/structured_log._SECRET_PATTERNS` (structured_log.py:28-35), covers three more shapes — `\bssc_live_[A-Za-z0-9_-]{16,}\b`, `(?i)\bBearer\s+...` and credential-bearing query parameters. The voice DB writer never got those. SECURITY.md line 38 states as a tested product contract that 'credentials never appear in TOML, logs, diagnostics, replay records or the support bundle'; replay records are exactly what this module writes.
findings.impact: In team_gateway mode the credential is `ssc_live_...`, not `sk-...`. Any string reaching `_safe_message` that embeds it — a `TeamSyncError`/`TeamGatewayError` chained from a urllib or websockets exception whose message quotes the request headers, or a tool result echoing a request — is stored verbatim in the engineering SQLite database under %LOCALAPPDATA%. That DB is not encrypted, is backed up, and its recent rows are surfaced in the support bundle via `database_support_summary`, breaking the stated contract.
findings.fix: Delete `_SECRET_PATTERN` and import the single shared redactor: `from ..runtime.structured_log import redact_log_value`, then `_safe_message = lambda v: str(redact_log_value(str(v)))[:2000]` and `_safe_json = lambda v: redact_log_value(json.dumps(...))`. Having two divergent secret patterns in one codebase guarantees they drift again.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed. voice/persistence.py:23 is verbatim `_SECRET_PATTERN = re.compile(r"(?:sk-[A-Za-z0-9_-]{8,}|OPENAI_API_KEY\s*=\s*\S+)")`, applied by `_safe_message` (line 26) and `_safe_json` (line 30). runtime/structured_log.py:28-35 genuinely carries three additional patterns the voice writer lacks: `\bssc_live_[A-Za-z0-9_-]{16,}\b`, `(?i)\bBearer\s+[A-Za-z0-9._~+/=-]{8,}` and the query-parameter pattern. SECURITY.md:37-38 does state 'credentials never appear in TOML, logs, diagnostics, replay records or the support bundle' as a tested contract, and team_gateway.py:134 puts the code in an Authorization header, so a `Bearer ssc_live_...` string reaching an error path is not hypothetical. Two independent redactors with divergent pattern sets is a genuine gap. | The coverage gap is real (persistence.py:23 matches only sk- and OPENAI_API_KEY=, versus four patterns in structured_log.py:28-35) but I could not construct any path that puts an ssc_live_ code into a string reaching _safe_message. The access code exists only as the Authorization header value built at team_gateway.py:134; every TeamGatewayError raised in _request is a canned constant ('SSC team access was denied or revoked.', etc., lines 158-172) and the request URL carries no credential, so neither HTTPError nor URLError text can contain it. I grepped src/ssc_engineer/voice/*.py: the realtime backend passes credentials via api_key_provider (realtime_backend.py:190-194), never into transcripts, tool arguments or playback reasons. The 'exception whose message quotes the request headers' the finding relies on does not exist in this code.

findings.title: redact_log_value silently bypasses all redaction for non-str, non-dict, non-list values
findings.why_wrong: The function's docstring promises 'Recursively redact known credential shapes and explicitly supplied values.' The str branch at line 55 does the redaction and returns early, so line 66's `isinstance(value, str)` is dead. Everything that is not a dict, list/tuple/set, Path, str, int, float, bool or None falls through to line 68 and is stringified with neither `_SECRET_PATTERNS` nor `extra_secrets` applied. I confirmed this against the real module: `redact_log_value(Exception('auth failed for Bearer sk-proj-ABCDEFGH12345678'))` returns `'auth failed for Bearer sk-proj-ABCDEFGH12345678'` verbatim, and `redact_log_value(b'sk-proj-ABCDEFGH12345678')` returns `"b'sk-proj-ABCDEFGH12345678'"`. Both are shapes the very next lines of the file are written to catch.
findings.impact: `StructuredLogger.log` accepts `data: dict[str, object]` and `CrashReporter.capture` feeds arbitrary payloads through the same helper. The moment any caller puts an exception instance, a bytes payload, a dataclass or a custom object into `data=` rather than pre-stringifying it — which the type signature explicitly permits — the secret is written unredacted to the JSONL runtime log, then copied into the support bundle, under a manifest that asserts `"credentials_included": False`. This is a booby trap in the one function the whole codebase trusts.
findings.fix: Recurse instead of returning raw: `return redact_log_value(str(value), extra_secrets=extra_secrets)` at line 68, and decode bytes explicitly (`if isinstance(value, (bytes, bytearray)): return redact_log_value(value.decode('utf-8', 'replace'), ...)`) before the fallback. Delete the dead `isinstance(value, str)` from line 66.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed by reading structured_log.py:38-69. The str branch at line 55 handles and returns, so line 66's `isinstance(value, str)` is unreachable, and line 68 `return str(value)` stringifies exceptions, bytes, dataclasses and custom objects with neither `_SECRET_PATTERNS` nor `extra_secrets` applied. `StructuredLogger.log` (line 254) feeds the whole record including `"data": data or {}` through this function, and `data` is typed `dict[str, object]`, so an exception instance as a value is an ordinary, permitted call. Dict-key redaction only saves it if the key name happens to match `_SENSITIVE_KEY`. Real booby trap in the project's single trusted redaction helper. | The mechanics check out - I ran it: redact_log_value(Exception('auth failed for Bearer sk-proj-ABCDEFGH12345678')) returns the string verbatim and redact_log_value(b'sk-proj-...') returns the repr - and the isinstance(value, str) at line 66 is indeed dead. But there is no caller that feeds it a non-primitive. I grepped every redact_log_value call site: structured_log.py:254 (record built from strings), support.py:125/127/130/137/142/152 (dicts of str/int from to_dict(), database_support_summary, collect_device_inventory, _read_json), crash_reporting.py:137 whose payload (lines 106-127) is entirely _bounded_text strings, bools and ints with exception_type already reduced to a name. The two logger calls that touch exceptions pre-stringify: runtime/service.py:1585 data={"exception_type": type(exc).__name__} and soak.py:512 data={"type": type(exc).__name__}. A hypothetical future caller is not a repro.

findings.title: Sensitive-key regex misses the bare keys 'token', 'bearer' and vendor-prefixed *_key
findings.quote: r"(?:api[_-]?key|access[_-]?(?:code|token)|authorization|cookie|credential|password|secret)",
findings.why_wrong: Dict-key-based redaction is the only defence for a secret whose *value* does not match one of the four `_SECRET_PATTERNS`. The alternation requires the literal 'api' before 'key' and the literal 'access' before 'token', so the single most common credential key name in JSON — a bare `token` — is not matched, nor is `bearer`, `session_key`, `client_secret`'s sibling `client_id`, or a vendor-prefixed `openai_key`. I verified against the real module: `redact_log_value({"token": "abcdefghijklmnop"})` returns `{'token': 'abcdefghijklmnop'}` and `redact_log_value({"openai_key": "secretvalue"})` returns `{'openai_key': 'secretvalue'}`. Note also that the loopback API's own credential is literally named `token` (api/__main__.py:35 emits `{"port": ..., "token": ...}`).
findings.impact: Any diagnostic payload shaped `{"token": "<opaque value>"}` — the loopback API handshake, an OpenAI ephemeral `ek_...` client secret, a Cloudflare share token — passes through the support bundle and the JSONL log in the clear, because neither the key name nor the value shape is recognised. The redaction is advertised as complete and is not.
findings.fix: Broaden to `(?:(?:^|[_-])(?:token|key|secret|bearer)(?:$|[_-])|api[_-]?key|access[_-]?(?:code|token)|authorization|cookie|credential|password)` with re.IGNORECASE, and add `ek_[A-Za-z0-9_-]{8,}` to `_SECRET_PATTERNS` to cover OpenAI ephemeral Realtime client secrets.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed by running the real regex from structured_log.py:24-27. `_SENSITIVE_KEY.search()` returns False for 'token', 'bearer', 'openai_key', 'session_key' and 'client_id', and True only for 'api_key' and 'access_token' — the alternation does require the literal 'api' before 'key' and 'access' before 'token'. This matters because key-name matching is the only defence for a value that no `_SECRET_PATTERNS` entry recognises (e.g. an OpenAI `ek_...` ephemeral secret, which none of the four patterns match). Note one shaky sub-claim: `client_secret` IS matched by the `secret` alternative, so only its sibling `client_id` is missed — the finder half-acknowledges this. Core defect stands. | The regex behaviour is as described - I confirmed redact_log_value({"token": "abcdefghijklmnop"}) and {"openai_key": ...} both pass through unredacted - but the claimed payload does not exist in this app. I grepped the whole of src/ssc_engineer for "token"/'token' as a dict key: the only hit is api/__main__.py:35, sys.stdout.write(json.dumps({"port": server.port, "token": server.token})), which writes to the shell host's own stdout for the Electron parent to read and never passes through StructuredLogger or create_support_bundle (RuntimeController._capture_runtime_output logs the runtime child's stdout, a different process). api/server.py uses the token only in a compare_digest at line 581. No diagnostic payload shaped {"token": ...} reaches either sink, so the impact is unrealisable as written.

findings.title: Support bundle exports absolute Windows profile paths that the release validator treats as disqualifying
findings.quote: entries["effective-config.json"] = _json_bytes(redact_log_value(effective_config))
findings.why_wrong: `export_support_bundle` (ui/controller.py:164) passes `load_effective_config(...).to_dict()`, and `EffectiveConfig.to_dict` (config.py:547) includes `self.voice.to_dict()` plus `voice_sources`/`engineering_sources`. `VoiceConfig` carries `results_directory` and `telemetry_directory` (config.py:350-351), which are user-chosen absolute LMU paths, and the `*_sources` tuples are the resolved config-file paths under `%LOCALAPPDATA%`. `redact_log_value` does nothing to these — I confirmed `redact_log_value({"results_directory": r"C:\Users\Moritz\Documents\LMU"})` returns the path unchanged, because no `_SECRET_PATTERNS` entry matches a filesystem path and no key name matches. Meanwhile `distribution_privacy._WINDOWS_PROFILE_PATH` exists solely to make `C:\Users\<name>\` a hard release blocker, so the project does classify this string as private.
findings.impact: A driver exports a support bundle to send to the team owner for a voice problem. `effective-config.json` inside it contains `"results_directory": "C:\\Users\\<their real Windows account>\\Documents\\Le Mans Ultimate\\..."` and `"voice_sources": ["C:\\Users\\<name>\\AppData\\Local\\SSC Race Engineer\\config\\voice.toml"]`, alongside `driver_name`. The bundle's own manifest advertises a privacy block, and the app's privacy dialog (ui/privacy.py:135) tells the user exports are clean. The same string is a release blocker two modules away.
findings.fix: Normalise before export: map any `%USERPROFILE%`/`C:\Users\<name>` prefix to `<user>` in `effective_config`, `*_sources` and the health/crash payloads, e.g. a `_strip_profile_paths` pass using `distribution_privacy._WINDOWS_PROFILE_PATH.sub("<user-profile>/", ...)` applied to the JSON text before `_json_bytes`. Add the profile-path regex to `_SECRET_PATTERNS` so one change covers logs too.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed with one citation drift. support.py:125 is verbatim `entries["effective-config.json"] = _json_bytes(redact_log_value(effective_config))`; ui/controller.py:164 `export_support_bundle` builds it from `load_effective_config(...)`; config.py:547 `EffectiveConfig.to_dict` includes `"voice": self.voice.to_dict()` plus `engineering_sources`/`voice_sources`. `results_directory` and `telemetry_directory` are at config.py:369-370, not 350-351 as cited — minor drift, the fields exist. `redact_log_value` provably leaves filesystem paths untouched (no pattern matches, no key matches — same regex run as finding 9). The inconsistency with `_WINDOWS_PROFILE_PATH` is real. Severity trimmed: the bundle is an explicit, user-initiated export sent to the user's own team owner, and the leaked datum is a Windows account name, not a credential. | Verified end to end: ui/controller.py:164-181 passes effective.to_dict() into create_support_bundle, support.py:125 writes redact_log_value(effective_config) to effective-config.json, and I confirmed redact_log_value({"results_directory": r"C:\Users\Moritz\Documents\LMU"}) returns the path unchanged (no _SECRET_PATTERNS match, no _SENSITIVE_KEY match). So a user's Windows account name does leave the machine in a bundle. Downgrading to low: the manifest's privacy block (support.py:118-123) claims only database/microphone/credentials/auth_headers exclusion and the privacy dialog text (ui/privacy.py:134-136) says 'Credentials are never written to ... exports' - a filesystem path is not a credential, so nothing is actually contradicted, and the recipient is the team owner the user chose to send it to.

findings.title: Team access code is transmitted to the gateway before its format is validated
findings.quote:
if self.voice_config.auth_mode == "team_gateway":
                candidate = self.key_entry.get()
                access = TeamGatewayClient(self.voice_config, candidate).validate_access()
                store_team_access_code(candidate)
findings.why_wrong: The raw contents of the credential entry box go straight into `TeamGatewayClient`, whose `__init__` (team_gateway.py:111) only strips whitespace and checks non-empty — it never calls `validate_team_access_code`. `validate_access()` then sends `Authorization: Bearer <whatever the user typed>` over the network. The format check via `store_team_access_code` → `validate_team_access_code` (credentials.py:79) happens only on line 804, *after* the value has already left the machine. The direct-OpenAI branch on line 806 has the opposite, correct ordering: `store_api_key` validates before doing anything. The onboarding path also gets it right (`onboarding.py:135` validates first). This one screen is the outlier.
findings.impact: The credential card is titled 'SSC TEAM ACCESS' when auth_mode is team_gateway and 'OWNER CREDENTIAL' otherwise (control_center.py:1052) — the same masked box, same Save button. A user who pastes their OpenAI `sk-proj-...` key into the team box has that key sent as a Bearer token to the Cloudflare gateway. The gateway's `bearerToken` regex `^Bearer ([A-Za-z0-9_-]{24,160})$` matches an OpenAI key, so it is parsed and hashed before `authenticate` rejects it on the `ssc_live_` prefix — the key has already traversed the network and reached third-party infrastructure. The subsequent error message gives the user no hint that their OpenAI key was just transmitted.
findings.fix: Validate first: `candidate = validate_team_access_code(self.key_entry.get())` before constructing the client, so a malformed value raises `CredentialError` locally and never leaves the process. Better still, make `TeamGatewayClient.__init__` itself call `validate_team_access_code(self._access_code)` so no caller can skip it.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed verbatim at ui/application.py:800-804: `candidate = self.key_entry.get()` then `access = TeamGatewayClient(self.voice_config, candidate).validate_access()` then `store_team_access_code(candidate)`. TeamGatewayClient.__init__ (team_gateway.py:108-114) only does `.strip()` and a non-empty check — it never calls `validate_team_access_code`, and `_request` sends `Bearer <candidate>` immediately. The ordering contrast is accurate: the else branch at application.py:806 is `store_api_key(self.key_entry.get())` (validate-then-store), and onboarding.py:154 validates first. The gateway's `bearerToken` regex at index.js:115 `/^Bearer ([A-Za-z0-9_-]{24,160})$/` does match an `sk-proj-...` key, so a mistyped OpenAI key does reach Cloudflare before index.js:169 rejects it on the prefix. | Ordering confirmed at ui/application.py:800-804: TeamGatewayClient(self.voice_config, candidate).validate_access() runs on line 802, store_team_access_code(candidate) (which is the only caller of validate_team_access_code, credentials.py:79) on line 804; TeamGatewayClient.__init__ (team_gateway.py:108-114) only strips and checks non-empty. The contrast with the direct branch (line 806 store_api_key validates first) and onboarding.py is accurate, so this is a genuine inverted check. Downgrading from medium: the destination is the team's own Cloudflare Worker over TLS, bearerToken (index.js:115) only regex-matches then SHA-256s the value, Cloudflare invocation logs record method/URL/status rather than request headers, and the mistyped key is rejected without being stored. Fix the ordering, but the realised harm is one TLS transit to the team's own infrastructure.

findings.title: Installer share token is carried in the URL path, and the Worker persists invocation logs
findings.quote: print(f"URL={GATEWAY}/v1/app/share/{token}")
findings.why_wrong: `token = secrets.token_urlsafe(32)` (line 21) is a genuine 256-bit bearer credential: `temporaryShareDownload` (index.js:335-349) hashes the path segment and constant-time-compares it against `grant.sha256`, and possession alone authorises the installer download with no other authentication. Putting a bearer in a URL path rather than a header means it is recorded wherever URLs are recorded. `wrangler.jsonc` lines 9-17 configure exactly that: `"observability": { "enabled": true, "logs": { "enabled": true, "invocation_logs": true, "persist": true } }` — Workers invocation logs record the request URL, and this config persists them. `wrangler.sync-only.jsonc` repeats the same block.
findings.impact: Every use of a share link writes the live share token into retained Cloudflare Workers logs, where it is readable by anyone with dashboard/Logpush access for the 7-day validity window (VALID_DAYS = 14 days? no — 7). The same token also lands in the recipient's browser history, in any `Referer` sent by a page that links it (the JSON routes set `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`, but a third-party page hosting the link does not), and in chat-app link previews. There is no revocation short of overwriting the `DOWNLOAD_SHARE` secret.
findings.fix: Move the token off the path: accept it as `Authorization: Bearer <token>` or as a POST body on `/v1/app/share`, and have the share page exchange it for a short-lived signed redirect. If a link must remain one-click, at minimum set `"invocation_logs": false` for the gateway and add `Cache-Control: no-store` plus `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` to the download response (`downloadRelease` builds its headers from `responseHeaders`, which has no Cache-Control).
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed on both halves. create_phone_download.py:21 `token = secrets.token_urlsafe(32)` and line 46 `print(f"URL={GATEWAY}/v1/app/share/{token}")`; index.js:335-349 `temporaryShareDownload` hashes the path segment and constant-time-compares against `grant.sha256`, with possession as the sole authorisation. wrangler.jsonc:9-17 is verbatim `"observability": { "enabled": true, ... "logs": { "enabled": true, "invocation_logs": true, ... "persist": true } }`, and wrangler.sync-only.jsonc repeats it. VALID_DAYS = 7 (line 14) as the finder self-corrected. Bearer-in-URL plus persisted invocation logs is a genuine, if bounded, credential-in-logs defect. | Both halves verified: create_phone_download.py:21 mints secrets.token_urlsafe(32) and line 46 prints it as a path segment; temporaryShareDownload (index.js:337-350) authenticates on possession of that segment alone (sha256Hex + constantTimeEqual against grant.sha256); wrangler.jsonc:9-17 sets observability.logs {enabled, invocation_logs, persist: true}. A bearer in a URL path plus persisted invocation logs is a real, citable practice defect. Downgrading to low: head_sampling_rate is 0.1 so most invocations are not logged, the only capability the token grants is downloading the same installer the team is already entitled to (downloadRelease on a fixed channel/version - no secrets, no account access), the grant self-expires after 7 days, and it is revocable by overwriting DOWNLOAD_SHARE, contrary to the finding's 'no revocation' claim.

findings.title: Source-archive privacy filter misses .pem, .crt, id_rsa, .venv and log files
findings.quote:
PRIVATE_SUFFIXES = (
    ".pyc",
    ".pyo",
    ".pfx",
    ".p12",
    ".key",
findings.why_wrong: This tuple is the allowlist gate for every source release. It covers `.pfx`, `.p12` and `.key` but omits `.pem`, which is the single most common private-key extension and which the project's own `.gitignore` line 27 (`*.pem`) explicitly treats as a credential — so the two policies disagree. `PRIVATE_DIRECTORY_PARTS` (line 9) likewise omits `.venv`/`venv` although .gitignore lines 2-3 exclude them. I ran `private_distribution_path` against realistic names and every one of these returned False: `ssl/server.pem`, `id_rsa`, `certs/client.crt`, `secrets.toml`, `credentials.json`, `team-codes.txt`, `runtime.jsonl`, `app.log`, `.venv/pyvenv.cfg`.
findings.impact: An operator zips the working tree (rather than using `git archive`) and runs `scripts/release/validate_source_archive.py`. A stray `server.pem`, an `id_rsa`, a `.venv` containing the developer's pip cache and site-packages, or the JSONL runtime logs from `logs/` all sail through and are published in the source release, while the script prints a passing file count. The validator's guarantee is materially narrower than its name and its use as a release gate imply.
findings.fix: Add `".pem", ".crt", ".cer", ".p8", ".ppk", ".jks", ".keystore", ".asc", ".jsonl", ".log"` to PRIVATE_SUFFIXES; add `".venv", "venv", ".idea", ".vscode", "logs", "recordings"` to PRIVATE_DIRECTORY_PARTS; add `"id_rsa", "id_ed25519", "secrets.toml", "credentials.json", ".npmrc", ".netrc"` to PRIVATE_FILENAMES. Derive the list from .gitignore in a test so the two cannot drift.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified by executing the real function, not by reading. distribution_privacy.py:26-39 `PRIVATE_SUFFIXES` contains `.pfx`, `.p12`, `.key` and no `.pem`; `PRIVATE_DIRECTORY_PARTS` (line 9-21) has no `.venv`/`venv`. I ran `private_distribution_path` and every one of the finder's examples returned False: ssl/server.pem, id_rsa, certs/client.crt, secrets.toml, credentials.json, team-codes.txt, runtime.jsonl, app.log, .venv/pyvenv.cfg. The policy conflict is also real — .gitignore:2-3 excludes `.venv/` and `venv/`, and .gitignore:27 is `*.pem`, so the release validator is strictly laxer than the repo's own ignore rules. | The gaps are real - I ran private_distribution_path and got False for ssl/server.pem, id_rsa, certs/client.crt, .venv/pyvenv.cfg and app.log - but the repro ('an operator zips the working tree') contradicts the actual release path. scripts/windows/BUILD_SOURCE_ARCHIVE.bat is the documented builder (docs/release/RELEASE_PROCESS.md:134-143) and it hard-fails before archiving on any uncommitted change ('git diff --quiet --exit-code HEAD --') and on any untracked file at all ('git status --porcelain --untracked-files=all' -> ERROR: Commit, stash, or remove untracked source changes), then archives the tagged commit. tests/release/test_source_archive.py:145 states the same invariant: 'Ignored files cannot leak through git archive'. Since *.pem, .venv and logs are gitignored, none of the listed files can reach an archive; the scenario requires force-adding an ignored credential, which is a different (and unobserved) failure.

findings.title: Source-archive validator never inspects file contents for secrets, only filenames and prose paths
findings.why_wrong: This is the only content-level check in `validate_source_archive`, and it is doubly narrow. First, it returns False for anything that is not `.md`, `.txt` or `.rst` (DOCUMENT_SUFFIXES, line 42), so a personal path or a hardcoded key inside a `.py`, `.toml`, `.json`, `.jsonc`, `.ps1`, `.iss`, `.cjs` or `.tsx` file is never looked at — I confirmed `document_has_personal_path('docs/BUILD.py', ...)` short-circuits to False. Second, the only pattern it looks for is `_WINDOWS_PROFILE_PATH` (line 43), which matches `X:\Users\<name>\` and nothing else: not `/home/<user>/`, not macOS `/Users/<name>/`, not UNC `\\NAS\share`, and crucially not any credential shape at all. There is no `sk-`, `ssc_live_`, `AKIA`, `-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----` or bearer scan anywhere in the release path.
findings.impact: The function that gates 'clean source provenance' for publication (BUILD_INFO.txt names this as a release requirement) would not stop a live OpenAI key hardcoded in a `.py` module, a team access code pasted into a `.toml` fixture, or a developer path in a build script. Combined with the absence of any secret scanning in CI, nothing in this project's release pipeline would catch a committed credential.
findings.fix: Scan all text members, not just DOCUMENT_SUFFIXES: decode any member under a size cap and run both `_WINDOWS_PROFILE_PATH` and the credential patterns from `runtime.structured_log._SECRET_PATTERNS` over it, raising `DistributionPrivacyError` on a hit. Keep an explicit allowlist for the known test fixtures (tests/release/, services/team-gateway/test/) rather than allowlisting by file extension.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed. distribution_privacy.py:64-68 is the only content-level check and begins `if PurePosixPath(name).suffix.casefold() not in DOCUMENT_SUFFIXES: return False` against `DOCUMENT_SUFFIXES = frozenset({".md", ".txt", ".rst"})` (line 42) — I ran `document_has_personal_path('docs/BUILD.py', b'C:\\Users\\leonl\\x')` and it returns False. The only pattern applied is `_WINDOWS_PROFILE_PATH` (line 43), which matches drive-letter user paths and nothing credential-shaped: no sk-, no ssc_live_, no PEM header. Combined with the confirmed absence of any secret scanner in CI (finding 16), nothing in the release path would stop a committed credential. | The description of the code is accurate (DOCUMENT_SUFFIXES is .md/.txt/.rst only, distribution_privacy.py:42, and _WINDOWS_PROFILE_PATH at line 43 is the sole content pattern), but this is an absent feature, not a defect with a repro. Every consequence listed is conditional on a secret that does not exist: I found no sk-, ssc_live_ or key material committed in any .py/.toml/.json. The one real committed privacy violation in this repo (the handoff docs, finding 6) is precisely the case this function does catch. 'Would not stop a hypothetical future hardcoded key' is a wish for a secret scanner, which is finding 16's subject, not a confirmable defect in this code.

findings.title: Re-running deploy_for_team silently revokes every previously issued team code and forces every code to the 'driver' role
findings.why_wrong: Two separate defects in three lines. (1) `wrangler secret put TEAM_ACCESS_SHA256` replaces the secret wholesale; the script builds `hash_map` only from the `--driver` arguments of this invocation and never reads the existing value. Adding one teammate therefore invalidates every code already issued. (2) The map values are bare driver strings. On the gateway, `normalizeAccess` (index.js:137) has a string branch that returns `{ driver: value, role: "driver", room: TEAM_ROOM_DEFAULT }` — so every code provisioned by this script is hardcoded to the `driver` role and the default room. The companion `issue_access.py` (line 77) correctly emits `{"driver": ..., "role": ..., "room": ...}` objects and supports `--room` and `DRIVER:ROLE`; the deploy script cannot express either.
findings.impact: (1) The owner runs `deploy_for_team.py --driver newguy` mid-season to onboard one person. Every existing teammate's code stops authenticating at the next request — team radio, mobile pit wall and voice all fail simultaneously, potentially during a race, with only a generic 'SSC team access was denied or revoked' message. (2) There is no supported way to provision a `race_engineer` or `administrator` through this script, so the capabilities in ROLE_CAPABILITIES that gate `approve_high_impact_strategy`, `publish_engineer_radio`, `revoke_sessions` etc. are unreachable for anyone deployed this way.
findings.fix: Read the current secret first (`wrangler secret list` does not return values, so keep the authoritative hash map in a local restricted file or use `TEAM_ACCESS_ADDITIONAL_SHA256` for incremental adds) and merge rather than replace. Emit the same object shape as issue_access.py: `hash_map[digest] = {"driver": driver, "role": role, "room": args.room}`, and add `--driver DRIVER:ROLE` and `--room` arguments to match.
findings.verifier_notes: Both halves confirmed, and this is more operationally severe than rated. (1) deploy_for_team.py:135-136: `hash_map = {digest: driver for driver, (_, digest) in issued.items()}` built only from this invocation's `--driver` args, pushed via `_put_secret(..., "TEAM_ACCESS_SHA256", json.dumps(hash_map))`; `_put_secret` (line 20-31) runs `wrangler secret put`, which replaces wholesale, and nothing reads the existing value first. (2) Values are bare strings, and index.js:137-139 `normalizeAccess` has `if (typeof value === "string" && /^[A-Za-z0-9._-]{1,64}$/.test(value)) return { driver: value, role: "driver", room: TEAM_ROOM_DEFAULT };` — so every code from this script is pinned to `driver` and the default room, and no `race_engineer`/`administrator` is reachable. issue_access.py:80 does emit `{"driver":..., "role":..., "room":...}` as claimed. Silent mass revocation of every teammate credential mid-season warrants high. | Both halves confirmed by reading deploy_for_team.py:134-137: issued/hash_map are built solely from this invocation's drivers, _put_secret writes TEAM_ACCESS_SHA256 with json.dumps(hash_map), and nothing anywhere in the script reads the current secret value first - wrangler secret put replaces wholesale, so prior codes are destroyed. The values are bare driver strings, and normalizeAccess (index.js:137-139) has exactly the string branch quoted, returning role 'driver' and TEAM_ROOM_DEFAULT, so no race_engineer/administrator/observer can be provisioned this way while issue_access.py:77 correctly emits {driver, role, room}. The mid-season repro is realistic and the consequence (whole-team auth outage, possibly during a race) is concrete.

findings.title: CI runs no secret scanning and skips two of the three gateway auth test suites
findings.quote:
- name: Test Cloudflare gateway contract
        run: node --test test/gateway.test.mjs
findings.why_wrong: Two gaps in one pipeline. (1) I grepped the whole `.github/` tree for `gitleaks`, `trufflehog` and `secret` and found no scanner step — the workflow runs compileall, unittest, ruff, mypy, the gateway contract test, a fault campaign, the frozen build, the shell smoke and the installer, but nothing that would catch a committed credential. SECURITY.md line 38 declares 'credentials never appear in TOML, logs, diagnostics, replay records or the support bundle' as a contract 'tested in tests/', yet the repo has no automated gate protecting it at commit time. (2) `services/team-gateway/test/` contains three suites — gateway.test.mjs, coordination.test.mjs and mobile.test.mjs — and only the first is executed. `mobile.test.mjs` covers `/v1/mobile/snapshot`, the route that serves race data to a phone on the strength of an access code, and `coordination.test.mjs` covers the Durable Object that enforces per-role team actions.
findings.impact: A credential accidentally committed in a future change ships without any automated objection — the three handoff docs with the developer's real profile path are live proof that content-level review is not catching this class of problem. Separately, regressions in the mobile authentication/capability-filtering path and in the coordination room's role enforcement will not fail CI, even though both are explicitly in scope per SECURITY.md line 10.
findings.fix: Add a `gitleaks/gitleaks-action` (or `trufflehog filesystem --only-verified`) step to the source-suite job, and change line 78 to `node --test test/` so all three gateway suites run. Add a unit test that asserts `redact_log_value` and `voice.persistence._SECRET_PATTERN` both suppress an `ssc_live_` code, which would have caught finding 7.
findings.verifier_notes: Both halves verified. .github/workflows/windows-ci.yml:76-78 is verbatim `- name: Test Cloudflare gateway contract` / `working-directory: services/team-gateway` / `run: node --test test/gateway.test.mjs`, and `ls services/team-gateway/test/` shows coordination.test.mjs, gateway.test.mjs, mobile.test.mjs — a repo-wide grep for `node --test` finds that one line only, so mobile and coordination never run. A case-insensitive grep of the whole .github/ tree for gitleaks/trufflehog/secret-scan/detect-secrets returns nothing. Findings 4 and 15 are exactly the classes of regression the two unrun suites would cover, and finding 6 is live evidence that manual review is not catching committed personal data. | Verified: services/team-gateway/test/ contains coordination.test.mjs, gateway.test.mjs and mobile.test.mjs, and .github/workflows/windows-ci.yml:78 runs only 'node --test test/gateway.test.mjs'; .github/workflows/ contains a single file and grepping it for gitleaks/trufflehog/secret returns nothing. The skipped-suites half is a concrete, checkable gap: a regression in /v1/mobile/snapshot capability filtering or in the coordination Durable Object's role enforcement (the very gap finding 4 documents) would not fail CI. Downgrading from medium: no defect exists today because both suites pass locally, and 'no secret scanner' is a missing control rather than a bug - this is process risk, correctly reportable but not production-biting.

findings.title: Three different length bounds for the same access code; the gateway's floor is the weakest
findings.quote: if not re.fullmatch(r"ssc_live_[A-Za-z0-9_-]{32,128}", clean):
findings.why_wrong: The same credential is length-checked three times with three different bounds. The desktop requires 32-128 characters after the `ssc_live_` prefix (here). The gateway's `bearerToken` (index.js:115) accepts `^Bearer ([A-Za-z0-9_-]{24,160})$` on the *whole* token — and since `_` is in the character class, `ssc_live_` counts toward the 24, so a token with only 15 characters of entropy after the prefix is accepted. The mobile client (mobile-client.js:112) uses a third bound, `^ssc_live_[A-Za-z0-9_-]{16,151}$`. Codes actually issued are `secrets.token_urlsafe(32)` = 43 characters, so nothing in production is weak today, but the authoritative minimum is set by the weakest of the three, and that is the server.
findings.impact: If a code is ever issued or migrated by any path other than issue_access.py/deploy_for_team.py — a hand-written test credential promoted to production, a shortened legacy code, a future script — the gateway will happily authenticate a token with roughly 90 bits instead of 256 bits of entropy, and the desktop's stricter check provides no protection because it is client-side. Three independent regexes for one format is also a standing source of 'works on the phone, rejected on the desktop' support load.
findings.fix: Define the format once and enforce the strict bound server-side: change the gateway regex to `^Bearer (ssc_live_[A-Za-z0-9_-]{32,128})$` so the server is the strictest party, and align mobile-client.js to the same pattern. Add an assertion in issue_access.py that the generated code matches the canonical regex.
findings.verifier_notes: All three bounds confirmed: credentials.py:81 `if not re.fullmatch(r"ssc_live_[A-Za-z0-9_-]{32,128}", clean)`, index.js:115 `/^Bearer ([A-Za-z0-9_-]{24,160})$/` applied to the whole token (and `_` is in the class, so the 9-char `ssc_live_` prefix counts toward the 24), and services/team-gateway/src/mobile-client.js:112 `/^ssc_live_[A-Za-z0-9_-]{16,151}$/`. The finder is honest that production is unaffected — `_issue` at deploy_for_team.py:37 and issue_access.py both emit `"ssc_live_" + secrets.token_urlsafe(32)`. Correctly rated low: a latent consistency defect, not an exploitable one today. | The three bounds are as quoted - credentials.py:81 requires ssc_live_ + 32-128, index.js:115 accepts /^Bearer ([A-Za-z0-9_-]{24,160})$/ over the whole token, and the mobile client uses a third. The finding is honest that no weak code exists in production, and it correctly notes the desktop check is client-side only. It survives as a low-severity consistency defect because the loose server-side floor is real and is the authoritative one; note however that authentication ultimately requires the SHA-256 to appear in TEAM_ACCESS_SHA256, which only token_urlsafe(32) issuance populates, so the entropy floor is unreachable without an operator hand-minting a weak code.

findings.title: Storing a credential injects it into os.environ, where deletion cannot reach already-spawned children
findings.quote: os.environ[account] = value
findings.why_wrong: `_store` writes the secret into the parent process environment so that children inherit it, and `bootstrap_api_key` does the same at line 151. `_delete_stored` (line 129) removes it from the keyring and calls `os.environ.pop(account, None)`, and `_delete_windows_user_environment_key` additionally clears the HKCU Environment value and broadcasts WM_SETTINGCHANGE. None of that reaches a process that has already started: a child's environment block is a copy taken at CreateProcess time. `RuntimeController` spawns its runtime child with `env=os.environ.copy()` (controller.py:418) and that child can outlive the Remove-key action, since `_remove_key` (application.py:874) calls `self._stop()` but stop is asynchronous and the quiet-learning child may be restarted.
findings.impact: A user hits 'Remove key' after, say, a suspected key compromise.
