The Credential Manager entry and the parent's environment are cleared and the UI reports the credential is gone, but any runtime child still running — or any process the user launched from a shell that inherited the HKCU variable before it was deleted — still holds the plaintext key and can keep using it. The revocation is less complete than the UI states.
findings.fix: Stop propagating secrets through the environment: pass the credential to the child over its stdin pipe (the same mechanism `api/__main__.py` already uses for the loopback token) or have the child read it from Credential Manager itself, and strip `OPENAI_ACCOUNT`/`TEAM_ACCESS_ACCOUNT` from the `env=` dict in controller.py:418. Then make `_remove_key` block on child termination before reporting success.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed. credentials.py:62 `os.environ[account] = value` in `_store`, credentials.py:151 in `bootstrap_api_key`; `_delete_stored` (line 129) does `os.environ.pop(account, None)` and `_delete_windows_user_environment_key` clears HKCU and broadcasts WM_SETTINGCHANGE — none of which reaches an already-running child. ui/controller.py:418 `environment = os.environ.copy()` for the runtime child is verbatim. application.py:877 `_remove_key` does call `self._stop()` before deletion, which partly mitigates the runtime-child case, so the residual exposure is mainly unrelated inherited shells. Correctly rated low; it is an inherent property of environment inheritance rather than a coding mistake. | Mechanism confirmed: credentials.py:62 'os.environ[account] = value', _delete_stored at line 129 pops it from the parent only, and ui/controller.py:418 'environment = os.environ.copy()' hands the runtime child a snapshot. I also checked application.py:877-892: _remove_key calls self._stop(), which at line 777-786 first shows a confirmation dialog (declining returns early, leaving the child running) and then dispatches controller.stop through _run_transition on a worker thread - so the deletion genuinely proceeds while a child may still hold the key. Correctly filed as low: this is inherent to process environment inheritance, the surviving child is the app's own trusted runtime, and the real remedy for a compromised key is revocation at OpenAI.

findings.title: issue_access.py prints every plaintext team code to stdout
findings.why_wrong: The codes are 256-bit bearer credentials that the gateway stores only as SHA-256 hashes — the plaintext exists nowhere else, which is the right design. Emitting them to stdout puts them into terminal scrollback, the Windows Terminal / PowerShell session buffer, PSReadLine history if the command was piped, any CI or tmux capture, and any shell recording. The banner acknowledges the risk ('then clear this terminal') but pushes the entire mitigation onto the operator with no mechanism. The sibling `deploy_for_team.py` does better: it writes codes to a file and ACL-restricts it (albeit with the ordering bug in finding 5) and prints only the file path.
findings.impact: An owner runs `python issue_access.py leon:race_engineer marco:driver` in a PowerShell window, copies the codes into a chat app, and leaves the window open for the rest of the session. The codes remain in the console buffer and are recoverable by anything that can read the conversation host's buffer or a screen-capture/screen-share. If the invocation was scripted under CI or a logged shell, they are written to disk.
findings.fix: Take the deploy_for_team approach: require an `--out` path, create the file with 0600/restricted ACL *before* writing, emit the codes there, and print only the path and the TEAM_ACCESS_SHA256 payload to stdout. If interactive output is kept as an option, gate it behind an explicit `--print-codes` flag.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed verbatim at services/team-gateway/scripts/issue_access.py:79-81: `print("ONE-TIME DRIVER CODES - store privately, then clear this terminal")` / `for driver, role, code in codes:` / `print(f"{driver} [{role}]: {code}")`. The codes are `"ssc_live_" + secrets.token_urlsafe(32)` and the gateway stores only SHA-256 (index.js:167-176), so stdout is the only place the plaintext exists. The banner does push mitigation onto the operator with no mechanism, and the sibling deploy_for_team.py:178-184 demonstrates the better pattern. Correctly rated low — this is a deliberate design tradeoff for a one-time operator tool, not a bug, but the scrollback exposure is real. | Confirmed the code does this (issue_access.py:79-82, and lines 83-84 also print the hash map for pasting into wrangler), but there is no defect to fix: the gateway stores only SHA-256 digests, so the operator must see the plaintext exactly once in order to distribute it, and stdout on the owner's own machine is the delivery channel. The stated mitigations are speculative - PSReadLine records typed commands, not program output, and 'scripted under CI' is not how this admin script is used. The suggested alternative (deploy_for_team.py's file) is the script that carries the TOCTOU bug in finding 5 and the revocation bug in finding 15, so it is not obviously safer. No concrete exfiltration path, benign consequence.

findings.title: StructuredLogger snapshots the secret list at construction, so a credential saved later is only pattern-redacted
findings.why_wrong: `_extra_secrets` is read once in `__init__` and never refreshed; `log()` at line 254 passes that frozen tuple to every `redact_log_value` call for the logger's entire lifetime. But credentials are populated into `os.environ` at arbitrary later times — `credentials._store` (line 62) runs whenever the user clicks Save in the credential card, and `bootstrap_api_key` (line 151) runs on auth-mode changes. A logger constructed before that point (controller.py:414 builds one per runtime start, and the runtime child builds its own) holds an empty tuple.
findings.impact: A user starts the engineer, then saves a team access code from the Settings screen without restarting. For the rest of that run, exact-value redaction is disabled and the only protection is the four `_SECRET_PATTERNS` regexes — which, per findings 8 and 9, do not cover exception objects, bytes, dict keys named `token`, or OpenAI `ek_` ephemeral secrets. The belt-and-braces layer that exists precisely to catch what the patterns miss is silently inert.
findings.fix: Read the environment at log time rather than at construction: replace `self._extra_secrets` with a small helper `def _extra_secrets(self) -> tuple[str, ...]` that reads `os.environ` on each call (the cost is two dict lookups per log record, and records are explicitly 'infrequent runtime events' per the class docstring), and call it from `log()`.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed. structured_log.py:181-188 reads `os.environ.get("OPENAI_API_KEY", "")` and `os.environ.get("SSC_TEAM_ACCESS_CODE", "")` once inside `__init__`, and `log()` at line 254 passes that frozen `self._extra_secrets` to `redact_log_value` for the logger's whole lifetime. credentials.py:62 populates those variables at arbitrary later times (application.py:800-804 Save button, settings.py:835). ui/controller.py:412 `self._logger = StructuredLogger(self.paths.runtime_log)` builds one per runtime start. The exact-value belt-and-braces layer is genuinely inert for a credential saved after logger construction, leaving only the `_SECRET_PATTERNS` regexes — which findings 8 and 9 confirm are incomplete. Low is right: the pattern layer does cover the `ssc_live_` and `sk-` shapes in plain strings. | The snapshot is real (structured_log.py:181-189, consumed at line 254) but the consequence cannot be made concrete. Both credential shapes this app handles are fully covered by _SECRET_PATTERNS: I ran redact_log_value('code ssc_live_' + 'a'*40) and got 'code [REDACTED]', and sk- keys match the first pattern - so losing extra_secrets loses nothing for either credential in any string. The residual gaps it invokes (exception objects, bytes, bare 'token' keys) are findings 8 and 9, both of which I refuted as unreachable. Ordering also works against the finding: at runtime start _bootstrap_credential(import_environment=True) runs at controller.py:395 before StructuredLogger is constructed at line 412, so the common path captures the secret. No realisable leak.

findings.title: publish_state drops engineering_overview, so the mobile pit-wall overview card is permanently blank
findings.why_wrong: normalizeStatePayload (index.js:542) explicitly produces result.engineering_overview via mobileEngineeringOverview, and _snapshot reads this.state.engineering_overview at index.js:767, but the publish_state branch assigns only system_health, strategy_state and technical_alerts. this.state.engineering_overview is never written anywhere in the file (grep confirms the only three occurrences are the producer at 543, the reader at 767, and mobile.js:60), and defaultTeamState() at index.js:632 does not even declare the key. The normalized overview exists only inside the broadcast state_update event, which is never stored.
findings.impact: I ran this end to end against TeamRadioHub with stub storage: POST /internal/action action=publish_state with engineering_overview {position:3, fuel_laps:12.5} returns 200, the event carries the normalized overview, but the snapshot in the same response has engineering_overview = null, and a later GET /internal/snapshot also returns null, while system_health from the same payload persists as READY. Every /v1/mobile/snapshot poll therefore returns an all-null overview, so the pit wall's entire Race and pit overview card - position, gaps, fuel laps, VE laps, modelled stop window, green and caution pit loss, pit-open authority, observed lane and stationary time - renders Unavailable/UNAVAILABLE forever, and mobile-client.js:25 marks the card STALE - do not use for decisions. The feature is dead on arrival for anyone not holding an open WebSocket.
findings.fix: Add `if (state.engineering_overview) this.state.engineering_overview = state.engineering_overview;` to the publish_state branch, declare engineering_overview in defaultTeamState(), and add an end-to-end test that publishes state through /internal/action and asserts the field survives a subsequent /internal/snapshot.
findings.verifier_notes: Code-true and complete. index.js:911-915 assigns only system_health/strategy_state/technical_alerts; normalizeStatePayload does produce result.engineering_overview (index.js:542-544) and _snapshot reads `snapshot.engineering_overview = this.state.engineering_overview || null;` (index.js:767), but defaultTeamState() (index.js:632-...) never declares the key and nothing in the file ever writes this.state.engineering_overview. I confirmed the producer side too: runtime/service.py:343 `"engineering_overview": mobile_engineering_overview(context),` is published, and both consumers are dead - mobile.js:60 reads source.engineering_overview and ui/team_operations.py:59 reads team_state.get("engineering_overview"). So the desktop Team Operations view is affected as well, not just mobile. Severity corrected to high rather than critical: the failure is fail-safe (every field renders Unavailable and mobile-client.js:22-25 explicitly marks the card STALE/UNAVAILABLE), so it is a dead feature, not a wrong race-critical number or data loss. | Fully confirmed by reading the code end to end. index.js:541-544 normalizeStatePayload produces result.engineering_overview; the publish_state branch (index.js:913-920) assigns only system_health, strategy_state and technical_alerts; grep over the whole repo shows this.state.engineering_overview is written nowhere and defaultTeamState() (index.js:632-680) does not declare the key, so the reader at index.js:767 (`snapshot.engineering_overview = this.state.engineering_overview || null;`) always yields null. The producing side is real and in normal use: runtime/service.py:343 puts `"engineering_overview": mobile_engineering_overview(context)` into the published payload. mobile.js:60 then runs mobileEngineeringOverview(undefined), which returns an all-null object, and mobile-client.js:22 treats a present object with timestamp_utc null as stale, printing "STALE · do not use for decisions". The overview only ever exists inside the transient state_update broadcast. Race-critical data (position, fuel/VE laps, pit window, pit loss) is permanently unavailable to every polling client.

findings.title: webSocketMessage does not await this.loaded, so a hibernation wake overwrites stored team state with defaults
findings.why_wrong: The constructor sets this.state = defaultTeamState() and kicks off this.loaded = this._load() (index.js:678-679) without awaiting it. fetch() correctly guards with `await this.loaded` at index.js:951, but webSocketMessage does not. A hibernated Durable Object is reconstructed when a WebSocket frame arrives, so webSocketMessage runs while _load()'s storage.get is still in flight. _applyAction then mutates the default state and calls this._persist() at index.js:945, which writes team_state_v1 unconditionally.
findings.impact: I reproduced this with a 20 ms storage.get and a stored state of {revision: 9, notes: ["IMPORTANT stint plan"]}. A single team_action add_note frame delivered during the load window produced, in durable storage, revision 1 with the prior note gone - the stint plan, all acknowledgements, all strategy proposals and approvals, and the entire revoked_sessions map were destroyed and the revision counter went backwards. Because note/proposal/approval ids are derived from the revision (`note-${revision}`, index.js:821), the reset also reissues ids that already exist in clients' local histories, so approve_strategy at index.js:885 can match the wrong proposal. Revocation is part of the wiped state, so a revoked client also becomes un-revoked.
findings.fix: Add `await this.loaded;` as the first statement of webSocketMessage (and webSocketClose), exactly as fetch() does. Better still, route all state access through a single `async _state()` helper that awaits this.loaded, so no future entry point can skip it.
findings.verifier_notes: The code asymmetry is real: constructor(ctx) at index.js:675 sets this.state = defaultTeamState() and this.loaded = this._load() (679) without awaiting, fetch() guards with `await this.loaded;` at index.js:951, and webSocketMessage at index.js:1014 has no such guard before reaching _applyAction/_persist (945). But the claimed impact does not survive the platform: Cloudflare Durable Objects close the input gate while a storage operation is in flight ("no events shall be delivered to the object except storage completion events"), and this._load()'s storage.get is issued synchronously in the constructor, before any event can be delivered. The finder's reproduction used a hand-written 20 ms storage stub in Node with no input gate, so it demonstrates the test harness, not production. What remains is a genuine latent fragility (no ctx.blockConcurrencyWhile, inconsistent with fetch's own guard) that would bite the moment any non-storage await is added to _load. Downgraded from critical to low. | The missing `await this.loaded` at index.js:1014 is real, but the claimed failure cannot be constructed on the platform this code runs on. The reproduction was done against a hand-written storage stub with an artificial 20 ms delay; Durable Objects have automatic input gates ("while a storage operation is executing, no events shall be delivered to the object except storage completion events"). The constructor calls this._load() synchronously (index.js:679), so ctx.storage.get("team_state_v1") is already in flight when the constructor returns, the gate is closed, and the queued webSocketMessage delivery is deferred until the get completes; _load's continuation (a microtask on that completion) assigns this.state before any event task runs. There is exactly one await in _load and it is a storage op, so the gate never re-opens mid-initialisation. No concrete sequence on real workerd produces the revision rollback, note loss or un-revocation described. It is a latent fragility (blockConcurrencyWhile would make it explicit, and the asymmetry with fetch()'s guard at index.js:951 is sloppy), not a reproducible data-loss defect.

findings.title: WebSocket team_action path bypasses the action rate limiter entirely
findings.why_wrong: The HTTP route rate-limits the identical write path: teamRoomRequest at index.js:368-372 calls rateLimit(env.SESSION_RATE_LIMITER, `${access.driver}:team-actions`) before forwarding operation === "action" to the DO. The WebSocket handler reaches the same _applyAction with no limiter at all. It structurally cannot have one: TeamRadioHub's constructor takes only ctx (index.js:675) and never receives env, so the rate-limiter bindings are not reachable from inside the Durable Object.
findings.impact: Any authenticated client with add_notes (race_engineer, strategist, administrator) opens one WebSocket to /v1/sync/connect - itself unlimited, see index.js:446 - and then sends team_action frames as fast as the socket allows. Each one runs `await this._persist()` (index.js:945) and `this._broadcast(event)` (946), so a single teammate can drive unbounded Durable Object storage writes and fan-out to every connected peer, at zero cost to their HTTP action quota. The same handler at index.js:1043-1059 relays engineer_call radio messages of up to 1200 characters with no limiter either. Meanwhile _snapshot advertises `actions_per_minute: 12` (index.js:749) as a hard limit, which is false for every WebSocket client.
findings.fix: Pass env (or just the limiter binding) into the Durable Object and apply the same `${access.driver}:team-actions` limit inside _applyAction, or maintain a per-socket token bucket in the serialized attachment and reject frames that exceed it; either way the advertised actions_per_minute must match reality.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified. teamRoomRequest rate-limits only the HTTP path (`operation === "action" && !(await rateLimit(env.SESSION_RATE_LIMITER, `${access.driver}:team-actions`))`, index.js:368-372) while webSocketMessage:1031-1033 calls the identical `await this._applyAction(access, payload)` with no limiter, and each success runs `await this._persist()` (945) and `this._broadcast(event)` (946). teamRadio (index.js:351-363) also has no limiter, so opening the socket is free too. One overstatement: "structurally cannot have one" - the constructor is declared `constructor(ctx)` (index.js:675) so env is ignored, but the DO runtime passes (ctx, env); the binding is one parameter away, so this is an omission, not a structural impossibility. Abuse also requires a code that already holds add_notes (observer/driver get ACTION_DENIED at index.js:809 before any persist), which bounds it to an authenticated teammate. Downgraded to medium. | Confirmed. teamRoomRequest rate-limits only when operation === "action" (index.js:368-372, `rateLimit(env.SESSION_RATE_LIMITER, `${access.driver}:team-actions`)`), while webSocketMessage reaches the identical _applyAction with no limiter (index.js:1031-1033), and each accepted action performs `await this._persist()` (index.js:945, a full rewrite of team_state_v1) plus `this._broadcast(event)` (946). /v1/sync/connect itself is unmetered (index.js:446). _snapshot advertises `actions_per_minute: 12` (index.js:749), which is untrue for any WebSocket client - that part is directly verifiable. One inaccuracy in the rationale: the claim that it "structurally cannot have one" is wrong - Durable Object constructors are invoked as (ctx, env) by the runtime, and this class simply ignores the second argument (`constructor(ctx)` at index.js:675), so the limiter binding is reachable with a one-line change. The bypass and the false advertised quota stand; the abuse requires an already-authenticated add_notes-capable code, so this is insider/leaked-credential abuse rather than an anonymous attack.

findings.title: /v1/realtime-token and /v1/tts are not capability-checked, so any role can spend the owner's OpenAI budget
findings.why_wrong: Every other privileged operation is checked against the server-owned capability matrix via hasCapability (index.js:809). These two routes are dispatched on path alone - neither realtimeToken (index.js:206) nor speech (index.js:237) consults access.role, and there is no realtime or TTS capability in ROLE_CAPABILITIES at all. The observer role is defined at index.js:56-61 with only four view/receive capabilities and explicitly no publish rights.
findings.impact: A holder of an `observer` or `driver` code - the roles the README calls least-privilege and which are denied even add_notes - can POST /v1/realtime-token and receive a live OpenAI Realtime client secret minted against the owner's OPENAI_API_KEY (index.js:213). That secret is used directly against api.openai.com, so the gateway cannot meter or filter it, and the session is created with only model and voice pinned (index.js:217-223), leaving instructions and tools for the client to choose - i.e. the owner's paid account becomes a general-purpose LLM for anyone holding any team code. The 12/min limit at index.js:207 caps token issuance, not the usage each token authorises.
findings.fix: Add explicit `use_realtime_voice` and `use_tts` capabilities, grant them only to race_engineer and administrator, and gate both routes with hasCapability(access, ...) before the upstream fetch.
findings.verifier_notes: Fully confirmed. index.js:482-485 dispatches on path alone: `if (url.pathname === "/v1/realtime-token") { return realtimeToken(request, env, access.driver); }` and `if (url.pathname === "/v1/tts") return speech(request, env, access.driver);`. realtimeToken (206-235) and speech (237-273) receive only `access.driver` - the role never reaches them - and ROLE_CAPABILITIES (index.js:24-74) contains no realtime or TTS capability, so hasCapability cannot gate them. observer is defined at index.js:56-61 with only four view/receive capabilities, yet a valid observer bearer token reaches the upstream POST to api.openai.com/v1/realtime/client_secrets with `Authorization: Bearer ${env.OPENAI_API_KEY}` (index.js:211-213). The session body pins only type/model/audio.output.voice (217-222), so the minted client secret is used directly against OpenAI outside the gateway's view. Severity confirmed. | Confirmed by reading the dispatcher. After `const access = await authenticate(request, env)` (index.js:431-432) the two money-spending routes are dispatched on path alone: index.js:482-486 `if (url.pathname === "/v1/realtime-token") { return realtimeToken(request, env, access.driver); } if (url.pathname === "/v1/tts") return speech(request, env, access.driver);`. Neither realtimeToken (index.js:206-235) nor speech (index.js:237-272) reads access.role, and ROLE_CAPABILITIES (index.js:24-74) contains no realtime or TTS capability, so hasCapability cannot gate them. observer is defined with four view/receive capabilities only (index.js:56-61). Concrete path: an observer code POSTs /v1/realtime-token, gets 200 with a client secret minted against env.OPENAI_API_KEY, and uses it directly against api.openai.com where the gateway can no longer meter or filter it. This also directly contradicts the project's own stated security contract at services/team-gateway/README.md:26 ("Every operation is checked against a server-owned capability matrix").

findings.title: TEAM_ACCESS_ADDITIONAL_SHA256 can never be revoked; the README's revocation procedure silently fails
findings.why_wrong: authenticate() unions two independent secrets. A grep across the whole repository for TEAM_ACCESS_ADDITIONAL_SHA256 returns exactly four hits: this line, one README paragraph, and two test lines. No script writes, reads, prunes or even warns about it - deploy_for_team.py:136 and upgrade_team_services_v08.py:76 both call `_put_secret(..., "TEAM_ACCESS_SHA256", ...)` only. Yet README.md:117-120 states: "Generate a new code set containing every driver who should remain authorized, then replace only TEAM_ACCESS_SHA256 with the new hash map. The removed code fails immediately on its next gateway request to every service."
findings.impact: An administrator who provisioned an emergency code into the additional map (the exact scenario README.md:108-112 recommends it for) and later revokes a compromised teammate by regenerating TEAM_ACCESS_SHA256 believes access is gone. It is not: the digest still lives in the additional secret and authenticate() still returns a valid access object with its original role - including `administrator`, since the test at gateway.test.mjs:51-56 confirms an additional entry with role "owner" resolves to administrator. The credential retains realtime-token, TTS, release download, radio and full team-operations access indefinitely, and nothing in the product surfaces that the second map exists.
findings.fix: Make every provisioning script read, edit and rewrite both maps together (or refuse to run while the additional map is non-empty), and correct README.md:117-120, which currently contradicts README.md:110-112.
findings.verifier_notes: The code claim holds: authenticate() unions both maps at index.js:171-174 with no distinction, and gateway.test.mjs:51-57 confirms an additional entry with role "owner" resolves to administrator. Grep confirms no script touches the additional secret (deploy_for_team.py:136 and upgrade_team_services_v08.py:76 both put only TEAM_ACCESS_SHA256). But the finder's central claim - that nothing warns - is a misread of the README it cites: README.md:111-112 says explicitly "Treat both maps as part of the access list when revoking a code." The contradiction with README.md:117-120 ("replace only TEAM_ACCESS_SHA256 ... fails immediately ... to every service") is real and is the actual defect, together with the absence of any tooling or surface for the second map. That is a documentation inconsistency with a security consequence, not an undisclosed backdoor. Downgraded to medium. | The code fact is confirmed: authenticate() unions both maps (index.js:171-175) and the repo-wide grep returns only index.js:173, README.md:108, and gateway.test.mjs:51/64 - no script writes, prunes or warns about the second secret, and both deploy_for_team.py:136 and upgrade_team_services_v08.py:76 push TEAM_ACCESS_SHA256 only. But the finding's supporting claim that "nothing in the product surfaces that the second map exists" is false, and it materially changes severity: README.md:110-111 in the very same section says "Treat both maps as part of the access list when revoking a code." The revocation paragraph (actually README.md:120-123, not 117-120) does contradict that with "replace only TEAM_ACCESS_SHA256 ... fails immediately on its next gateway request to every service", so an operator reading only the last paragraph is misled. This is a documentation self-contradiction plus a missing tooling guard, not an unwarned trap.

findings.title: Access tokens have no expiry and no revocation path short of a secret redeploy
findings.why_wrong: The access record schema is {driver, role, room} and nothing else - there is no issued_at, expires_at, key_id or version field, and authenticate() (index.js:166-180) performs no time check. The only in-band revocation is the Durable Object's revoked_sessions, and it is checked solely in TeamRadioHub.fetch (index.js:956), which covers /v1/sync/connect, /v1/team/*, /v1/mobile/snapshot and coordination - but not /v1/realtime-token, /v1/tts, /v1/app/latest or /v1/app/download/*. README.md:114-116 concedes this: room revocation "deliberately does not claim to revoke the same code from update, TTS, or Realtime services."
findings.impact: A leaked ssc_live_ code - typed into a phone browser at mobile.js:84, pasted into chat, or left in the plaintext handoff file - is valid forever. Revoking it requires an administrator with Cloudflare credentials to regenerate the whole map and run `wrangler secret put`, which rotates every teammate's code at once (issue_access.py mints fresh codes for all entries). Room revocation, the only self-service control, leaves the attacker full access to the owner's paid OpenAI Realtime and TTS endpoints and to the signed installer downloads.
findings.fix: Add an `expires_unix` field to the access record, reject expired entries in authenticate(), and check revoked_sessions (or a KV deny-list keyed by access_id) in the Worker before dispatching to /v1/realtime-token, /v1/tts and the release routes rather than only inside the Durable Object.
findings.verifier_notes: Code-true. normalizeAccess (index.js:137-146) returns exactly {driver, role, room} - no issued_at/expires_at/key_id - and authenticate (166-180) does no time check. revoked_sessions is consulted only in TeamRadioHub.fetch (index.js:956), which the realtime-token, TTS, /v1/app/latest and /v1/app/download/* paths never reach. Two deductions from the finder's own evidence, though: README.md:114-116 discloses the limit rather than hiding it, and the practical blast radius is largely the same hole already counted in finding 4 (any code reaching the paid endpoints). Rotation is possible, just coarse. Downgraded to medium to avoid double-counting the same exposure as high twice. | Confirmed by code. normalizeAccess returns exactly {driver, role, room} (index.js:137-147) with no issued_at/expires_at/key_id, and authenticate (index.js:166-180) does only a digest comparison - no time check anywhere. revoked_sessions is consulted solely in TeamRadioHub.fetch (index.js:956, `if (this.state.revoked_sessions[access.access_id])`), which is unreachable from /v1/realtime-token, /v1/tts, /v1/app/latest and /v1/app/download/* because those never touch the Durable Object (index.js:482-490). README.md:115-118 concedes room revocation "deliberately does not claim to revoke the same code from update, TTS, or Realtime services." Combined with finding 4, a leaked ssc_live_ code gives permanent access to the owner's paid Realtime/TTS endpoints, and the only fix rotates every teammate's code at once.

findings.title: deploy_for_team.py rewrites the access map with legacy string entries, demoting every role and forcing the default room
findings.why_wrong: The map values are bare driver-name strings, which normalizeAccess (index.js:138-140) treats as the legacy form and resolves to role "driver" and room TEAM_ROOM_DEFAULT. The script has no --role or --room argument at all, and _put_secret replaces the entire TEAM_ACCESS_SHA256 secret rather than merging. It also runs at line 136, before any of the validation at lines 137-165.
findings.impact: Running the documented provisioning script against a live gateway destroys the existing access map: every previously issued race_engineer, strategist, observer and administrator code stops working, and the newly issued codes are all plain drivers in room `ssc-team-radio`. If the team was issued with `--room race-room` (the exact example in README.md:75) the new codes land in a different Durable Object and cannot see any existing team state. There is now no administrator code at all, so nobody can disconnect or revoke a client, and recovery requires re-running issue_access.py and a second secret push. If the script then fails at the health check on line 137 or the per-driver authorization loop on line 144, the team is locked out with no rollback.
findings.fix: Emit the object form {driver, role, room} with --role and --room arguments, merge into the existing map instead of replacing it (or refuse to run when the fetched map is non-empty without an explicit --replace flag), and push the secret only after all validation has passed.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified at deploy_for_team.py:134-136: `hash_map = {digest: driver for driver, (_, digest) in issued.items()}` then `_put_secret(..., "TEAM_ACCESS_SHA256", json.dumps(hash_map))` - bare string values, which normalizeAccess (index.js:138-140) resolves to role "driver" and room TEAM_ROOM_DEFAULT. The script has no --role/--room, contrasting with issue_access.py:77 which writes `{"driver": driver, "role": role, "room": args.room}`, and README.md:75 uses `--room race-room` as the example. The secret is replaced wholesale, not merged. One claim is wrong: driver validation is NOT skipped - validate_driver runs at deploy_for_team.py:114-118, well before line 136; what follows the write at 137-165 is post-write verification, which necessarily comes after the secret exists. There is also a partial guard against casual re-runs (line 103-104 refuses to overwrite an existing handoff file). Downgraded to medium. | Confirmed verbatim at deploy_for_team.py:134-136: `hash_map = {digest: driver for driver, (_, digest) in issued.items()}` followed by `_put_secret(wrangler, gateway_root, "TEAM_ACCESS_SHA256", json.dumps(hash_map))`. Values are bare strings, which normalizeAccess (index.js:138-140) resolves to role "driver" and room TEAM_ROOM_DEFAULT. argparse defines only --gateway, --driver and --handoff (lines 88-97) - no --role, no --room - and _put_secret replaces the whole secret (no merge). The ordering claim checks out: the secret push is line 136, the health wait is 137-138 and the per-driver authorization loop starts at 140, so a failure there leaves the team locked out with no rollback. Contrast issue_access.py, which does support DRIVER:ROLE and --room and emits structured entries, and README.md:63 whose documented example issues with `--room race-room`; running deploy_for_team.py afterwards silently relocates everyone to `ssc-team-radio` and strips the administrator role, so nobody can disconnect or revoke.

findings.title: Every role, including observer, reads the full coordination state with operator identities and free-text decision reasons
findings.quote: return jsonResponse(200, { ...this._snapshot(access), coordination: await this.coordination.snapshot() });
findings.why_wrong: _snapshot carefully gates system_health, strategy_state and revoked_sessions behind capabilities (index.js:761-771), but the coordination block is spliced in unconditionally. TeamCoordination.snapshot() (coordination.js:24-29) performs no access check - the allowed() guard at coordination.js:6, which restricts to race_engineer and administrator, is only applied inside _apply(), i.e. to writes. There is no coordination-read capability in ROLE_CAPABILITIES at all.
findings.impact: I confirmed this against the real DO: an `observer` is correctly refused a coordination write with 403 ACTION_DENIED, then issues GET /v1/team/snapshot and receives the complete coordination view - the active lease {node_id: "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa:one", scope, epoch, expires_ms}, and the current HUMAN_DECISION record including operator, operator_access_id (another member's session identifier, from coordination.js:141), recommendation_key, model_preferred and the operator's 300-character free-text reason, which in my run read "secret team tactic: undercut on lap 40". recent_events replays the last 30 such records. An observer code - the role handed to guests and spotters - leaks the team's live strategy reasoning and another member's session id.
findings.fix: Add a `view_coordination` capability granted to race_engineer and administrator, and include the coordination block only when capabilities.includes("view_coordination"); also drop operator_access_id from the client-visible view.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed. index.js:961 is `return jsonResponse(200, { ...this._snapshot(access), coordination: await this.coordination.snapshot() });` with no capability test, while the three lines it sits beside (index.js:765-771) each gate on capabilities.includes(...). coordination.js:24-29 snapshot() takes no access argument, and `allowed` (coordination.js:6) is applied only inside _apply (line 44), i.e. writes. _view (coordination.js:31-41) returns the live lease, the decision record and recent_events.slice(-30), and the HUMAN_DECISION record built at coordination.js:139-145 carries operator, operator_access_id, recommendation_key, model_preferred and the 300-char reason. findings.title: Ranged release downloads emit Content-Range: bytes undefined-NaN and Content-Length: undefined
findings.why_wrong: Cloudflare's R2Range union is {offset, length?} | {offset?, length} | {suffix}. The code assumes both offset and length are always present. For a suffix request (Range: bytes=-N) neither exists; for an open-ended request (Range: bytes=N-) length is absent. String(undefined) yields the literal "undefined" and undefined + undefined - 1 yields NaN.
findings.impact: I ran the real handler with an R2 stub returning {suffix: 2} and {offset: 2}: `bytes=-2` produced status 206, Content-Length "undefined", Content-Range "bytes undefined-NaN/4"; `bytes=2-` produced Content-Length "undefined", Content-Range "bytes 2-NaN/4". Open-ended is exactly the form the desktop updater sends - team_gateway.py:316 builds `{"Range": f"bytes={start_byte}-"}`. Its resume guard at team_gateway.py:321-325 only checks that Content-Range startswith "bytes 2-", so the malformed header slips through and the client resumes against a response whose declared length is garbage, while any standards-conforming download manager or CDN rejects it outright. README.md:99-101 advertises "Ranged reads support resumable downloads" for a multi-hundred-megabyte installer.
findings.fix: Handle all three R2Range shapes: derive start and length from offset/length/suffix against object.size, fall back to the full object when the range cannot be resolved, and return 416 for an unsatisfiable range. Add tests for `bytes=N-` (no length) and `bytes=-N` (suffix) - gateway.test.mjs:456-460 currently stubs an impossible {offset: 2, length: 2} for an open-ended request, which is why this was never caught.
findings.verifier_notes: The code is exactly as quoted (index.js:309-314) and unguarded: it reads object.range.offset and object.range.length directly and does arithmetic on both, with no handling for the documented R2Range union's suffix-only or offset-only forms, and no fallback to object.size. The client side checks out too: team_gateway.py:316 sends `{"Range": f"bytes={start_byte}-"}` and the guard at :321-325 only tests `content_range.startswith(f"bytes {start_byte}-")`, so `bytes 2-NaN/4` passes. Downgraded from high to medium for one reason the finder glossed: the reproduction used a hand-made R2 stub returning {suffix: 2}/{offset: 2}, not the real binding, and workerd may resolve the range to {offset, length} before handing it back - which would make this a type-contract defect that only fires on a malformed or suffix range rather than on the updater's everyday resume. The missing guard is still real and one line to fix. | The code at index.js:309-313 does read object.range.offset and object.range.length unconditionally, and the workers-types R2Range union does permit {offset} or {suffix} alone - but the claimed failure was produced only against a hand-written R2 stub that returned {suffix: 2} and {offset: 2}. The call site passes `{ range: request.headers }` (index.js:301), i.e. R2 parses the Range header itself and the binding returns the resolved range it actually served; the repo's own fixture at gateway.test.mjs:454-458 returns `range: { offset: 2, length: 2 }` for a `bytes=2-` request, matching that behaviour. I could not establish that real R2 ever hands back a header-derived range with length absent, so the concrete NaN output is not demonstrated. Even granting it, the described consequence is benign for this product: the desktop updater only sends open-ended ranges (team_gateway.py:316) and its guard at 321-325 checks `status != 206 or not content_range.startswith(f"bytes {start_byte}-")`, which a "bytes 2-NaN/4" header passes, so the resume still completes. Refuted for lack of a constructible failure.

findings.title: rateLimit() fails open when a limiter binding is missing, on every route except mobile

The mobile route was deliberately hardened against this - index.js:437 reads `if (!env.SESSION_RATE_LIMITER?.limit) return jsonResponse(503, ...)` with a comment explaining the fail-closed choice - but /v1/realtime-token (index.js:207), /v1/tts (238), /v1/team/action (370) and /v1/team/coordination (453) all go straight through rateLimit and therefore fail open.

Any authenticated teammate can then mint OpenAI Realtime client secrets and stream TTS against the owner's key without limit, and there is no signal anywhere that protection is off: /health still reports READY, and _snapshot still advertises actions_per_minute: 12.

The contrast is genuine and deliberate: index.js:435-437 carries the comment "Fail closed without the existing configured limiter" and returns 503 MOBILE_RATE_LIMIT_UNAVAILABLE. So the codebase demonstrates it knows the correct behaviour and applies it to exactly one route. Requires a misconfigured deploy to trigger, which is what keeps it at medium rather than higher. | The code is exactly as quoted (index.js:200-204, `if (!binding || typeof binding.limit !== "function") return true;`) and the asymmetry with the deliberately fail-closed mobile route (index.js:437-440, with a comment explaining the choice) is real, as is the fact that /v1/realtime-token (207), /v1/tts (238), team actions (370) and coordination (453) go through the permissive helper. findings.title: /v1/team/snapshot and /v1/sync/connect have no rate limit at all
findings.why_wrong: teamRoomRequest only rate-limits when operation === "action" (index.js:368-372), so the "snapshot" operation passes through unmetered; teamRadio (index.js:351) has no limiter either. Every /v1/team/snapshot hits the Durable Object, which runs coordination.snapshot() - an `await this.chain` plus a storage.get (coordination.js:25-26) - and serialises the entire team state. The analogous mobile route was given both a fail-closed guard and a dedicated key at index.js:437-440; the desktop route was not.
findings.impact: One authenticated code, including an observer's, can issue unlimited /v1/team/snapshot requests and open unlimited WebSockets to the same Durable Object. Durable Objects are single-threaded, so this serialises into head-of-line blocking for the whole room: real teammates' actions and radio calls queue behind the flood during a race. Each accepted socket is also added to ctx.getWebSockets(), which _presence() (index.js:706) walks and _broadcast() (775) fans out to on every single action, making the cost quadratic.

findings.title: parseJson only pre-checks the Content-Length header, then buffers the whole body regardless
findings.why_wrong: A chunked request carries no Content-Length, so `Number(null || "0")` is 0 and the guard passes. The real size check on the following line runs only after `await request.text()` has already materialised the entire body in the isolate's memory. The 16 KiB MAX_JSON_BYTES limit is therefore advisory for any client that declines to send Content-Length.
findings.impact: An authenticated client POSTs a chunked body far larger than 16 KiB to /v1/tts, /v1/team/action or /v1/team/coordination. The Worker buffers all of it before rejecting with 413, so memory and CPU are consumed per request up to the platform's own request ceiling, not the application's. Combined with the fail-open limiter above and the unmetered WebSocket path, this is a cheap way to push a Worker isolate toward its memory limit; _snapshot nonetheless advertises `request_bytes: MAX_JSON_BYTES` (index.js:748) as an enforced bound.
findings.fix: Read the body through a size-capped reader that aborts once MAX_JSON_BYTES have been consumed, rather than calling request.text() and measuring afterwards.
findings.verifier_notes: Code-true: index.js:187-190 reads Content-Length, defaults to "0" when absent, and the authoritative byte check runs only after `const text = await request.text();`. Downgraded from medium to low because the finder overstates the consequence: the request IS rejected with 413 (index.js:190), the buffering ceiling is Cloudflare's own request body limit rather than anything the attacker chooses, the abuse requires an authenticated code, and no state is corrupted. This is a hardening gap - the size check should stream or trust the platform limit - not a usable memory-exhaustion vector on its own. | Confirmed at index.js:186-190: `const declared = Number(request.headers.get("Content-Length") || "0"); if (declared > MAX_JSON_BYTES) throw ...; const text = await request.text();` - a chunked request yields Number("0") and sails past, and the real byte check runs only after the body is fully materialised. So MAX_JSON_BYTES is advisory for the buffering step, and `request_bytes: MAX_JSON_BYTES` in the advertised limits (index.js:748) overstates what is enforced. Downgrading severity: the request still ends in a 413, the size is bounded above by Cloudflare's own request-body ceiling, and reaching a memory problem needs a sustained authenticated flood - a resource-consumption nuisance rather than a production-breaking defect.

findings.title: Cloudflare rate-limit bindings are per-location, but the protocol advertises them as absolute quotas
findings.why_wrong: The Workers rate-limiting API is documented as not globally coordinated - counters are maintained per Cloudflare location, so the effective ceiling is limit x (number of colos an attacker's traffic reaches). Nothing in the Worker compensates: index.js:749 hard-codes `actions_per_minute: 12` into the snapshot's `limits` block that clients display as a firm quota, and the README ("Every upstream Realtime and TTS request is rate-limited per driver identity") states it without qualification.
findings.impact: A single leaked ssc_live_ code driven from a handful of geographies gets 12 realtime-token issuances and 30 TTS calls per minute *per colo*, so the true ceiling on spend against the owner's OpenAI key is a multiple of the advertised one - and each realtime token authorises an unmetered upstream session. Anyone reading the snapshot's limits block or the README will size the blast radius wrong.
findings.fix: Either accept the per-colo semantics and document them in the README and in the snapshot's limits block, or back the quota with a Durable Object counter keyed by access_id, which is globally consistent.
findings.verifier_notes: The config is as quoted (wrangler.jsonc:45-52, limit 12 / period 60) and index.js:749 does hard-code `actions_per_minute: 12` into the snapshot's limits block that clients render as a firm quota. The per-location semantics of the Workers rate-limiting API are accurate. But this is a documentation/accuracy defect, not a code defect: the limiter still works, the multiplier is bounded by how many colos one client's traffic reaches, and no guard is missing from the code itself. Downgraded to low. | The configuration is as quoted (wrangler.jsonc:47-53, limit 12/60 for SESSION_RATE_LIMITER; 30/60 for TTS at 55-60; 180/60 for coordination at 43-46) and the Workers rate-limiting API is documented as not globally coordinated, so the effective ceiling scales with the number of Cloudflare locations the traffic reaches. findings.title: The unauthenticated share token travels in the URL path while invocation logs are persisted

It will equally appear in any Referer header, browser history and corporate proxy log.
findings.impact: Anyone with read access to the Worker's logs (a broader set than the Cloudflare secret holders) recovers a live, unauthenticated download token for the production installer for the remainder of its 7-day window (create_phone_download.py:14). Separately, the grant lives in a single DOWNLOAD_SHARE secret (create_phone_download.py:38), so issuing a link for a second teammate silently invalidates the first, and temporaryShareDownload applies no rate limit, so one leaked link permits unbounded R2 egress against the owner's account.

findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed. index.js:411-414 handles /v1/app/share/ before authenticate() at :431, so the path segment is the sole credential, and wrangler.jsonc:9-17 enables `"invocation_logs": true` with `"persist": true`. temporaryShareDownload (index.js:335-348) applies no rate limit. The single-grant claim checks out: create_phone_download.py:37-43 puts one DOWNLOAD_SHARE secret, so a second link overwrites the first, and VALID_DAYS = 7 at :14. Mitigations worth noting but not disqualifying: the token is a 32-byte urlsafe secret compared in constant time against a stored sha256 (index.js:344-347), Referrer-Policy is no-referrer on every response (index.js:92), and head_sampling_rate is 0.1 so only a fraction of requests are logged. | Confirmed on both halves. index.js:410-414 handles the share prefix before the authenticate() call at index.js:431, so the path segment is the sole credential (temporaryShareDownload, index.js:333-347, only hashes the token against the DOWNLOAD_SHARE grant and applies no rate limit). wrangler.jsonc:9-17 sets `"invocation_logs": true` with `"persist": true`, and invocation logs record the request URL, so the bearer-equivalent secret lands in retained logs (head_sampling_rate 0.1 reduces but does not remove this), plus Referer, browser history and proxy logs. create_phone_download.py:14 confirms the 7-day window and lines 20-40 confirm the single DOWNLOAD_SHARE secret, so issuing a second link invalidates the first. findings.title: revoked_sessions grows without bound and accepts arbitrary 96-character keys
findings.quote: this.state.revoked_sessions = { ...this.state.revoked_sessions, [target]: revoked };
findings.why_wrong: Every other retained collection is capped - notes .slice(-40), status_requests .slice(-20), proposals and approvals .slice(-30) - and those caps are advertised in the snapshot's limits block (index.js:743-747). revoked_sessions has no cap. The key comes from safeIdentifier(payload.client_id) (index.js:924), which permits /^[A-Za-z0-9._:-]{1,96}$/, whereas a genuine client_id is always the 24-hex access_id enforced at index.js:532. The entry also carries a 200-character attacker-supplied reason string.
findings.impact: An administrator code - or anyone who has escalated to one - issues repeated revoke_client actions with fabricated 96-character client_ids over the unmetered WebSocket path, each adding a permanent ~300-byte entry to team_state_v1, which is rewritten in full on every single action by _persist() (index.js:945). The Durable Object's stored value grows without limit and every subsequent action pays the serialisation cost, degrading the room for the whole team. Each entry is also returned verbatim to administrators in the snapshot (index.js:770).
findings.fix: Validate the revoke/disconnect target against /^[a-f0-9]{24}$/ rather than safeIdentifier, and bound revoked_sessions with an LRU cap and a TTL, mirroring the caps already applied to the other collections.
findings.verifier_notes: Code-true: index.js:932 `this.state.revoked_sessions = { ...this.state.revoked_sessions, [target]: revoked };` has no cap, unlike notes .slice(-40) (:822), status_requests .slice(-20) (:848), proposals/approvals .slice(-30) (:880, :906); the key comes from safeIdentifier (index.js:526-530, /^[A-Za-z0-9._:-]{1,96}$/) while a real client_id is the 24-hex access_id checked at index.js:532; the reason is 200 chars (:929); _persist rewrites the whole record each action (:945). Downgraded to low because the action requires the revoke_sessions capability, which index.js:62-74 grants to administrator alone - this is an administrator degrading their own team's room, not a teammate or outsider vector, and restore_client can remove entries. | The code facts hold - index.js:932 has no cap where notes/status_requests/proposals/approvals all use .slice() (index.js:822, 840, 861, 884), and safeIdentifier (index.js:526-530) permits 96 chars where a real client_id is the 24-hex access_id enforced at index.js:532 - but no realistic failure follows. revoke_client requires the revoke_sessions capability, which only `administrator` holds (index.js:63-74), and _applyAction rejects the caller's own id (index.js:926). In legitimate use the map gains one ~300-byte entry per genuinely revoked teammate, and restore_client (index.js:938-943) deletes entries, so it is self-limiting. The only path to unbounded growth is a hostile or compromised administrator - a principal who can already disconnect every client, revoke every session and publish arbitrary state, so degrading their own room's storage is not a meaningful escalation. Trusted input, no concrete victim.

findings.title: Coordination event, decision and outcome records are written forever with no pruning
findings.quote: await storage.put(`coordination_event:${String(event.revision).padStart(12, "0")}`, event);
findings.why_wrong: Three separate key families are appended to Durable Object storage and never deleted: coordination_event:<revision> here, coordination_decision:<id> at coordination.js:146, and coordination_outcome:<id>:<status> at coordination.js:118. The only bounded structure is the in-memory `state.events` mirror, capped at .slice(-30). The comment on line 53 - "Immutable records survive bounded snapshot retention" - documents the intent but no retention policy, eviction or storage accounting was implemented alongside it.
findings.impact: The route is rate-limited to 180 requests/minute (wrangler.jsonc:43), and each lease grant, recommendation change, supersede, expiry, replace, human decision and decision outcome writes a permanent row. Over a season of endurance events a single room's Durable Object accumulates unbounded storage that nothing can reclaim short of deleting the object, which would also destroy the live team state. There is no metric, alarm or listing endpoint that would reveal the growth before it hits the platform limit.
findings.fix: Add a retention policy - delete coordination_event rows below revision minus N on each write, or use storage.list with a prefix and a scheduled alarm - and expose the current row count in the coordination view.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified in full. Three key families are put and never deleted: coordination_event:<padded revision> (coordination.js:54), coordination_decision:<id> (:146) and coordination_outcome:<id>:<status> (:118). Nothing in the file calls storage.delete or storage.list for cleanup; the only bounded structure is state.events = [...].slice(-30) (:55), and the comment at :53 ("Immutable records survive bounded snapshot retention") documents intent without a retention policy. Writes are throttled to 180/min by COORDINATION_RATE_LIMITER (wrangler.jsonc:41-43) and heartbeats only append on lease grant, recommendation change, supersede/replace/expiry or decision outcome, so growth is bounded by real events rather than per-request - slow but genuinely monotonic, with no listing or metric to observe it. | Confirmed: coordination.js:54 `await storage.put(`coordination_event:${String(event.revision).padStart(12, "0")}`, event)`, coordination.js:146 `await storage.put(`coordination_decision:${event.decision_id}`, event)` and coordination.js:118 `await storage.put(key, event)` for outcomes. No delete() or list()-and-prune exists anywhere in the file; only the in-memory state.events mirror is bounded (`.slice(-30)`, line 55). Unlike finding 19 this accrues under normal operation - every LEASE_GRANTED, MODEL_RECOMMENDATION, SUPERSEDED, EXPIRED, REPLACED, HUMAN_DECISION and DECISION_OUTCOME appends a row, and heartbeats are permitted at 180/min (wrangler.jsonc:43). Severity lowered because the impact claim is overstated: the rows are small and a season of racing produces thousands, not a volume that approaches a Durable Object storage limit. The real defect is the absence of any retention policy behind the comment at coordination.js:53 and of any way to reclaim space without destroying live team state.

findings.title: Engineer radio messages have no replay protection and relay a client-chosen timestamp
findings.why_wrong: message_id is only shape-checked against /^[A-Za-z0-9._:-]{1,96}$/ (index.js:499); no seen-set, monotonic counter or nonce store exists, so the same message_id can be submitted repeatedly. timestamp_utc is checked only for parseability (index.js:503-504) and is then relayed verbatim to peers at index.js:1056, while the 60-second bound at index.js:507 is applied to expires_utc alone.
findings.impact: A publisher - or anyone who has captured a frame from a compromised race_engineer session - can re-broadcast an identical engineer call as many times as they like within its 60-second window, and can stamp it with any timestamp_utc that parses, including one far in the past or future. Receiving clients deduplicate on message_id only if they choose to; the server offers no guarantee. For a race-radio channel where a stale "BOX BOX" replayed a lap later is directly harmful, the protocol should not leave this to the client.
findings.fix: Keep a bounded set of recently seen message_ids per room in the Durable Object and reject duplicates, and require timestamp_utc to fall within the same 60-second window already enforced on expires_utc.
findings.verifier_notes: Accurate. validRadioPayload (index.js:492-509) shape-checks message_id against /^[A-Za-z0-9._:-]{1,96}$/ with no seen-set or nonce store anywhere in the file, checks timestamp_utc only for Number.isFinite(Date.parse(...)), and applies the `expiry > now && expiry <= now + 60_000` bound to expires_utc alone. index.js:1050-1058 then relays payload.timestamp_utc verbatim to peers. Correctly filed as low: the publisher must already hold publish_engineer_radio (index.js:1043), and clients can dedupe on message_id. | Confirmed. validRadioPayload (index.js:492-509) checks message_id only against /^[A-Za-z0-9._:-]{1,96}$/ and there is no seen-set, nonce store or counter anywhere in the module, so the same message_id is accepted repeatedly. timestamp_utc is checked only with Number.isFinite(Date.parse(...)) (index.js:503-504) and is relayed verbatim to peers at index.js:1056; the `expiry > now && expiry <= now + 60_000` bound (index.js:507) applies to expires_utc alone, so an arbitrary past or future timestamp_utc passes. Reaching this path needs publish_engineer_radio (checked at index.js:1039), i.e. a race_engineer or administrator credential, which is why low is the right level - but for a race-radio channel the server offering no dedup guarantee is a genuine protocol gap.

findings.title: webSocketClose echoes the peer's close code back into socket.close() and reports a ghost client in presence
findings.why_wrong: The close code delivered to this handler can be 1005 (no status received) or 1006 (abnormal closure), and neither may be passed to close() - the call throws. There is no try/catch here, unlike the defensive wrappers around peer.send at index.js:781 and peer.close at index.js:795. Separately, _presence() (index.js:706) is computed from ctx.getWebSockets(), which still includes the socket being closed at this point; the `excluded` argument only suppresses sending to it, it does not remove it from the roster being broadcast.
findings.impact: An abnormally dropped connection - a driver's phone losing signal mid-stint, precisely the common case - raises inside webSocketClose, so the presence broadcast on the next line never runs and every remaining teammate keeps showing the departed client as CONNECTED until some other event forces a refresh. Even when close() succeeds, the broadcast roster includes the closing socket, so the count is off by one. mobile-client.js:38 renders this directly as "N connected".
findings.fix: Wrap socket.close() in try/catch and skip the code when it is 1005 or 1006, and filter the closing socket out of _presence() before broadcasting (or broadcast from a queued microtask after the runtime has removed it).
findings.verifier_notes: The code is as quoted (index.js:1062-1065) with no try/catch, in contrast to the deliberate catches around peer.send (:780-782) and peer.close (:793-795). Passing 1005/1006 to close() is rejected by workerd, and the throw would skip the presence broadcast on the very next line. The off-by-one is real independently of the throw: _presence() (index.js:706) enumerates ctx.getWebSockets(), which still contains the closing socket, and the `excluded` argument only suppresses delivery to it - mobile-client.js:38 renders the count directly. Worth noting the pattern mirrors Cloudflare's own hibernation example, which is presumably where it came from; low is the right level. | Confirmed at index.js:1062-1065, with no try/catch, in contrast to the defensive wrappers around peer.send (index.js:779-783) and peer.close (index.js:791-797). The reachable trigger is ordinary: a client that closes without a status code surfaces as 1005 in this handler, and close() rejects any code outside 1000 and 3000-4999, so the call throws before the presence broadcast on the next line ever runs and remaining peers keep showing the departed client. The second half is independently true even when close() succeeds: _presence() (index.js:703-717) is built from ctx.getWebSockets(), which still contains the closing socket, and the `excluded` argument of _broadcast (index.js:774-776) only suppresses delivery to it - it does not remove it from the roster, so the count rendered at mobile-client.js:38 (`${snapshot.connected_count} connected`) is off by one.

findings.title: Coordination outcome dedup key is ambiguous because ident() permits the ':' delimiter
findings.quote:
const key = `coordination_outcome:${outcome.decision_id}:${outcome.status}`;
          if (!await storage.get(key)) {
findings.why_wrong: ident() at coordination.js:7 is /^[A-Za-z0-9_.:-]{1,128}$/ - it allows the same ':' used as the field separator here, and in the node key at coordination.js:66 (`${access.access_id}:${payload.node_id}`). The key is therefore not injective: a decision_id containing a colon can produce the same storage key as a different (decision_id, status) pair. The same construction appears in coordination_decision:<id> at line 146.
findings.impact: Not currently exploitable - decision_ids are server-generated as `decision-<revision>` (coordination.js:140) and contain no colon, and line 110 requires the decision to already exist in storage - but the idempotency guarantee that this key is the sole mechanism for (recording each DECISION_OUTCOME exactly once, per the comment at line 53) rests on an accident of the current id format rather than on validation. Any future change that admits a colon into decision ids, such as scoping them by node, silently breaks outcome deduplication and lets the same outcome be appended repeatedly.
findings.fix: Tighten ident() to exclude ':' and validate the composite node key separately, or length-prefix/percent-encode the segments so the key construction is injective by design.
findings.verifier_notes: Correct as written and correctly self-limited. coordination.js:7 `const ident = (value) => ... /^[A-Za-z0-9_.:-]{1,128}$/` permits the ':' used as a separator at :113 and :146 and in the node key at :66, so the key is not injective. The finder states plainly it is not currently exploitable - decision ids are server-generated `decision-${state.revision + 1}` at :140 and :110 requires the decision to pre-exist - which I confirmed. This is a latent-invariant note, which is what low means; keeping it is fair since the user asked for everything. | The finding refutes itself: it states "Not currently exploitable", and the code confirms why. decision_id values are server-generated as `decision-${state.revision + 1}` (coordination.js:140) where revision is an integer, so no colon can appear; outcome.decision_id is additionally required to resolve to an existing `coordination_decision:<id>` record (coordination.js:110-111) before the key at line 113 is built, so a client cannot introduce a foreign id. status is constrained to a five-value allowlist (coordination.js:112). No input, state or sequence produces a collision. This is a hypothetical future-refactor hazard, not a defect.

findings.title: Revocation and disconnect events, including the administrator's free-text reason, are broadcast to every client
findings.quote: event = { type: "client_revoked", ...revoked, closed };
findings.why_wrong: The `revoked` object spread here carries client_id, revoked_by, revoked_utc and a 200-character administrator-supplied reason (index.js:929). _applyAction ends with an unconditional this._broadcast(event) at index.js:946, which sends to every socket in the room. Yet _snapshot deliberately restricts the same information to administrators: `if (capabilities.includes("revoke_sessions")) snapshot.revoked_sessions = ...` (index.js:769-771). The client_disconnected event at index.js:922 is broadcast the same way.
findings.impact: The moderation channel is confidential by snapshot but public by broadcast. Any connected observer or driver receives the id of the revoked session, the administrator's identity and their free-text justification - typically the reason someone was ejected from the team room. The revoked party themselves receives the event too if the close at index.js:933 loses the race with the broadcast.
findings.fix: Filter _broadcast by capability - send client_revoked and client_disconnected only to sockets whose attachment role includes revoke_sessions, and send the target only a minimal close notice - matching the gating already applied in _snapshot.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed. index.js:929-934 builds `revoked` with client_id, revoked_by, revoked_utc and the 200-char reason, spreads it into the event, and _applyAction ends at :946 with an unconditional this._broadcast(event) to every socket; client_disconnected (:922) takes the same path. The asymmetry with _snapshot's `capabilities.includes("revoke_sessions")` gate at :769-771 is exactly as described. The close-vs-broadcast race is also plausible since _closeClient runs at :933 before the broadcast. Reasonable to argue broadcast is intentional so clients can update presence, but then the reason string should not ride along; low is right. | Confirmed. The revoked object built at index.js:927-931 carries client_id, revoked_by, the 200-char administrator reason and revoked_utc, is spread into the event at index.js:934, and _applyAction ends with an unconditional `this._broadcast(event)` at index.js:946 that fans out to every socket in the room; client_disconnected (index.js:922) goes the same way. That directly contradicts the snapshot gating at index.js:769-771, which restricts revoked_sessions to holders of revoke_sessions. The race with _closeClient (index.js:933, executed before the broadcast) means the revoked party is usually closed first, so the claim that they also receive it is the weakest part - but any connected observer or driver plainly does.

findings.title: Driver swap runs voice_bundle.close() inline on the telemetry thread (up to 15 s stall)
findings.quote:
if voice_bundle is not None:
                    voice_bundle.close()
                    voice_bundle = None
                    last_voice_status = None
findings.why_wrong: This sits inside `if active_identity != identity:` and `identity` includes `snapshot.driver` (_identity_from_snapshot, service.py:153-160), so it fires on every scoring-driver change. `voice_bundle.close()` -> `VoiceRuntime.close()` (voice/runtime.py:48-55) -> `VoiceOrchestrator.stop()`, which serially does `self._speech_thread.join(timeout=5.0)` (orchestrator.py:890), `future.result(timeout=5.0)` on the realtime close (orchestrator.py:898) and `self._loop_thread.join(timeout=5.0)` (orchestrator.py:902) — up to 15 s of blocking joins — then `persistence.end_session()` and `persistence.close()` (SQLite). Immediately afterwards the same thread calls `build_voice_runtime(...)` (service.py:1210), which resolves and opens audio devices. All of it runs inside the single telemetry frame loop that is also the safety loop.
findings.impact: Endurance driver change at a pit stop: the playback worker is mid-`_play_stream` on a gateway TTS HTTP stream that does not tear down instantly, so the join burns its full 5 s; the realtime websocket close burns 5 s more. The telemetry loop does not call `reader.read()` for ~10-15 s. `lmu_interface`, `shared_memory`, `player_vehicle` and `tracker` all have `failed_after_s` of 5-10 s (supervision.py:28-34), so health flips to FAILED, no fuel/energy/tyre/traffic numbers are produced for the incoming driver, and the desktop shows the engineer as failed during the most safety-critical 15 s of the race.
findings.fix: Hand the old bundle to a dedicated teardown thread (or a small single-slot executor) and build the new one asynchronously; keep the telemetry frame free of joins. Gate calls on the new bundle until it reports READY, and surface "voice restarting" through health instead of blocking the loop.
findings.verifier_notes: Code-true. service.py:1085 `if active_identity != identity:` with identity from `_identity_from_snapshot` which includes `driver=snapshot.driver` (service.py:158); the close is at 1107-1110 inside that branch, and `build_voice_runtime(...)` is re-invoked at 1210 on the same thread. runtime.py:48-55 `self.orchestrator.stop()` leads to orchestrator.py:890 `self._speech_thread.join(timeout=5.0)`, 898 `future.result(timeout=5.0)`, 902 `self._loop_thread.join(timeout=5.0)` — three serial 5 s budgets — then persistence.end_session/close at 906-910. This is the single `while not shutdown.requested.is_set():` frame loop (service.py:958) that also calls `reader.read()` (972) and the heartbeats at 1075-1082. supervision.py:29-33 confirms `("lmu_interface", 1.0, 10.0)`, `("tracker", 1.0, 5.0)`, so a 5-15 s stall does flip health. No guard, no worker thread, no timeout shortcut anywhere on the path. | Confirmed by reading the code. service.py:1085 `if active_identity != identity:` and _identity_from_snapshot (service.py:153-160) includes `driver=snapshot.driver`, so a scoring-driver change enters the block; service.py:1108 `voice_bundle.close()` runs inline, and service.py:1210 `voice_bundle = build_voice_runtime(...)` rebuilds on the same thread. VoiceRuntimeBundle.close -> orchestrator.stop() has three serial blocking joins: `self._speech_thread.join(timeout=5.0)`, `future.result(timeout=5.0)`, `self._loop_thread.join(timeout=5.0)`. The precondition is constructible: tts_backend.py:83 passes `timeout=self.config.connection_timeout_s` and config.py:424 sets `connection_timeout_s: float = 15.0`, so a stalled TTS response parks the playback worker well past the 5 s join (the `if interrupt.is_set(): return` check only runs between received chunks). supervision.py:28-34 does register lmu_interface/shared_memory/player_vehicle at failed_after_s 10.0 and tracker at 5.0, so a 10-15 s frame gap flips them to FAILED. Downgraded from critical: the stall is transient and self-recovering - no data loss, no crash, no wrong number persisted - so it is a severe availability gap, not a critical one.

findings.title: enable_learning() and shutdown() call stop() while holding the controller RLock
findings.why_wrong: `stop()` is written so the child drain happens outside the lock — it releases `self._lock` at line 494 and comments at line 499 "The wait runs outside the lock so the desktop poll never blocks behind it" before `process.wait(timeout=grace)` at line 503. But `self._lock` is an RLock (line 203) and `enable_learning` already holds it, so the release at 494 only drops the inner acquisition; the outer frame keeps the lock held for the entire `process.wait(timeout=grace)`. `shutdown()` at lines 284-287 has exactly the same shape with `FULL_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_S = 120.0`. `start()` at 380-383 gets this right (it drops the lock before calling stop); these two do not.
findings.impact: Driver unticks quiet learning while a quiet child is running. In the native app, application.py:592-596 calls `self.controller.enable_learning(...)` directly on the Tk main thread from `_poll`, so the whole window hangs for up to `QUIET_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_S = 45.0` s and Windows paints it "Not Responding". In the Electron shell, api/server.py:537 serves `/api/learning` on an HTTP handler thread; the SSE thread's next `desktop_snapshot()` blocks on the same lock, so the UI freezes on stale state for the same 45 s and the shell's 15 s abandon timer (main.cjs:81) can fire first.
findings.fix: Snapshot what stop() needs under the lock, then release it before waiting — i.e. make both callers do what start() does: set the flags inside `with self._lock:`, then call `self.stop(...)` after the `with` block. Alternatively give stop() a private `_begin_stop()`/`_await_stop()` pair and forbid calling stop() from a lock-holding frame.
findings.verifier_notes: Code-true. controller.py:203 `self._lock = threading.RLock()`; enable_learning holds it at 216 and calls `self.stop(...)` at 220; shutdown holds it at 284 and calls stop at 287. stop()'s deliberate release (the `with self._lock:` block ends at 493, comment at 499 'The wait runs outside the lock so the desktop poll never blocks behind it') only drops the inner RLock acquisition, so `process.wait(timeout=grace)` at 503 runs with the outer frame still holding it. start() at 380-383 does it correctly by computing `replace` then leaving the block. Callers confirmed: application.py:593 on the Tk thread, api/server.py:537 on an HTTP handler thread with api/server.py:519 `self.host.desktop_snapshot()` blocking behind the same lock. Severity lowered: the grace values are ceilings, not durations — a healthy quiet child exits in seconds, so the realistic effect is a UI/API hang (worst case 45 s), not data loss or a crash. | Confirmed. controller.py:203 `self._lock = threading.RLock()`; enable_learning holds it at line 216 and calls `self.stop(continue_learning=False)` at 220; shutdown() does the same at 284-287. stop()'s `with self._lock:` at 471 is an inner re-acquisition, so the release before the comment at 499 ("The wait runs outside the lock so the desktop poll never blocks behind it") does not actually drop the lock - `process.wait(timeout=grace)` at 503 runs with the outer frame's acquisition still held. start() at 380-383 genuinely drops the lock first, confirming the intended discipline. Reachability confirmed: application.py:592-596 calls enable_learning on the Tk thread from _poll, and api/server.py:537 calls it on an HTTP handler thread. Grace constants verified at controller.py:32-33. Downgraded from critical: the realistic freeze is a second or two (the quiet child exits promptly on the stop file); the full 45 s/120 s only materialises on a wedged child. It is a UI/API hang, not data loss or a crash.

findings.title: _poll never reschedules itself if any exception escapes; the desktop silently stops updating
findings.why_wrong: `_poll` clears `self._poll_after_id = None` at line 478 and only re-arms the `after` timer at the very end (623-626). The only `try` in the method is `except queue.Empty` around the action drain (479-585); lines 586-622 — `enable_learning`, `ensure_learning`, `desktop_snapshot`, `view.update_runtime`, `_refresh_team_operations_summary` — are unguarded. Tk routes the escaping exception to `self.root.report_callback_exception = self.crash_reporter.handle_tk_exception` (line 141), and `handle_tk_exception` (crash_reporting.py:202-215) only writes a report and shows a dialog; it does not re-arm anything. The window stays open with a dead poll loop.
findings.impact: `desktop_snapshot()` -> `_status_from_health` sees the child has exited and calls `self._close_log(*self._detach_log())` (controller.py:347) -> `logger.stop()` (controller.py:583), which raises `RuntimeError("Structured logger did not stop within its timeout.")` (structured_log.py:306) whenever the log worker cannot drain in 10 s — e.g. a full disk makes `_write` fail and sleep 0.05 s per record (structured_log.py:355), so a full 1024-entry queue needs ~51 s. The RuntimeError kills the poll. From then on runtime status, health, learning text and the tray title are frozen forever while the engineer keeps running; the driver believes the state they see on screen.
findings.fix: Wrap the body of `_poll` in `try/finally` and re-arm the `after` callback in the `finally`, logging any exception. Separately, make `_close_log` swallow/report `RuntimeError` from `logger.stop()` instead of propagating it into a Tk callback.
findings.verifier_notes: Code-true and I confirmed there is no second re-arm site: `_poll_after_id` is only assigned at application.py:192 (initial), 478 (cleared) and 624 (the sole re-arm inside `if not self._closing:`), plus the cancel at 995-998. The `try` covers only 479-585 (`except queue.Empty` at 584); 586-622 (`enable_learning`, `ensure_learning`, `desktop_snapshot`, `view.update_runtime`, `_refresh_team_operations_summary`) are unguarded. crash_reporting.py:202-215 `handle_tk_exception` only calls `self.capture(...)` and `self.show_dialog(report)` — it re-arms nothing. The cited trigger is real: controller.py:347 `self._close_log(*self._detach_log())` → 583 `logger.stop()` → structured_log.py:305-306 `if thread.is_alive(): raise RuntimeError("Structured logger did not stop within its timeout.")`, and structured_log.py:350-355 `except OSError ... time.sleep(0.05)` per record. findings.title: Playback worker clears both interrupt flags after its generation check, so stale calls get spoken

with self._condition:
                    held = self._mode_suppression(item)

findings.title: stop() nulls the thread handles after a timed-out join, so wedged voice threads report as stopped
findings.why_wrong: The return of `join(timeout=...)` is not checked and `is_alive()` is never consulted; the handle is dropped unconditionally. Same pattern for the asyncio loop thread at lines 901-903, and `self._loop` is never cleared either. Everything downstream then believes the worker is gone: `start()` guards only on `if self._speech_thread is not None: return` (line 272), and `diagnostics()` reports `"tts_worker_running": bool(self._speech_thread is not None and self._speech_thread.is_alive())` (lines 847-849), which becomes False purely because the handle was nulled. Worse, `stop()` goes on to call `self.persistence.end_session(...)` and `self.persistence.close()` (lines 906-910) on a SQLite handle the still-live worker keeps using via `_ensure_persistence_session`/`update_turn`.
findings.impact: The playback worker is blocked in a gateway TTS `output.write(block)` on a wedged WASAPI endpoint and does not return within 5 s. `stop()` returns claiming success; `report_voice_health` reads `tts_worker_running: False` and reports `TTS_BACKEND_UNAVAILABLE` (supervision.py:395-403) even though audio is still being written to the device; and the leaked worker's next `persistence.update_turn` hits a closed connection. If the same orchestrator is ever restarted, `start()` spawns a second playback thread alongside the first and two radio calls play simultaneously.
findings.fix: Check the join: only null the handle when `not thread.is_alive()`. Otherwise keep it, mark the orchestrator state DEGRADED with an explicit reason code, refuse `start()` until the old thread exits, and skip `persistence.close()` (or fence it) while a worker is still referencing it.
