findings.title: Persisted projection evidence is keyed by a per-process UUID, so it is unreadable after restart
findings.quote: self._run_id = uuid.uuid4().hex
findings.why_wrong: `identity = f"{base_identity}:{self._run_id}:{self._epoch}"` (line 522) is what gets stored as `strategy_projection_runs.identity` (projections.py:185), and `_run_id` is a fresh uuid4 generated once per process while `_epoch` increments on every `invalidate()`. Every read path is identity-scoped: `get_digital_twin_runs(identity)` (projections.py:191-206), `get_lico_plan_runs`, `get_traffic_interception_runs` all require an exact `WHERE identity = ?` match. Once the process exits, that `_run_id` is gone and no caller can ever reconstruct the identity string, so the rows become permanently unreachable. The `idx_projection_identity_time` index on a near-unique column is likewise dead weight.
findings.impact: Strategy projections, traffic interception evidence and LICO plans — written continuously at 2-10 s intervals through the whole race with payloads up to 256 KB — are write-only. They occupy the database forever (nothing prunes them, see the retention finding) yet cannot be queried for post-race review or for the outcome-scoring the module docstring claims they enable ("Append-only bounded strategy inputs/results for replay and later outcome scoring", projections.py:1).
findings.fix: Store the stable `base_identity` in the `identity` column and put the ephemeral `run_id`/`epoch` in separate columns (or inside `payload_json`), so post-race queries can scope by track/session/car and optionally narrow by run. Keep the composite string only as the in-memory worker cache key where it is actually needed for invalidation.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed and, if anything, understated. strategy_projection_live.py:474 `self._run_id = uuid.uuid4().hex` is set once in __init__, and line 522 builds `identity = f"{base_identity}:{self._run_id}:{self._epoch}"`, which is what projections.py:185 stores as strategy_projection_runs.identity. Every reader is exact-match identity-scoped (projections.py:191-206 get_digital_twin_runs, :111 get_lico_plan_runs, :151 get_traffic_interception_runs, all `WHERE identity = ?`). I additionally grepped for callers of those three readers across src/ — there are none outside their own definitions, so the evidence is write-only even within a single process, not merely after restart. | Confirmed and stronger than claimed. strategy_projection_live.py:474 `self._run_id = uuid.uuid4().hex` is generated once per process and baked into `identity = f"{base_identity}:{self._run_id}:{self._epoch}"` (line 522), which is stored as strategy_projection_runs.identity (projections.py:185). Every reader requires an exact `WHERE identity = ?` (projections.py:201-203, and likewise get_lico_plan_runs:111, get_traffic_interception_runs:151), and the string cannot be reconstructed after the process exits. Additionally, `grep -rn 'get_digital_twin_runs|get_lico_plan_runs|get_traffic_interception_runs' src/` finds only the three definitions - there is not a single caller anywhere in the product, so this evidence is unambiguously write-only.

findings.title: engineer_replay stores an unbounded full telemetry snapshot per arbitration decision, duplicated per decision
findings.quote:
for decision in result.decisions:
            self._connection.execute(
                """
                INSERT INTO engineer_replay (
                    session_id, timestamp_utc, telemetry_json, context_json,
findings.why_wrong: `telemetry_json` and `context_json` are serialised once (lines 94-103) and then inserted once *per decision* in the loop — so N arbitration decisions produced in a single telemetry frame write N identical copies of the entire `RaceSnapshot` and `EngineerContext`. Unlike every other JSON-bearing table added in v9+ (which all carry `CHECK(length(CAST(payload_json AS BLOB)) <= 262144)`, schema.py:474, 484, 494, 504, 515...), `engineer_replay` has no size CHECK at all (schema.py:216-226). Decisions include suppressed outcomes — DUPLICATE_SUPPRESSED, COOLDOWN_SUPPRESSED, CALL_EXPIRED (referenced in replay.py:170-172) — so the rows are dominated by calls that were never even spoken.
findings.impact: `engineer_replay` is the fastest-growing table in the schema and the one with the least value per byte: in a 24 h race, every suppressed duplicate call persists a full copy of the car's entire telemetry state. Combined with the absent retention policy, this is the primary driver of database bloat, and `get_replay` (storage.py:413) deserialises those blobs for review.
findings.fix: Normalise: insert one `engineer_replay_frames` row per frame holding `telemetry_json`/`context_json` and have the per-decision rows reference it by id. Add the same `CHECK(length(CAST(telemetry_json AS BLOB)) <= 262144)` bound the newer tables use, and consider storing only the decision-relevant subset of the snapshot for suppressed outcomes.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed at src/ssc_engineer/persistence/calls.py:94-103 (telemetry_json and context_json serialised once) followed by `for decision in result.decisions:` at :104 with the INSERT INTO engineer_replay at :106-112 inside the loop — N decisions in one frame write N identical copies of both blobs. The CHECK asymmetry is real: the engineer_replay DDL (schema.py:216-226) has telemetry_json/context_json/event_json/call_json as bare `TEXT NOT NULL` with no length CHECK, while every v9+ JSON table (schema.py:474, 484, 494, 504, 515) carries `CHECK(length(CAST(payload_json AS BLOB)) <= 262144)`. Suppressed outcomes are indeed persisted — the loop is unconditional on decision.outcome. | Confirmed: persistence/calls.py:94-103 serialises telemetry_json and context_json once, then the `for decision in result.decisions:` loop at 105-130 inserts both blobs again for each decision, so N decisions in one frame write N identical full RaceSnapshot + EngineerContext copies. schema.py:216-226 shows engineer_replay carries no `CHECK(length(CAST(... AS BLOB)) <= 262144)` unlike the v9+ payload tables (schema.py:474, 484, 494, 504, 515). Suppressed outcomes are persisted too - the loop is unconditional, and replay.py:170-172 aggregates DUPLICATE_SUPPRESSED/COOLDOWN_SUPPRESSED/EXPIRED from those rows. With no retention path anywhere (see finding 10) this is unbounded.

findings.title: Acknowledgement UPDATE cannot use the engineer_calls index and is not scoped to a session
findings.quote:
UPDATE engineer_calls
                SET status = ?, acknowledged_utc = ?
                WHERE call_id = ?
findings.why_wrong: The only index covering `call_id` is `UNIQUE(session_id, call_id)` (schema.py:213). SQLite cannot use a composite index without its leading column, so `WHERE call_id = ?` degrades to a full scan of `engineer_calls` — a table that is never pruned. The predicate is also not scoped by `session_id` even though the uniqueness constraint is per-session, so the statement's contract silently assumes `call_id` is globally unique; it is a 20-hex-char truncated sha256 (arbitration.py:283), which happens to include the event timestamp and therefore does not collide in practice, but the query is written against an invariant the schema does not guarantee.
findings.impact: Every push-to-talk acknowledgement scans the whole call history on the voice thread while the DatabaseWriter holds an open transaction on a different connection to the same file. After a season of racing that is hundreds of thousands of rows scanned per acknowledgement, adding latency to exactly the interaction that must feel instant.
findings.fix: Add `CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_calls_call_id ON engineer_calls(call_id);` to `_SCHEMA`, and scope the UPDATE with `WHERE session_id = ? AND call_id = ?` using the voice session's `engineering_session_id` so it matches the table's actual uniqueness contract.
findings.verifier_notes: Code confirmed at voice/persistence.py:394-399 — `UPDATE engineer_calls SET status = ?, acknowledged_utc = ? WHERE call_id = ?`. I grepped every call_id reference in schema.py: engineer_calls has `call_id TEXT NOT NULL` (195) and `UNIQUE(session_id, call_id)` (213), plus idx_calls_session on (session_id, timestamp_utc) — nothing leads with call_id, so SQLite must scan. Correcting severity: the finder concedes the collision risk is theoretical (call_id is a timestamp-bearing sha256 prefix), so the whole impact is a full scan of one modestly-sized table on a user-initiated action, which is a low, not a medium. | Confirmed and reachable: voice/persistence.py:390-402 runs `UPDATE engineer_calls SET status=?, acknowledged_utc=? WHERE call_id=?`, wired into production at voice/runtime.py:80 as acknowledgement_sink. The only call_id-bearing index is `UNIQUE(session_id, call_id)` (schema.py:213) plus idx_calls_session on (session_id, timestamp_utc), so with no leading session_id the statement scans engineer_calls. Severity corrected to low: the row count reached in practice makes this a sub-100 ms scan, and the unscoped-predicate concern is theoretical - call_id is a truncated sha256 that embeds the event timestamp, so the cross-session collision the finding itself calls out as not occurring in practice remains hypothetical.

findings.title: Scheduled and manual backups run against a live writer with no runtime guard and no timeout
findings.quote:
source = self._connect_read_only()
            target = sqlite3.connect(str(temporary), timeout=10.0)
            source.backup(target, pages=256, sleep=0.05)
findings.why_wrong: `compact_database` (line 834) and `delete_personal_data` (line 792) both take a `runtime_active` flag and refuse when the engineer is running; `create_verified_backup` takes no such guard. It is reachable both from the manual button (ui/storage_management.py:288-292 wires `service.create_verified_backup` with no guard, in contrast to line 427 which passes `runtime_active=self.controller.status().running` for compaction) and from `run_scheduled_backup` at UI startup (ui/application.py:193). SQLite's online-backup API restarts the copy from the beginning whenever the source database is modified by another connection — and the runtime child process commits roughly once per second (writer.py:232 `commit_interval_s: float = 1.0`). With `pages=256, sleep=0.05` the copy advances about 1 MB per 50 ms, so it makes ~20 MB of progress per commit interval before restarting. There is no iteration cap and no deadline.
findings.impact: A user presses "Create verified backup" during a race on a database larger than roughly 20 MB and the background thread loops indefinitely, never completing and never reporting an error, holding a read connection open (which also blocks WAL checkpointing). The UI shows "Creating and verifying database backup…" forever.
findings.fix: Give `create_verified_backup` the same `runtime_active: bool` parameter as `compact_database` and refuse when the engineer is running; pass `self.controller.status().running` at ui/storage_management.py:291 exactly as line 427 already does for compaction. If live backups must be supported, add a wall-clock deadline around the `backup()` call and surface a clear "database too busy" error instead of spinning.
findings.verifier_notes: The guard asymmetry is real and correctly cited: compact_database (storage_management.py:834) and delete_personal_data (:792) both open with `if runtime_active: raise`, create_verified_backup takes no such parameter, and ui/storage_management.py:288-292 wires it with no guard while :427 passes `runtime_active=self.controller.status().running` for compaction. There is no deadline or iteration cap around storage_management.py:605. But the quantitative reasoning is wrong and I am correcting it: CPython's Connection.backup only sleeps on SQLITE_BUSY/SQLITE_LOCKED, not between successful steps, so `sleep=0.05` does not throttle progress to ~1 MB/50 ms. I measured the exact call on a 61.6 MB WAL database: `source.backup(target, pages=256, sleep=0.05)` completed in 0.111 s, about 550 MB/s. With the writer committing once per second (writer.py commit_interval_s=1.0), a realistic database finishes well inside one commit interval, so the claim that anything over ~20 MB "loops indefinitely" and hangs the UI forever is false. What survives is the missing runtime guard and missing deadline — a low. | The asymmetry is real: compact_database (storage_management.py:834) and delete_personal_data (:792) both take and enforce runtime_active, create_verified_backup (:588) does not, and ui/storage_management.py:287-292 wires the manual button with no guard while :427 passes runtime_active=self.controller.status().running for compaction; ui/application.py:193 also runs it at startup via _refresh_storage_summary(scheduled_backup=True). There is no iteration cap or deadline around `source.backup(target, pages=256, sleep=0.05)`. But the impact analysis is wrong by more than an order of magnitude, so I am downgrading rather than confirming as stated: CPython only sleeps on SQLITE_BUSY/LOCKED, never between successful backup_step calls. I measured a 123 MB database copied in 118 steps in 0.24 s with exactly these parameters - roughly 500 MB/s, not the claimed ~20 MB per commit interval. With the runtime committing once per second (writer.py:232) a database would need to be several hundred MB before restart-on-write could outrun the copy, so 'larger than roughly 20 MB loops indefinitely' does not hold.

findings.title: JSONL calibration import runs the whole file in one uncommitted transaction
findings.quote:
outcome = database.import_completed_lap_payload(
                payload,
                source_uid=digest.hexdigest(),
            )
findings.why_wrong: `import_completed_lap_payload` never commits (it ends at calibration.py:313 with a bare `return "accepted"`), and the loop at calibration.py:720-742 iterates the entire file before the single `finalize_calibration_import` call at line 755 issues `self._connection.commit()` (calibration.py:410). Every lap's session/stint/lap/lap_conditions/tyre_data/tyre_calibration_samples/fuel_data inserts therefore accumulate in one open transaction for the whole file. The function also relies on bare `assert` statements for database invariants (calibration.py:133 `assert session_row is not None`, line 156), which are stripped when Python runs under `-O`.
findings.impact: Importing a large recorder capture builds an arbitrarily large WAL before any commit, and any unexpected exception inside the loop — an IntegrityError, a bad row, a disk-full — discards the entire import with no partial progress and leaves the transaction open on a shared connection. `import_jsonl_directory` (calibration.py:766-775) additionally re-runs the whole-database baseline rebuild once per file.
findings.fix: Commit in batches (e.g. every 500 accepted laps) inside `import_jsonl_completed_laps`, and wrap each record in a SAVEPOINT so one malformed payload is counted as rejected rather than aborting the import — the same pattern `_store_lap` already uses for optional evidence (records.py:140-151). Replace the asserts with explicit raises. Hoist `finalize_calibration_import` out of the per-file loop in `import_jsonl_directory`.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed. import_completed_lap_payload ends at persistence/calibration.py:313 with a bare `return "accepted"` and a grep for commit() in that file shows only lines 410 and 585 — nothing inside the per-lap path. The loop at calibration.py:715-741 iterates the whole file calling it (the cited line 733 is `outcome = database.import_completed_lap_payload(`), and the single finalize_calibration_import at :755 reaches the commit at persistence/calibration.py:410. The bare asserts are real — `assert session_row is not None` and `assert stint_row is not None` — with one cite correction that does not affect the finding: they are at persistence/calibration.py:133 and :156, not src/ssc_engineer/calibration.py:133/156 as the prose implies. import_jsonl_directory (calibration.py:766-775) does re-run the whole-database baseline rebuild once per file. | Confirmed: persistence/calibration.py:313 ends import_completed_lap_payload with a bare `return "accepted"` and no commit, the loop at calibration.py:718-742 iterates the whole file, and only finalize_calibration_import commits (persistence/calibration.py:410). The bare asserts are there as cited (persistence/calibration.py:133 `assert session_row is not None`, :156 `assert stint_row is not None`). Severity corrected to low: whole-file atomicity is a defensible design choice rather than a defect, the connection is per-CLI-instance so a left-open transaction is rolled back at close, and the concrete cost is WAL growth proportional to one capture file plus the redundant per-file baseline rebuild - which is already the substance of finding 5.

findings.title: save_race_plan and save_policy claim atomic persistence but never fsync
findings.quote:
temporary.write_text(
            json.dumps(payload, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False, sort_keys=False) + "\n",
            encoding="utf-8",
        )
        temporary.replace(selected)
findings.why_wrong: The module docstring promises "Strict race-plan JSON parsing, atomic persistence, and human approval" (race_plan_io.py:1). `write_text` closes the handle but issues no `os.fsync` on the file descriptor, and there is no fsync of the containing directory after `replace`. `Path.replace` maps to `MoveFileEx(..., MOVEFILE_REPLACE_EXISTING)` on Windows, which is atomic in the directory namespace but says nothing about the new file's data having reached disk. `StorageManagementService.save_policy` (storage_management.py:338-349) has the identical pattern. The temp name also uses `os.getpid()` as its only uniquifier, so two concurrent saves from one process collide — note `save_policy` uses `uuid4().hex` for exactly this reason, an inconsistency between the two.
findings.impact: A power loss or hard reset shortly after approving a race plan can leave a zero-length or truncated plan file where a valid one used to be — `load_race_plan` then raises RacePlanError on the JSON decode and the approved strategy for the event is gone. The same applies to storage-policy.json, whose loader treats any parse failure as a hard `StorageManagementError` (storage_management.py:220-227).
findings.fix: Open the temp file explicitly, `write()`, `flush()`, `os.fsync(handle.fileno())`, close, then `replace`, then open the parent directory and fsync it where the platform supports it. Switch the temp suffix to `uuid4().hex` to match save_policy.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed at race_plan_io.py:294-299: `temporary.write_text(...)` then `temporary.replace(selected)` with no os.fsync of the file descriptor and none of the parent directory; the module docstring at race_plan_io.py:1 does promise "atomic persistence". The identical pattern is at storage_management.py:340-345, and the uniquifier inconsistency is real — race_plan_io.py:292 uses `f".{selected.name}.{os.getpid()}.tmp"` while storage_management.py:338-340 uses `uuid.uuid4().hex`. The loader's hard-failure behaviour also checks out (storage_management.py:215-222 raises StorageManagementError on any JSON decode error). Correcting severity: rename-without-fsync is a genuine durability gap but requires an unclean power loss inside a narrow window, so low rather than medium. | Confirmed: race_plan_io.py:292-301 writes via `temporary.write_text(...)` then `temporary.replace(selected)` with no os.fsync on the file descriptor and none on the containing directory, under a module docstring promising 'atomic persistence'; storage_management.py:338-349 repeats the pattern, and the temp-name inconsistency is real (os.getpid() at race_plan_io.py:292 vs uuid4().hex at storage_management.py:338). Severity corrected to low: the pid-collision half is not reachable in practice (saves are issued from a single UI action path, not concurrently), and the durability half requires a power loss inside a millisecond-scale window between rename and writeback.

findings.title: Lap-time standard deviation uses the population formula and reports 0.0 from a single lap
findings.why_wrong: `lap_time_m2` is accumulated by Welford's algorithm in `_update_profile_row` (profiles.py:141-144), where M2 is the sum of squared deviations. Dividing by `count` gives the *population* variance; the sample variance needs `count - 1`. More damagingly, the guard is `count > 0` rather than `count > 1`, so a profile built from exactly one clean lap has `lap_time_m2 = 0.0` (set explicitly on line 139) and yields `stddev = 0.0` — reported not as "unknown" but as a hard zero. The confidence label computed alongside it does distinguish this case (`_profile_confidence` returns "LOW" for 1 lap, profiles.py:329-330), but the stddev value itself is emitted as a real number with no qualification.
findings.impact: `DriverConditionProfile.lap_time_stddev_s` is the driver-consistency figure the engineering pipeline reads. After a single clean lap in a new condition — the normal state early in a wet session or at a new track — the profile reports perfect consistency (0.000 s spread), which is the strongest possible signal in the wrong direction for any pace or stint-length reasoning that keys off variance.
findings.fix: Use `count > 1` as the guard and divide by `count - 1` for the sample standard deviation, returning `None` for a single sample so downstream code treats it as unavailable rather than as zero spread.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed at persistence/profiles.py:338-340: `math.sqrt(max(0.0, float(row["lap_time_m2"] or 0.0) / count)) if count > 0 else None` — divides M2 by count (population) and guards on count > 0 rather than count > 1. The Welford accumulation is as described at profiles.py:136-144, where the first lap explicitly sets `lap_m2 = 0.0`, so a one-lap profile emits a hard 0.0 rather than None. _profile_confidence (profiles.py:324-331) does return "LOW" for one lap, but that is a separate field and does not qualify the stddev value itself. | Confirmed: profiles.py:338-340 is `math.sqrt(max(0.0, float(row['lap_time_m2'] or 0.0) / count)) if count > 0 else None` - divided by count (population, not sample) and guarded on count > 0, while profiles.py:137-139 explicitly sets lap_m2 = 0.0 for the first lap, so a one-lap profile emits a hard 0.0 rather than None. The value does reach a consumer: it is set on DriverConditionProfile (profiles.py:354), which is a Serializable carried as matching_base/matching_detail (communication/contracts.py:118-119) and returned wholesale to the voice engineer via `context.driver_profile.to_dict()` at voice/tool_history.py:222 (get_driver_profile / get_best_matching_baseline, registered in voice/tools.py:270-276). So the AI engineer is handed 0.000 s spread as a fact after one clean lap in a new condition. The finding's phrasing that 'the engineering pipeline reads' it overstates it slightly - no deterministic module computes on the field - but the tool-surface exposure is real.

findings.title: Personal-data export embeds every previous backup and archive of the same database
findings.quote: _PERSONAL_AREA_NAMES = ("config", "data", "logs", "reports", "cache")
findings.why_wrong: `_personal_roots` returns `root/data` as an export area and `_personal_files` (lines 266-303) walks it recursively, excluding only the live database and its -wal/-shm (lines 267-271). But `backup_directory = self.data_directory / "backups"` and `archive_directory = self.data_directory / "archives"` (lines 247-248) live inside that same `data` directory, so every historical `ssc-engineering-backup-*.db` and every previously exported archive .zip is enumerated and deflated into the export — on top of the fresh verified backup the method takes at line 745.
findings.impact: A user who has been running the weekly scheduled backup for a year and then requests a GDPR-style personal-data export gets an archive containing 52 full copies of the engineering database plus any prior archives, each of which itself contains a full database copy. The export is orders of magnitude larger than the data it is supposed to represent and can exhaust the destination disk.
findings.fix: Exclude `self.backup_directory` and `self.archive_directory` from the `_personal_files` walk (they are derived copies, not distinct personal data), and note their existence and count in manifest.json instead. The README text at lines 771-774 should be updated to match, since it currently advertises that backups and archives are included.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed. _PERSONAL_AREA_NAMES at storage_management.py:24 includes "data", _personal_roots (247-259) returns root/data as an export area, and _personal_files (261-303) walks each area recursively with an excluded set (263-267) containing only the live database and its -wal/-shm. backup_directory and archive_directory are defined at storage_management.py:246-247 as `self.data_directory / "backups"` and `/ "archives"`, i.e. inside that same walked tree, so every historical backup .db and prior archive .zip is enumerated. export_personal_data additionally takes a fresh verified backup and appends it as a source at :744-746. | Confirmed: _PERSONAL_AREA_NAMES includes 'data' (storage_management.py:24), _personal_roots returns root/'data' (:252-264), and _personal_files (:266-303) walks each area recursively excluding only {database_path, -wal, -shm} (:267-271). backup_directory and archive_directory are self.data_directory/'backups' and /'archives' (:247-248), i.e. inside that same walked tree, so every ssc-engineering-backup-*.db and every prior export .zip is enumerated and deflated - on top of the fresh snapshot the export takes at :745. Only the 50,000-file _DIRECTORY_ENTRY_LIMIT bounds it, and full database copies are few and large, so that limit does not help.

findings.title: ensure_column silently depends on row_factory being sqlite3.Row and crashes without it
findings.quote: columns = {str(row["name"]) for row in connection.execute(f"PRAGMA table_info({table})")}
findings.why_wrong: `migrate_schema` is a module-level entry point exported in `__all__` (migrations.py:307) and takes a bare `sqlite3.Connection`, but subscripting a PRAGMA result row by name requires `connection.row_factory = sqlite3.Row`. With the default tuple factory it raises `TypeError: tuple indices must be integers or slices, not str` — I hit exactly this when driving `migrate_schema` from a plain connection. The identical PRAGMA is read positionally in `StorageManagementService._column_names` (storage_management.py:379: `str(row[1])`), so the codebase already contains both conventions.
findings.impact: Any future caller, tool or test that opens the database without setting `row_factory` — the natural default — gets a TypeError from inside the migration rather than a working migration, and the failure points at a set comprehension rather than at the missing precondition. Today only `EngineeringDatabase.__init__` calls it (storage.py:104 sets the factory just in time), so it is latent rather than live.
findings.fix: Index the PRAGMA result positionally (`row[1]` is the column name) so `ensure_column` works on any connection, matching storage_management.py:379. Alternatively assert the precondition explicitly at the top of `migrate_schema`.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed at persistence/migrations.py:16: `columns = {str(row["name"]) for row in connection.execute(f"PRAGMA table_info({table})")}` — name-subscripting a result row requires row_factory = sqlite3.Row, which the function neither sets nor documents, while migrate_schema is exported in __all__ (migrations.py:307) and typed to take a bare sqlite3.Connection. The inconsistency cite holds: storage_management.py:379 reads the same PRAGMA positionally as `str(row[1])`. The finder correctly labels this latent — storage.py:104 sets the factory before the only current call site — so low is right. | No failure is constructible in this product. migrations.py:16 does subscript the PRAGMA row by name, but the only caller anywhere is storage.py:117, and storage.py:105 sets `self._connection.row_factory = sqlite3.Row` twelve lines earlier on the very connection it passes; `grep -rn 'migrate_schema' src/` returns only the definition, the storage.py import/call, and a literal string in cli.py:400's import-manifest list. The described victim is 'any future caller, tool or test' - a hypothetical actor, not a path that exists - and the finding concedes it is latent. Under an exploit-or-repro standard this is a style preference about which PRAGMA-reading convention the codebase should settle on, not a defect.

findings.title: Duplicate laps keep the old lap row but have all their child evidence overwritten
findings.quote:
INSERT OR IGNORE INTO laps (
                session_id, stint_id, stint_number, lap_number, completed_utc,
findings.why_wrong: `_store_lap` resolves a conflict on `UNIQUE(session_id, stint_number, lap_number)` with OR IGNORE — keep the existing row — and then re-reads the existing `lap_id` (lines 130-139). But every child write for that same lap uses the opposite policy: `INSERT OR REPLACE INTO lap_conditions` (line 214), `INSERT OR REPLACE INTO tyre_data` (line 247), `INSERT OR REPLACE INTO tyre_calibration_samples` (line 283), `INSERT OR REPLACE INTO fuel_data` (line 310). The parent keeps the first observation while all of its evidence is replaced by the second. The import path has the same split (calibration.py:159 OR IGNORE for laps, lines 233/260/308 OR REPLACE for children).
findings.impact: If the same (session, stint, lap) tuple is ever observed twice with different data — a lap-counter reset, a stint restart, or a re-import of overlapping JSONL — the stored lap keeps lap A's time, fuel and clean flag while its tyre wear, temperatures, conditions and calibration sample all describe lap B. The row looks internally consistent but mixes two laps, and the calibration sample derived from it is attributed to the wrong lap time via `pace_delta_s`.
findings.fix: Pick one policy and apply it to the whole entity. Either use OR REPLACE for `laps` too (last observation wins throughout), or detect the ignored insert via `lap_cursor.rowcount == 0` and skip the child writes entirely, logging the duplicate — the rowcount is already captured on line 108 and used for the baseline guard on line 375.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed by grepping every conflict clause in persistence/records.py: line 110 `INSERT OR IGNORE INTO laps`, then 214 `INSERT OR REPLACE INTO lap_conditions`, 247 `INSERT OR REPLACE INTO tyre_data`, 283 `INSERT OR REPLACE INTO tyre_calibration_samples`, 310 `INSERT OR REPLACE INTO fuel_data` — the parent keeps the first observation while all children are replaced by the second. records.py:130-139 does re-read the surviving lap_id, confirming the second observation proceeds against the first row. The import path mirrors the split (persistence/calibration.py:159 OR IGNORE for laps, :233/:260/:308 OR REPLACE for children). | The import half of the claim is factually wrong and the live half has no reachable trigger. In the import path, persistence/calibration.py:179-181 is `if cursor.rowcount <= 0: return "duplicate"` immediately after the INSERT OR IGNORE INTO laps - the function returns before reaching any of the OR REPLACE child writes at :233/:260/:308, so a re-imported overlapping JSONL never overwrites a kept lap's evidence. In the live path the mix requires the same (session_id, stint_number, lap_number) to be observed twice with different data inside one session row, and I could not construct that: storage.py:353-379 _ensure_session ends the session and calls _begin_session (new session_uid, new id) on either an identity change or `snapshot.session_elapsed_s + 1.0 < self._last_observed_elapsed_s`, so a race restart or lap-counter reset produces a fresh session_id and the UNIQUE(session_id, stint_number, lap_number) constraint is not hit; a re-delivered identical frame writes identical children. The finding's own wording ('If the same tuple is ever observed twice') concedes the trigger is hypothetical.

findings.title: counts() performs 28 unbounded COUNT(*) full scans on the writer connection
findings.quote:
table: int(self._connection.execute(f"SELECT COUNT(*) FROM {table}").fetchone()[0])
            for table in tables
findings.why_wrong: The comprehension issues an unqualified `COUNT(*)` against each of the 28 tables listed on lines 578-607. SQLite has no cached row count, so each is a full scan of the table or its smallest index. The method also does not acquire `self._access_lock`, unlike `owned_completed_session_ids` immediately below it (line 623), even though `access_lock`'s own docstring says it exists to "Serialize the writer connection with infrequent cached reads" (line 145). The table names are interpolated, but from a hardcoded literal tuple, so there is no injection exposure.
findings.impact: A diagnostics call scans the entire database — including `engineer_replay`, `laps`, `tyre_calibration_samples` and `prediction_records`, none of which are ever pruned — on the shared writer connection. On a multi-season database this is seconds of I/O that can interleave with the writer's own statements on the same connection object.
findings.fix: Take `self._access_lock` around the loop for consistency with the other accessors, and either accept an approximate count or bound the expensive tables (`COUNT(*)` over `sqlite_stat1`, or `SELECT MAX(rowid)` where a row count is only needed for scale). Move the call off the writer connection onto a short-lived read-only one, as `StorageManagementService.inventory` already does.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed at storage.py:577-612: a literal tuple of 28 table names followed by `{table: int(self._connection.execute(f"SELECT COUNT(*) FROM {table}").fetchone()[0]) for table in tables}` at line 610, with no `with self._access_lock:` — in direct contrast to owned_completed_session_ids immediately below at line 623 which does acquire it. The injection note is also correct: the names come from a hardcoded tuple. The unpruned-table premise is independently confirmed by the zero-hit `DELETE FROM` grep. | The stated impact - 'a diagnostics call scans the entire database ... on the shared writer connection' - has no production path. `grep -rn 'counts()' . --include=*.py` outside .venv returns hits only under tests/ (tests/persistence/test_storage.py, test_persistence_writer.py, test_replay_review_v05.py, tests/voice/, tests/engineering/); nothing in src/ calls EngineeringDatabase.counts, and no UI, CLI, API or voice surface exposes it. It is a test-only assertion helper running against small in-memory or temp databases, where the missing _access_lock and the unqualified COUNT(*)s cost nothing and race with no concurrent writer. The table tuple at storage.py:579-607 also lists 29 tables, not 28.

findings.title: Mandatory pit-stop call only fires when ≤1 lap remains to the finish
findings.why_wrong: This is the only place in the codebase that produces a mandatory-stop recommendation (`grep` for STRATEGY_MANDATORY_STOP_THIS_LAP / required_stops_remaining confirms `strategy_recommendations.py:56` is the sole producer). It is gated on `laps_to_finish <= 1.0`, i.e. it only raises the call once the car is on its final lap. A mandatory stop served on the final lap cannot be recovered from: the car loses the pit-lane delta plus stationary time (the project's own default green pit loss is 45 s, `config.py:85`) with no racing laps left to recover, and in a timed race it will still be in the pit lane when the flag falls. The call needs to be raised with enough remaining distance to serve the stop, not as a terminal alarm.
findings.impact: 6h race, `strategy_required_pit_stops = 2`, driver has made 1 stop. For the whole race the engine returns STAY_OUT (because `finish_safe` at line 92 requires `required_stops_remaining == 0`, so it falls through to NO_DOMINANT_SCENARIO). The first and only "box, mandatory stop outstanding" call arrives when `laps_to_finish` drops to 1.0 — on the last lap. The car boxes, serves a ~45 s stop, and either finishes a lap down or is classified as not having completed the distance. The team loses the result to a rule it configured into the app.
findings.fix: Gate the call on the remaining distance actually needed to serve the stop, not on the final lap: raise it once `laps_to_finish <= required_stops_remaining * (planned_stint_laps) + margin`, and escalate through advisory → warning → critical as that margin shrinks. At minimum add a separate early advisory (e.g. when `laps_to_finish` falls below two stint lengths) so the stop is never first mentioned on the last lap.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified: strategy_recommendations.py:56 reads exactly `if required_stops_remaining > 0 and laps_to_finish is not None and laps_to_finish <= 1.0:`, and grep confirms required_stops_remaining is consumed only here (strategy_recommendations.py:28/56/92). So the only mandatory-stop recommendation is a terminal, final-lap alarm. Two corrections that lower severity: (a) the impact text is self-contradicting — it says 'the engine returns STAY_OUT' and then correctly explains that finish_safe at line 92 requires required_stops_remaining == 0, so the engine does NOT emit STAY OUT while a stop is owed; it falls through to no dominant scenario. The app therefore fails to raise a timely call rather than actively advising a wrong one. (b) Another surface does flag it: strategy_projection.py:242 `rejected.append("Mandatory stops are not fulfilled")`. The event code itself is STRATEGY_MANDATORY_STOP_THIS_LAP (strategy_evaluation.py:337), i.e. this is written as a last-chance backstop, not the planner. Real defect (a backstop that fires too late to be served), but not data-loss/wrong-number class. | Confirmed by reading src/ssc_engineer/strategy_recommendations.py:56 — the only branch keyed on `required_stops_remaining > 0` is additionally gated on `laps_to_finish <= 1.0`, and strategy_evaluation.py:328-333 is its sole caller (grep confirms no other producer of the mandatory-stop path; the STRATEGY_MANDATORY_STOP_THIS_LAP code at strategy_evaluation.py:337 is derived from this rationale string). finish_safe at line 92 does require `required_stops_remaining == 0`, so while a stop is owed the engine falls through to NO_DOMINANT_SCENARIO. A last-lap PIT_NOW with `automatic_call_authorized=not pit_lane_closed` is genuinely reachable and useless. Severity lowered from critical: the stated impact (6h race, 1 stop made) is not constructible — `snapshot.pitstops` counts every stop, and a 6h LMU race forces ~6 fuel stops, so a default-config car satisfies 2 required stops long before the end. The reachable repro is narrower: a sprint/short race (or a stint-length-limited car) where `strategy_required_pit_stops` exceeds the fuel-driven stop count, which does produce the terminal alarm.

findings.title: Timed-race laps_to_finish uses own clock, not the leader's flag — off by one full lap
findings.quote:
distance_until_clock = snapshot.session_time_remaining_s / pace_s
finish_crossing = math.ceil(progress + distance_until_clock - 1e-9)
candidates.append(max(0.0, finish_crossing - progress))
findings.why_wrong: In WEC/LMU a timed race ends at the *leader's* first line crossing at or after the clock expires; every other car then takes the flag at its own next crossing. This function computes the player's own first crossing after its own clock expiry, with no reference to the leader at all. Whenever the player crosses the line after clock zero but *before* the leader has taken the flag — the normal case for anyone behind the leader on the road, and universal for lapped cars in a multi-class field — the real requirement is one full lap more than this returns. The developers clearly knew this: `strategy_projection_live.py:253-285` goes to considerable trouble to derive `finish_clock` from the observed leader's position and pace, but that leader-aware clock is never fed back into `_laps_to_finish`, which is the value the whole fuel/VE model runs on (`engineering/models.py:121-123`, `engineering/fuel.py:51-56`).
findings.impact: 24h Le Mans, LMGT3 car one lap down, 4.3 L/lap. Clock hits zero while the car is at `lap_progress = 0.10`; the Hypercar leader is at 0.60 and will not cross for another ~90 s. `laps_to_finish` returns 0.90, so `required_to_finish_l` = 0.90*4.3 + reserve. `strategy_recommendations.finish_safe` (line 81) is satisfied and the app says "STAY OUT TO FINISH". The car crosses the line without the flag, has to run a full extra lap, and needs ~4.3 L more than modelled against a reserve of 0.5 laps + 2σ ≈ 2.4 L. The car runs dry on the last lap.
findings.fix: Pass the leader-derived checkered clock (the value `strategy_projection_live.py:275-280` already computes) into `_laps_to_finish`, and compute the crossing against `max(own_clock, leader_flag_clock)`. When the leader's position/pace is unavailable, add one conservative lap rather than assuming the player's own clock, since the error is always in the run-out-of-fuel direction.
findings.verifier_notes: Code verified: engineering/pace.py:35-36 `distance_until_clock = snapshot.session_time_remaining_s / pace_s` / `finish_crossing = math.ceil(progress + distance_until_clock - 1e-9)`, with no leader term anywhere in _laps_to_finish (signature is `(self, snapshot, pace_s)`). The leader-aware clock at strategy_projection_live.py:253-285 is real and is indeed never fed back. The defect is genuine and one-sided: the function can only ever be correct or one lap short, never long. BUT the worked impact example is backwards. With player at lap_progress 0.10 and the leader at 0.60, the leader is FURTHER along the lap and crosses the line first, takes the flag first, and the player's own next crossing is after the flag — the code is right in exactly the case cited. The undercount occurs only when the player is AHEAD of the leader on the road at clock expiry (player fraction > leader fraction), which is roughly half of configurations, not 'universal for lapped cars'. Confirmed as a modelling gap, with the cited scenario and 'normal case' framing refuted. | Confirmed. engineering/pace.py:34-37 computes `distance_until_clock = session_time_remaining_s / pace_s` then `finish_crossing = math.ceil(progress + distance_until_clock - 1e-9)` with no leader term, and engineering/models.py:121-123 feeds that value straight into `_fuel_model(snapshot, laps_to_finish)` / `_ve_model(...)`, where fuel.py:51-54 turns it into `required_to_finish_l`. The repro is concrete and common: whenever the player's lap_progress at clock expiry exceeds the leader's, the player crosses the line before the leader takes the flag and must run one more lap; the model returns exactly one lap too few. The team's own code shows they know the rule — strategy_projection_live.py:260-280 derives `finish_clock` from the observed leader (`first_crossing = (1 - leader.lap_distance_m / track_length_m) * leader_pace`, then rounds up in leader laps) with the caveat string "no extra timed lap" — and that leader-aware clock is never passed back into `_laps_to_finish`. Under-stating the finish distance by a full lap against a reserve of 0.5 laps + 2σ is a wrong race-critical number.

findings.title: Self-referential plausibility filter permanently locks out pace, fuel and VE evidence
findings.quote:
if len(history) < 3:
        return True
    center = median(history)
    return center * 0.65 <= value <= center * 1.35
findings.why_wrong: `_reasonable_sample` accepts a sample only if it is within ±35% of the median of `history`. For lap times the history passed in is `self._session_lap_samples` (`stint.py:324-329`), and that deque is appended to *only inside the branch that the same test guards* (`stint.py:334`). The acceptance band is therefore computed from a population that only accepted samples can join, so it can never track a sustained regime change larger than ±35% — it is a closed loop. Worse, the lap-time verdict also gates the fuel and VE samples: lines 338-363 (`self._fuel_samples.append(...)`, `self._ve_samples.append(...)`) sit inside the same `else: clean = True` block, so one rejected lap time discards that lap's consumption evidence too. The same self-referential structure is repeated for `_session_fuel_samples` (stint.py:340-348) and `_session_ve_samples` (stint.py:353-361).
findings.impact: Heavy rain arrives at Le Mans: lap times step from 3:30 to 4:45 (+36%). Every subsequent lap fails `center * 0.65 <= value <= center * 1.35`, so it is marked "IMPLAUSIBLE PACE SAMPLE", never enters `_session_lap_samples`, and the median never moves. From that moment the pace model, the fuel rate and the VE rate are frozen on dry-weather values for the rest of the race, while `_fuel_model` keeps publishing `estimated_per_lap_l`, `laps_to_finish` and `margin_to_finish_l` as if nothing had changed. The same lock-out hits fuel directly: a driver put on a 40% fuel-save programme has every saved lap rejected, so `saving_required_l_per_lap` never falls and the engineer keeps demanding saving that is already being delivered.
findings.fix: Break the loop: keep an unfiltered rolling history for the band and filter only what is *published*, or widen/re-seed the band when N consecutive samples are rejected in the same direction (a sustained one-sided rejection run is evidence of a regime change, not of bad data). Separately, decouple the fuel/VE sample capture from the lap-time verdict — consumption over a slow-but-valid lap is real consumption.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified exactly: engineering/lap.py:35-38 `if len(history) < 3: return True` / `center = median(history)` / `return center * 0.65 <= value <= center * 1.35`, and engineering/stint.py:323-334 shows the accepted sample is appended to `self._session_lap_samples` only inside the `else: clean = True` branch that the same test guards — a closed loop with no reset path (deques are created once in engineering/session.py:46-51). The coupling claim is also exactly right and is the strongest part: the fuel test (stint.py:340-348) and VE test (stint.py:353-361) sit inside that same `clean = True` block, so one rejected lap time silently discards that lap's consumption evidence. Severity lowered because the lock-out needs a sustained STEP larger than ±35%: a gradual regime change is absorbed as the rolling median drifts, and the band does legitimate work rejecting FCY/SC laps (which `lap_excluded` at stint.py:301-307 does not catch, since it only covers invalid/pit/new-stint). | Structurally confirmed. engineering/lap.py:34-38 accepts only `center * 0.65 <= value <= center * 1.35` where `center = median(history)`, and engineering/stint.py:323-334 passes `self._session_lap_samples` as that history while appending to the same deque only inside the `else: clean = True` branch the test guards — a closed loop; a sustained >35% step can never be re-entered because no new sample can move the median (the deque has maxlen but nothing new enters it). The cascade is also real: the fuel append (stint.py:338-347) and VE append (stint.py:351-362) are nested inside that same `else`, so a rejected lap time discards that lap's consumption evidence. Severity lowered from critical: the filter is doing useful work for the common confounds (FCY/SC laps are ~+60-100% and correctly rejected), and the lock-out needs a sustained regime change beyond ±35%. The stated 40%-fuel-save repro is not realistic (endurance lift-and-coast is single-digit percent); the realistic repro is a torrential-rain step at a long circuit, which is a tail case but does occur in the 24h races this app targets.

findings.title: Virtual Energy reserve is silently discarded in the box-now trigger
findings.quote:
if derived.ve_model.applicable and derived.ve_model.laps_remaining is not None:
            resources.append(
                (
                    derived.ve_model.laps_remaining,
                    "VIRTUAL ENERGY",
findings.why_wrong: `_resource_laps` mixes two different quantities. The fuel entry (line 59) uses `projected_usable_laps`, which is net of the reserve (`fuel.py:36-38`: `max(0.0, fuel_l - reserve_l) / rate`). The VE entry uses `laps_remaining`, which is the *gross* figure (`virtual_energy.py:158`: `virtual_energy_pct / rate`), not the reserve-aware `usable_laps` computed two lines below it at `virtual_energy.py:160-164`. `min(resources)` therefore compares net-of-reserve fuel laps against gross VE laps, and the result drives the PIT_NOW trigger at `strategy_recommendations.py:34` (`resource_laps < 1.0`). The identical mistake appears in `engineering/models.py:128-130`, which publishes `strategy_laps_remaining` and `limiting_resource` from the same mismatched pair.
findings.impact: LMH/LMDh Hypercar, VE-limited, team sets `ve_reserve_laps = 0.5` to match the fuel policy. The box-now call is issued when *gross* VE drops below 1.0 lap — i.e. with the entire 0.5-lap reserve already spent. The car has exactly one lap of energy to cover the remainder of the current lap plus the run to pit entry, with zero margin for a heavy lap, traffic or a deployment mistake, and drops into limp mode before reaching the box. It also biases `limiting_resource` toward reporting FUEL when VE is genuinely the binding constraint.
findings.fix: Expose `usable_laps` on `VirtualEnergyModelState` (it is already computed at `virtual_energy.py:160`) and use it in both `strategy_scenarios._resource_laps` and `engineering/models._derived`, so fuel and VE are compared on the same net-of-reserve basis.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified: strategy_scenarios.py:59 uses `derived.fuel_model.projected_usable_laps` (net of reserve per engineering/fuel.py:36-38) while :62/:65 use `derived.ve_model.laps_remaining`, which is gross — engineering/virtual_energy.py:86 `laps_remaining=gross_laps`, whereas the reserve-aware figure is `usable_laps` at virtual_energy.py:40-41. min() therefore mixes net and gross. The duplicate at engineering/models.py:127-130 is confirmed. Note the finder's virtual_energy.py line citations (158, 160-164) do not exist — that file is 111 lines; the substance is nevertheless correct at lines 40/86. Severity lowered because the default `ve_reserve_laps` is 0.1, not 0.5 (config.py:63), so out of the box the discarded reserve is one tenth of a lap; the impact scenario assumes a team-configured 0.5 to reach fuel parity. | Confirmed. strategy_scenarios.py:57-67 appends `derived.fuel_model.projected_usable_laps` for FUEL and `derived.ve_model.laps_remaining` for VE, then takes `min(resources, key=...)`. engineering/fuel.py:36-38 sets `projected_usable_laps = max(0.0, fuel_l - reserve_l) / rate` (net of reserve) while engineering/virtual_energy.py:38/86 sets `laps_remaining = gross_laps` where `gross_laps = snapshot.virtual_energy_pct / rate` (gross) — the reserve-aware `usable_laps` computed two lines below at virtual_energy.py:40-44 is never used for this field. So `min()` compares net against gross and drives `resource_laps < 1.0` at strategy_recommendations.py:34. The same mismatched pair is republished at engineering/models.py:125-130 as `strategy_laps_remaining` / `limiting_resource`. Severity lowered from high: `ve_reserve_laps` defaults to 0.1 (config.py:63), so by default the call is late by ~0.1 lap; the '0.5-lap reserve already spent' impact is config-dependent, not the out-of-box behaviour.

findings.title: "Stay out to the finish with configured reserves" ignores the VE reserve it claims to honour
findings.quote:
derived.ve_model.laps_remaining is not None
                    and derived.ve_model.laps_remaining >= laps_to_finish
findings.why_wrong: The `finish_safe` test uses `projected_usable_laps` for fuel (line 84, net of reserve) but `laps_remaining` for VE (line 89, gross). The VE model already publishes a reserve-aware finish margin — `margin_to_finish_pct` at `virtual_energy.py:195-197`, computed as `virtual_energy_pct - (laps_to_finish * rate + reserve_pct)` — and it is not used here. The recommendation that this branch returns states in its own rationale (lines 115-117) "Current fuel and Virtual Energy projections reach the finish with configured reserves", which is false for VE: the test permits a finish with VE margin anywhere down to zero.
findings.impact: Hypercar, `ve_reserve_laps` configured to 1.0 by the team as its safety policy. With exactly `laps_to_finish` of gross VE left and no reserve remaining, the app returns preferred_scenario STAY_OUT and, if confidence is MEDIUM or better, sets `automatic_call_authorized=True` (line 103-107), so the voice adapter reads out "stay out to the finish" with a stated reserve the car does not actually have. Any VE consumption above the modelled mean on the closing laps leaves the car short of the line.
findings.fix: Replace `derived.ve_model.laps_remaining >= laps_to_finish` with the reserve-aware check, e.g. `(derived.ve_model.margin_to_finish_pct or -1.0) >= 0.0`, mirroring what the fuel branch already does.

The reserve-aware alternative exists and is unused — `margin_to_finish_pct=finish_margin` at virtual_energy.py:89, built from `laps_to_finish * rate + reserve_pct` at virtual_energy.py:71 (again, the finder's cited lines 195-197 do not exist in a 111-line file, but the code does). Same severity correction as finding 4: default ve_reserve_laps is 0.1 (config.py:63), so the unhonoured reserve is 0.1 lap unless the team raises it. | Confirmed. strategy_recommendations.py:81-92: fuel is tested with `projected_usable_laps >= laps_to_finish` (net of reserve) while VE is tested with `derived.ve_model.laps_remaining >= laps_to_finish` (gross, virtual_energy.py:86). The reserve-aware `margin_to_finish_pct` (virtual_energy.py:76-78/89, `virtual_energy_pct - (laps_to_finish * rate + reserve_pct)`) exists and is not consulted, and the returned rationale at lines 113-117 literally asserts "reach the finish with configured reserves" — false for VE. With confidence >= MEDIUM and an advantage clearing the threshold, lines 100-107 set `automatic_call_authorized=True`, so a voice call can be made on a zero-VE-margin finish. Severity lowered from high for the same reason as #4: the default `ve_reserve_laps` is 0.1, so the out-of-box error is small and only becomes material when a team configures a real reserve.

findings.title: Opponent "relative distance" is cumulative race distance, not on-track gap — traffic model blind to lapped cars
findings.quote:
absolute = (
                observation.completed_laps * snapshot.track_length_m
                + observation.lap_distance_m
            )
            relative = absolute - player_absolute if valid else None
findings.why_wrong: `relative_lap_distance_m` is the difference in *total race distance*, but every consumer treats it as an on-track gap. There is no modulo of the track length anywhere in this module (verified by grepping `track_length_m` across `src/ssc_engineer/*.py`). A car one lap ahead on the road right next to you gets `relative ≈ +13626 m` at Le Mans; a lapped car 200 m in front of you gets `relative ≈ -13426 m`. The consumers then break: line 537 selects "cars ahead" with `0.0 < relative_lap_distance_m < 1500.0`; line 494 sets `direction = "behind" if relative < 0 else "ahead"`; lines 474-491 classify FASTER_CLASS_APPROACHING on `relative < 0.0`. And `closing_speed_mps` is d(relative)/dt, which for a lap-offset car is the *pace difference*, not a closing rate, so `catch_s = abs(relative)/closing` is enormous and is thrown away by the `catch_s > 300.0` filter at line 259 — the car is dropped entirely at line 471. The project's own newer LICO predictor does this correctly (`lico/prediction.py:115` uses `(car.fraction - previous.fraction + 0.5) % 1` and line 418-421 uses `(opponent.fraction - player.fraction) % 1 * length`), which confirms the intended semantics.
findings.impact: LMGT3 car at Le Mans, one lap down. A Hypercar closing to lap it has `relative ≈ +13600 m`, so it is classified "ahead", excluded from the `< 1500.0` pack window, given a nonsensical catch time that the 300 s filter discards, and never produces a FASTER_CLASS_APPROACHING contact. The blue-flag/faster-class-approaching warning — the single most safety-relevant traffic call in multi-class endurance racing — never fires for exactly the cars it exists for. Symmetrically, a lapped car directly in front of the player is reported as "behind".
findings.fix: Compute the signed on-track gap as `((absolute - player_absolute + L/2) % L) - L/2` and carry the lap offset as a separate field, so proximity logic uses the circular gap while cycle/position logic keeps the cumulative distance. Alternatively route the traffic contacts through the already-correct LICO `Frame`/`fraction` geometry.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified at opponents.py:170-174: `absolute = observation.completed_laps * snapshot.track_length_m + observation.lap_distance_m` then `relative = absolute - player_absolute if valid else None`. Grep for track_length_m in opponents.py returns only lines 95/103/105/159/168/171/446/580 — no modulo normalisation anywhere; line 446 is only a half-track sanity bound inside the undercut branch, not a wrap. The consumers do treat it as an on-track gap: line 537 `0.0 < item.relative_lap_distance_m < 1500.0`, line 494 `direction = "behind" if relative < 0 else "ahead"`, lines 474-479 the FASTER_CLASS_APPROACHING gate, and line 259 drops catch_s > 300.0. The contrast with lico/prediction.py:115 `(car.fraction - self.previous.fraction + 0.5) % 1 - 0.5` and :421 `... % 1 * frame.track.length_m` confirms the intended semantics exist elsewhere in the same repo. Holds as written. | Confirmed exactly as described. opponents.py:171-175 computes `absolute = observation.completed_laps * track_length_m + observation.lap_distance_m` and `relative = absolute - player_absolute`, with no wrap anywhere in the module. Consumers treat it as an on-track gap: opponents.py:474/479/486 gate contacts on `relative < 0.0` / `relative > 0.0`, line 494 sets `direction = "behind" if relative < 0 else "ahead"`, and line 537 selects the pack window with `0.0 < item.relative_lap_distance_m < 1500.0`.
