findings.title: "Pit window" is a fuel-exhaustion band; the radio announces CLOSED after the car is already past empty
findings.why_wrong: `pit_window_open_lap` and `pit_window_close_lap` are not a strategic pit window. `engineering/fuel.py:48-49` defines them as `completed_laps + usable_fuel / pessimistic` and `completed_laps + usable_fuel / optimistic` — i.e. the earliest and latest lap at which the *usable* fuel runs out. So the window "opens" at the earliest possible fuel-out lap and "closes" at the latest one. In race-engineering usage a pit window opens when a stop becomes strategically viable and closes when it is no longer possible; here "CLOSED" means the opposite — the car is past the last modelled lap it could reach and is running on reserve. The radio phrase at `communication/phrases.py:260` compounds this: `return "Pit window is open.", tuple(facts), "Pit when strategically suitable."` tells the driver a stop is optional at the exact moment the fuel model says the tank is on its last laps. Nothing about `laps_to_finish`, mandatory stops or tyre life enters this calculation.
findings.impact: A driver hears "pit window is open, pit when strategically suitable" and elects to stay out for track position. Two laps later the status silently flips to CLOSED — which an engineer reads as "the window has passed, stay out" — while it actually means the modelled usable fuel is gone and only `fuel_reserve_laps + 2σ` remains. The naming inverts the urgency at precisely the moment urgency is maximal.
findings.fix: Rename these fields to what they are (`fuel_exhaustion_earliest_lap` / `fuel_exhaustion_latest_lap`) and invert the status semantics so the terminal state reads as an escalation (e.g. NOT_YET / OPEN / OVERDUE), or build a genuine pit window from `laps_to_finish`, tank capacity and mandatory stops and keep the fuel band as a separate readout.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified: communication/context.py:109-113 is quoted correctly, and engineering/fuel.py:46-49 defines `open_lap = snapshot.completed_laps + usable_fuel / pessimistic` / `close_lap = ... / optimistic` from `usable_fuel = max(0.0, snapshot.fuel_l - reserve_l)` — so the band really is earliest/latest usable-fuel-out lap, with no term for laps_to_finish, mandatory stops or tyre life. The phrase at communication/phrases.py:260 exists verbatim. Downgraded because this is a naming/semantics defect, not a missing call: urgency is still carried independently by the fuel status ladder (fuel.py:79-86 MARGINAL when `usable_laps < 1.0`) and by the PIT_NOW trigger at strategy_recommendations.py:34, neither of which depends on this string. | Confirmed. engineering/fuel.py:44-49 defines `open_lap = completed_laps + usable_fuel / pessimistic` and `close_lap = completed_laps + usable_fuel / optimistic` where `usable_fuel = max(0.0, fuel_l - reserve_l)` — i.e. earliest and latest modelled usable-fuel exhaustion lap — and communication/context.py:105-113 maps the current lap into NOT OPEN / OPEN / CLOSED against those. The advisory really is emitted on the transition: communication/arbitration.py:439-448 fires `PIT_WINDOW_OPEN` with action "Pit when strategically suitable.", and phrases.py:260 returns "Pit window is open." plus "Pit when strategically suitable.". Nothing about mandatory stops, laps_to_finish or tyre life enters it. Severity lowered from high: it is a semantics/naming defect rather than a wrong number, and the same state simultaneously drives FUEL_MARGIN_MARGINAL (arbitration.py:341-344, fuel status MARGINAL from fuel.py:83-85), so the urgency is not entirely absent from the radio — but the phrase itself is inverted and misleading.

findings.title: Fuel target is floor(usable_laps), making the fuel-saving advisory unreachable outside the final stint
findings.quote: target = float(max(1, math.floor(usable_laps)))
findings.why_wrong: Outside the final stint the target is defined as the largest whole number of laps the current fuel can already cover with the reserve intact. Substituting `fuel_l = usable_laps * rate + reserve_l` into `margin = fuel_l - (target * rate + reserve_l)` (lines 70-73) gives `margin = (usable_laps - floor(usable_laps)) * rate`, which is non-negative by construction for any `usable_laps >= 1`. Consequently `status` can never become "FUEL SAVING REQUIRED" (line 81-82) and `saving_required_l_per_lap` (line 74-78) is always 0.0 unless `usable_laps < 1` — and in that case `strategy_recommendations.py:34` has already returned PIT_NOW, so the SAVE_FUEL branch at `strategy_recommendations.py:124-132` is dead. Separately, the comment at lines 65-66 says "Without a configured strategy target…", but no configured target path exists: `_fuel_model(snapshot, laps_to_finish)` takes no target argument, and the approved plan's per-stint `fuel_target_laps` (`race_plan_core.py:65`, surfaced on `PlannedDriverStintState`) never reaches this module (confirmed by grepping `fuel_target_laps` under `engineering/`).
findings.impact: Team plans a 14-lap stint at Le Mans to line up with the driver-change schedule, but the car is running 4.6 L/lap against a 4.3 L/lap plan and will only reach 13. The app computes `target = floor(13.2) = 13`, reports `margin = +0.86 L` and status SAFE, and never issues a fuel-save call. The engineer gets no warning that the approved stint length is unachievable until the car is a lap short of the planned box lap.
findings.fix: Feed the approved plan's `fuel_target_laps` for the current/next stint into `_fuel_model` and use it as `target` when present, falling back to `floor(usable_laps)` only when no plan target exists. As written, the model can only ever confirm what the car can already do, never flag what the plan asks for.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified: engineering/fuel.py:67 `target = float(max(1, math.floor(usable_laps)))` under the comment at :65-66, and the algebra holds — with `usable_laps = (fuel_l - reserve_l)/rate`, `margin = fuel_l - (floor(usable_laps)*rate + reserve_l) >= 0` for usable_laps >= 1, so `saving_required_l_per_lap` (fuel.py:74-78) is pinned at 0.0 and 'FUEL SAVING REQUIRED' (fuel.py:81-82) is unreachable outside the final stint. The dead-configured-target claim also checks out: `_fuel_model(self, snapshot, laps_to_finish)` takes no target and grep for fuel_target_laps under src/ssc_engineer/engineering/ returns nothing. One overstatement corrected: the finder claims the SAVE_FUEL branch is entirely dead, considering only usable_laps < 1. It is not — the `final_stint` branch at fuel.py:62-63 sets `target = laps_to_finish`, which can produce a negative margin with usable_laps well above 1, so SAVE_FUEL does fire through the whole closing stint (`laps_to_finish <= gross_laps + 1.0`). The defect is confined to mid-race saving against a planned stint length. | Headline confirmed by algebra on the real code. engineering/fuel.py:60-78: outside the final stint `target = float(max(1, math.floor(usable_laps)))`, and since `usable_laps = max(0, fuel_l - reserve_l)/rate` implies `fuel_l = usable_laps*rate + reserve_l`, `margin = fuel_l - (target*rate + reserve_l) = (usable_laps - floor(usable_laps))*rate >= 0` for `usable_laps >= 1`, so `saving` (lines 74-78) is always 0.0 and status can never be "FUEL SAVING REQUIRED" (lines 81-82). The comment at lines 65-66 about "a configured strategy target" is indeed vestigial — `_fuel_model(snapshot, laps_to_finish)` takes no target and the plan's `fuel_target_laps` never reaches this module. One sub-claim in the rationale is wrong and I am not endorsing it: the SAVE_FUEL branch at strategy_recommendations.py:120-127 is NOT dead, because in the final stint `target = laps_to_finish` (line 63) and `margin` can go negative with `usable_laps >= 1`. Severity lowered to medium accordingly: the advisory works when it matters most (final stint), it is the mid-race stint-target warning that is missing.

findings.title: Approved stint windows converted to laps without deducting pit-stop time, then the pit loss is added again
findings.quote: laps = min(distance, duration / pace)
findings.why_wrong: `duration` is a wall-clock stint window taken from the approved schedule (lines 147-149). `schedule_bounds` (`race_plan_core.py:485-492`) tiles those windows back-to-back with `elapsed += item.duration_s` and no gap, and `build_round_robin_schedule` (line 372-389) makes their sum equal the full race duration — so the pit-lane time is inside those windows, not between them. Dividing the whole window by lap pace therefore counts the stationary and pit-lane time as racing laps. The projection then double-counts: `strategy_projection._propagate` adds `pick(stop.total_loss_s)` to elapsed at line 182 *and* `leg.laps * pick(leg.pace_s)` at line 194, so the modelled elapsed time is Σduration + Σpit_loss, longer than the race.
findings.impact: 6h race, 6 stops at the configured 45 s green pit loss, 100 s laps: each leg is credited with ~0.45 laps it will not actually run, so the schedule appears to cover the remaining-distance horizon with roughly two to three fewer laps of running than reality, and the check at line 204 (`if distance > 1e-6: rejected.append("Approved schedule ends before the conditional remaining-distance horizon")`) fails to fire when it should. Projected race time is simultaneously ~4.5 minutes too long.
findings.fix: Subtract the modelled stop loss from the stint window before converting to laps: `laps = min(distance, max(0.0, duration - stop_loss_expected) / pace)`, using the same `green_pit_loss` distribution that is already attached to `stop_before`.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified on all three legs. strategy_projection_live.py:155 `laps = min(distance, duration / pace)` where duration comes from the plan's wall-clock boundaries (lines 147-149). race_plan_core.py:485-492 `elapsed += item.duration_s` tiles windows with no gap, and build_round_robin_schedule (race_plan_core.py:372-389) makes them sum to the race duration, so pit time is inside the windows. The double-count is exact: strategy_projection.py:182 `elapsed += pick(stop.total_loss_s)` and strategy_projection.py:194 `elapsed += leg.laps * pick(leg.pace_s)`. The rejection check at strategy_projection_live.py:204 is as quoted. Holds as written. | Confirmed. strategy_projection_live.py:146-155 derives `duration` from the approved plan's `planned_start/end_elapsed_s` and does `laps = min(distance, duration / pace)`. race_plan_core.py:486-492 (`schedule_bounds`) tiles those windows with `elapsed += item.duration_s` and no gap, and build_round_robin_schedule (lines 371-388) fills `race_duration_s` exactly, so pit-lane time is inside the windows, not between them — dividing the whole window by lap pace credits stationary time as racing laps. The double count is real too: strategy_projection.py:179-182 adds `elapsed += pick(stop.total_loss_s)` and lines 193-194 add `elapsed += leg.laps * pick(leg.pace_s)`, so modelled elapsed is Σduration + Σpit_loss. The under-fill also silences the `distance > 1e-6` rejection at strategy_projection_live.py:203-205.

findings.title: Fuel reserve adds a fixed 2σ of a single lap regardless of how many laps it must cover
findings.why_wrong: `deviation` is `pstdev(self._fuel_samples)` — the per-lap standard deviation of consumption (line 31). Adding a flat `2.0 * deviation` treats the uncertainty of one lap as the uncertainty of the entire remaining run. For N laps of independent per-lap variation the uncertainty of the total grows as √N·σ, so the buffer is under-sized by a factor of about √N. The same `reserve_l` is used both for the short-horizon `usable_laps` (line 36) and for `finish_required` over the whole remaining distance (line 51-54), where N can be 30+.
findings.impact: Hypercar at Le Mans, rate 4.3 L/lap, σ 0.15 L/lap, 30 laps to the finish. The reserve is 4.3*0.5 + 0.30 = 2.45 L. The actual 2σ uncertainty on 30 laps of burn is 2*0.15*√30 ≈ 1.64 L on top of the 0.5-lap policy buffer, i.e. roughly double the variance allowance the model provides. `margin_to_finish_l` is reported as safe when the true one-in-twenty outcome is short of the line.
findings.fix: Scale the statistical component with the horizon: `reserve_l = rate * fuel_reserve_laps + 2.0 * deviation * sqrt(max(1.0, laps_to_cover))`, using `laps_to_finish` for the finish calculation and the stint target for the stint calculation.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified: engineering/fuel.py:33-35 `reserve_l = (rate * self.policy.fuel_reserve_laps + 2.0 * deviation if rate is not None else None)` with `deviation = pstdev(self._fuel_samples)` at fuel.py:31 (per-lap σ), and the same reserve_l feeds both the one-lap-horizon `usable_laps` (fuel.py:36-38) and the whole-race `finish_required` (fuel.py:51-54). The √N scaling argument is correct statistics, not opinion. Context that tempers it: fuel_reserve_laps defaults to 0.5 (config.py:62), so the policy term (≈2.15 L in the cited case) still carries most of the buffer and the shortfall is ≈1.3 L / 0.3 laps, not a total absence of margin. A real quantitative deficiency in tail-risk coverage; medium is the right level. | Confirmed. engineering/fuel.py:31 sets `deviation = pstdev(self._fuel_samples)` (per-lap population σ) and lines 33-35 build `reserve_l = rate * self.policy.fuel_reserve_laps + 2.0 * deviation`. That same constant-width buffer is used both for the one-lap horizon (`usable_laps`, line 36-38) and for the whole-race `finish_required = laps_to_finish * rate + reserve_l` (lines 51-54), where `laps_to_finish` can be 30+. Independent per-lap variation accumulates as √N·σ, so the allowance is under-sized by roughly √N over a long horizon and `margin_to_finish_l` reads safe in tail outcomes that are not. This is a modelling-rigour defect rather than a coding error — the configured `fuel_reserve_laps` term still scales with rate — so medium is the right band, not higher.

findings.title: Night is hard-coded as 19:00-07:00 in driver allocation, contradicting the configurable twilight used elsewhere
findings.why_wrong: The same app defines night twice, differently. `opponent_strategy.py:345-346` uses the configurable policy: `night = not self.config.twilight_start_hour <= hour < self.config.twilight_end_hour`, with defaults 5.0 and 20.0 (`config.py:124-125`). This function hard-codes 07:00/19:00. Neither accounts for track latitude or date, but the two disagree with each other for four hours of every day. The NIGHT condition is not cosmetic — it feeds `_evidence_score` at line 113-114, where `_PREFERENCE_SCORE` contributes ±2.0, and the preferred-alternative threshold is `score >= 1.0` (line 304). A single mislabelled condition can therefore flip a driver-change proposal on its own.
findings.impact: Le Mans in mid-June: sunset is ~22:00 local and sunrise ~06:00. At 19:30 in full daylight, a driver flagged AVOID for night is penalised -2.0 and a driver flagged PREFER is credited +2.0, which alone clears the 1.0 threshold and produces a "Consider X next" proposal for conditions that do not exist. Meanwhile `opponent_strategy` is still recording those same laps as daytime pace, so the two subsystems disagree about the same snapshot.
findings.fix: Use `self.config.twilight_start_hour` / `twilight_end_hour` here as `opponent_strategy.py:346` does, and ideally derive the boundary from the observed track light state or from track latitude and date rather than a fixed clock.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified: driver_allocation.py:34-36 `hour = (snapshot.time_of_day_s % 86400.0) / 3600.0` / `if hour < 7.0 or hour >= 19.0:` / `conditions.append("NIGHT")`, against opponent_strategy.py:345-346 `night = not self.config.twilight_start_hour <= hour < self.config.twilight_end_hour` with defaults 5.0/20.0 at config.py:124-125. The four-hour daily disagreement is real. The scoring path is confirmed: _PREFERENCE_SCORE = {"PREFER": 2.0, "NEUTRAL": 0.0, "AVOID": -2.0} at driver_allocation.py:23, applied on the NIGHT condition at :113-114, against the `if score >= 1.0` bar at :304 on a candidate-minus-planned differential — so a ±2.0 swing can cross the threshold on its own. Holds; effect requires the team to have set non-NEUTRAL night preferences. | Confirmed on both sides. driver_allocation.py:34-37: `hour = (snapshot.time_of_day_s % 86400.0) / 3600.0; if hour < 7.0 or hour >= 19.0: conditions.append("NIGHT")`, versus opponent_strategy.py:345-346 `night = not self.config.twilight_start_hour <= hour < self.config.twilight_end_hour` with defaults 5.0/20.0 (config.py:124-125) — the two disagree for four hours every day on the same snapshot. The consequence chain checks out: `_evidence_score` (driver_allocation.py:112-114) adds `_PREFERENCE_SCORE[night_preference]` only when NIGHT is in conditions, and the proposal bar is `if score >= 1.0` on the candidate-minus-planned delta (lines 301-304), so a spurious NIGHT can flip a driver-change proposal on its own.

findings.title: Fatigue proxy requires 24 confound-free laps under one driver identity and resets at every driver change
findings.quote:
required = self.BASELINE_LAPS + self.RECENT_LAPS
        if len(accepted) < required:
findings.why_wrong: `BASELINE_LAPS = 10` and `RECENT_LAPS = 14` (lines 32-33), so 24 *accepted* laps are needed before any assessment. `observe` keys identity on `(track, session, driver)` and calls `self.reset(snapshot)` whenever it changes (lines 332-334), and `reset` clears `self._accepted` (line 63) — so the counter restarts at every driver swap, including when a driver returns for a later stint. Acceptance additionally requires no traffic confound, where traffic is any gap ≤ 2.5 s to any of four neighbours at any point in the lap (`_nearby`, line 84). A Le Mans stint is ~11-14 laps, so 24 accepted laps can never accumulate within one driver's stint, and in a multi-class field almost every lap carries a traffic confound anyway.
findings.impact: The whole subsystem is dead in the race it was built for. `DriverFatigueProxyState.status` stays BASELINE_BUILDING for the entire 24h, which also disables the fatigue-triggered driver-change path at `driver_allocation.py:306-312`. Worse, resetting the baseline at every swap makes the accumulated-hours fatigue the model is named for structurally undetectable: the only comparison it can ever make is within a single stint.
findings.fix: Persist per-driver accepted-lap history across stints (key on driver, not on the driver-plus-session tuple, and do not clear it on a swap), and compare a driver's current stint against their own earlier stints in the same event. Loosen the traffic gate to exclude only laps where the exposure actually overlapped the timed portion, rather than any 2.5 s proximity anywhere on the lap.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified in full: fatigue.py:32-33 BASELINE_LAPS = 10 / RECENT_LAPS = 14; fatigue.py:213-214 `required = self.BASELINE_LAPS + self.RECENT_LAPS` / `if len(accepted) < required:` returning BASELINE_BUILDING; fatigue.py:331-333 `identity = (snapshot.track, snapshot.session, snapshot.driver)` / `if self._identity != identity: self.reset(snapshot)` and reset clearing `self._accepted` at fatigue.py:62. The traffic confound is also as described — fatigue.py:84 `return any(value is not None and 0.0 <= value <= 2.5 for value in gaps)` over four neighbour gaps, latched for the whole lap at fatigue.py:107 and turned into a rejection at fatigue.py:142-143 `reasons.append("TRAFFIC CONFOUND")` with `accepted=not reasons`. 24 accepted laps inside one ~11-14 lap Le Mans stint is unreachable, and the per-swap reset does make multi-hour fatigue structurally undetectable. Holds as written. | Confirmed. fatigue.py:29-30 `BASELINE_LAPS = 10` / `RECENT_LAPS = 14`, and line 213-214 `required = self.BASELINE_LAPS + self.RECENT_LAPS; if len(accepted) < required:` returns BASELINE_BUILDING. observe() at lines 332-334 keys identity on `(snapshot.track, snapshot.session, snapshot.driver)` and calls `self.reset(snapshot)` on change, and reset clears `self._accepted` (line 63). Acceptance in `_complete` (lines 128-145) rejects on any of MECHANICAL/WEATHER/TRAFFIC/CAUTION confounds, with traffic being `any gap <= 2.5 s` to four neighbours at any frame (`_nearby`, lines 77-84, set at line 107) — in a multi-class field that alone kills most laps. So the subsystem is effectively pinned at BASELINE_BUILDING, which also disables the fatigue branch at driver_allocation.py:306-312. One nuance the finding overstates: identity is per driver, not per stint, so a driver double- or triple-stinting keeps accumulating across the stop — 24 laps is not strictly unreachable, just very unlikely once the traffic confound is applied.

findings.title: Fatigue-triggered driver change picks an arbitrary alternative instead of the best-scoring one
findings.why_wrong: Ten lines earlier the code deliberately selects the best candidate with `max(ranked, key=lambda item: (item[0], item[1].alternative_id))` and applies a `score >= 1.0` quality bar (lines 301-304). This block overwrites that with `compliant[0]`, the first element in list-append order — which is the iteration order of `allocation.drivers`, not any measure of suitability. The filter is also a no-op: entries only reach `ranked` when `not reasons` (line 297-298), so every entry already has `regulation_compliant=True`. Both the ranking and the advantage threshold are silently discarded.
findings.impact: The current driver's consistency degrades and the app must propose a replacement. Instead of the highest-scoring compliant candidate, it proposes whichever driver happens to sit first in the allocation list — potentially one with an AVOID night preference (-2.0), an AVOID wet preference (-2.0) and a CAUTION fatigue flag (-2.0), while the best candidate is ignored. The recommendation is then surfaced as PROPOSAL_REQUIRES_APPROVAL with a rationale implying evidence supported it.
findings.fix: Reuse the existing ranking: `preferred = max(ranked, key=lambda item: (item[0], item[1].alternative_id))[1]`, keeping the fatigue trigger as the reason to bypass the `score >= 1.0` bar rather than as a reason to abandon the ranking.

findings.title: Tyre pressure-loss warning has no temperature compensation and fires on ordinary thermal cycling
findings.quote:
recent_peak = observed_peak if observed_peak is not None else pressure or 0.0

                max(0.0, recent_peak - pressure)
                if pressure is not None and samples
                else None

findings.why_wrong: `observed_peak` is the maximum pressure over the rolling window (`car_health_trend_window_s` defaults to 120 s, `config.py:101`), and any drop of `car_health_pressure_loss_kpa` (default 12.0 kPa, `config.py:104`) from that peak is reported as PRESSURE LOSS OBSERVED with status WARNING (lines 293-311) and escalated to a DamageHealthState WARNING (lines 507-510). Tyre pressure is dominated by carcass temperature, not by leaks: at a typical ~170 kPa gauge (≈270 kPa absolute, ≈350 K), the ideal-gas relation gives ΔP ≈ P·ΔT/T ≈ 270·20/350 ≈ 15 kPa for a 20 °C carcass-temperature swing. The model compares a hot peak against a cooler current reading with no temperature term, and the only gates are `speed_kmh >= 50.0` and `not in_pits` (lines 296-298) — both satisfied under a full-course yellow, which is exactly when tyres cool fastest. History is cleared only on pit entry (line 567-568), so the hot peak from a push phase persists for the full window.
findings.impact: FCY at Le Mans: the field drops to slow-zone speed above 50 km/h, carcass temperature falls 20-30 °C over a minute or two, pressures drop 15-20 kPa from the pre-yellow peak, and all four corners simultaneously report PRESSURE LOSS OBSERVED / damage WARNING. The engineer gets a four-wheel puncture alarm during a caution — the one moment where a genuine call has to cut through — and the crying-wolf effect trains the team to ignore the real one.
findings.fix: Compare pressure against a temperature-normalised reference (use the already-collected `BRAKE_`/tyre carcass series to correct P by T, or regress pressure on carcass temperature within the window), require the loss to be isolated to one corner rather than all four, and require a sustained monotonic decline rather than a single peak-to-current delta.

findings.title: Class relationship compares the player's single last lap against the opponent's rolling mean
findings.why_wrong: The player side is one raw lap time with no cleanliness filter — it includes in-laps, out-laps, laps under local yellow and laps ruined by traffic — while the opponent side is `recent_pace_s`, the mean of the last several laps (`opponents.py:253`, `_mean(recent)`). The two sides are not comparable estimators, and the classification threshold is only ±3%. The identical asymmetry appears in `strategy_gap.py:72` (`own_pace = snapshot.last_lap_s`) feeding the gap forecast at line 151. The tracker already maintains a filtered clean-lap history (`_stint_clean_lap_times`, `PaceModelState.rolling_5_lap_s`) that is not used here.
findings.impact: The player completes an out-lap after a stop: at Le Mans that is ~30 s slower than a green lap on a 3:30 baseline, roughly +14%, far beyond the 3% band. For the whole of the next lap every same-speed and even slower opponent is reclassified FASTER_CLASS, which then drives the FASTER_CLASS_APPROACHING contact at `opponents.py:474-479` and the caution/threat text built from `class_relationship`. The car is told a GT3 field is faster than it immediately after every pit stop.
findings.fix: Use `derived.pace.rolling_5_lap_s` (or the clean-lap stint average) for the player side in both `_relationship` and `strategy_gap.forecast_effective_gaps`, so both sides of the comparison are filtered rolling estimates.

findings.title: Opponent green-pace average is contaminated by out-laps; in-lap pace is never recorded at all

accumulator.add_lap(
                            state.last_lap_s,

                            night=night,

findings.why_wrong: `add_lap` unconditionally folds the lap into `green_mean` (line 192, `self.green_mean = _mean_update(...)`), and only *afterwards* is the same lap additionally tagged as an out-lap. So every out-lap is counted twice: once as an ordinary green lap and once as an out-lap. Out-laps in LMU carry cold tyres and a pit-lane-exit penalty and are tens of seconds off green pace. Separately, `in_lap_mean` / `in_lap_count` (lines 105-106) are read in `restore` (169-170) and published in `contract` as `in_lap_pace_s` / `in_lap_sample_count` (277-278) but are never incremented anywhere in the codebase — there is no `add_in_lap` method (verified by grep). So in-laps also pollute `green_mean` while the dedicated in-lap field is permanently null.
findings.impact: An opponent stopping every 12 laps contributes one out-lap and one in-lap per 12 green laps, each ~20-40 s off pace at Le Mans, inflating `observed_green_pace_s` by roughly 3-6 s/lap. That figure is published as the opponent's green pace and is the basis for stint and gap reasoning, and `in_lap_pace_s` is surfaced as evidence while always being `None`.

findings.title: Crossover estimates are rounded up to a 0.5 minimum and a 0.5-wide band, understating imminent tyre calls
findings.quote:
rounded_low = max(0.5, math.floor(low * 2.0) / 2.0)
    rounded_high = max(rounded_low + 0.5, math.ceil(high * 2.0) / 2.0)
findings.why_wrong: `_round_range` is applied both to minutes (`_crossover_range`, line 131) and to laps (line 236-239). The `max(0.5, ...)` floor means a crossover that is 6 seconds away is reported as "0.5 minutes", and the forced `rounded_low + 0.5` span means `estimated_min_laps` can never be below 0.5 and `estimated_max_laps` never below 1.0. Rounding always moves the estimate away from now, i.e. always in the less-urgent direction.
findings.impact: Wetness crosses the configured threshold in 8 seconds. The app reports `estimated_min_minutes = 0.5, estimated_max_minutes = 1.0` and the crossover event text says "within five minutes". An engineer reading 0.5-1.0 minutes has a materially different picture from 0.1 minutes when deciding whether to bring the car in this lap or next. The same floor makes `_weather_risk` HIGH (`strategy_scenario_support.py:71-74`, `estimated_max_laps <= 1.0`) reachable only at the exact boundary value 1.0.
findings.fix: Round toward the present for the lower bound (or do not floor it at all) and let the band width follow the actual slope uncertainty rather than forcing a 0.5-unit minimum span; surface sub-half-minute crossovers as "imminent" rather than rounding them up.

One stated rationale is wrong: 'Rounding always moves the estimate away from now' is false — `math.floor` on rounded_low moves toward now (more urgent); only the 0.5 clamp moves away from now. The finding survives on the clamp alone. | Confirmed. weather.py:114-117 `rounded_low = max(0.5, math.floor(low * 2.0) / 2.0); rounded_high = max(rounded_low + 0.5, math.ceil(high * 2.0) / 2.0)`, applied to minutes at line 131 (`_crossover_range`) and to laps at lines 236-239. So a crossover 8 s away reports 0.5-1.0 minutes, and rounding always moves away from now. findings.why_wrong: `build_round_robin_schedule` fills `race_duration_s` with back-to-back `nominal_stint_s` blocks and `schedule_bounds` (line 485-492) accumulates them with `elapsed += item.duration_s`, so the planned stint boundaries carry no explicit pit-stop allowance. findings.title: Numeric guardrail pools every number in every tool result, so a value from the wrong field passes
findings.quote: allowed_numbers = list(_numbers_from([result.get("data") for result in tool_results]))
findings.why_wrong: _numbers_from (guardrails.py:121-131) recurses through every nested dict and list of every tool result's `data` and flattens it into one unordered list of floats. The check at lines 379-384 then only asks whether each spoken number is close to *some* member of that pool. There is no association between a number and the field it came from, and no unit is consulted even though _result() carries a `units` map (tool_status.py:118). A single get_fuel_status call already contributes current_l, estimated_per_lap_l, laps_remaining, target_margin_l and saving_required_l_per_lap; get_tyre_status contributes four wheel dicts. Any of those numbers may legally be spoken as any quantity.
findings.impact: Verified by running the real guardrail in the project venv. With tool results {get_fuel_status: {current_l: 42.5, estimated_per_lap_l: 3.41, laps_remaining: 12.4}} and {get_position_and_gaps: {gap_ahead_s: 12.4, gap_behind_s: 3.41}}, the transcript "Gap ahead is 3.41 seconds, fuel 12.4 litres per lap." — both numbers swapped between fields — returns allowed=True. Likewise "You have 42.5 laps of fuel remaining." (42.5 is litres in the tank, not laps) returns allowed=True against the fuel result alone. The driver hears a fluent, confident and completely wrong race-critical number, and the turn is persisted with guardrail_outcome='PASS'.
findings.fix: Validate per-field, not against a pool. Have the model emit a structured answer naming the tool and field for each quantity (or tag each number in the transcript), then check value AND unit against that specific field via the `units` map. At minimum, restrict the allow-list to the fields of the single most recent tool result and require an adjacent unit token matching that field's declared unit.
findings.verifier_notes: Code-true. guardrails.py:366 is verbatim `allowed_numbers = list(_numbers_from([result.get("data") for result in tool_results]))`, _numbers_from (121-131) recurses into every dict/list and yields a flat float stream, and the only test at 379-384 is `math.isclose(value, allowed, ...) for allowed in allowed_numbers` — no field, no unit, no ordering. tool_status.py:118 does carry a `units` map that the validator never reads. Re-ran the finder's cases in .venv: swapped fuel/gap transcript -> allowed=True; 'You have 42.5 laps of fuel remaining.' against {current_l:42.5, estimated_per_lap_l:3.41, laps_remaining:12.4} -> allowed=True. Nothing upstream constrains which tool results are pooled (orchestrator.py:686 passes every trace result). | Confirmed by execution in .venv against src/ssc_engineer/voice/guardrails.py:366. _numbers_from (121-131) flattens every nested value of every result['data'] into one pool; the check at 379-384 only asks `any(math.isclose(value, allowed, ...))`. Repro run: with get_fuel_status {current_l:42.5, estimated_per_lap_l:3.41, laps_remaining:12.4} and get_position_and_gaps {position:5, gap_ahead_s:12.4, gap_behind_s:3.41}, validate('Gap ahead is 3.41 seconds, fuel 12.4 litres per lap.') -> allowed=True (both values swapped between fields). Also validate('You have 42.5 laps of fuel remaining.', tool_results=(fuel,)) -> allowed=True. No field association, no unit consulted. orchestrator.py:691 is the live call site and passes exactly these tool_results, and guardrail_outcome stays 'PASS' (orchestrator.py:663, 719-727), so the wrong number is spoken as OPENAI_REALTIME audio and persisted as passing.

findings.title: Action guardrail authorises "Box, box, box" from any tool status string containing the substring "pit"
findings.quote:
if action in {"box", "pit"}:
        return "box" in evidence or "pit" in evidence
findings.why_wrong: `evidence` is built by _permitted_actions (guardrails.py:134-162) by concatenating and case-folding data["recommended_action"], data["exact_text"] and data["status"] from every tool result. Those are free-form observational strings, not authorisations. PitExecutionState.status is literally assigned "PIT ENTRY OBSERVED" (src/ssc_engineer/pit_operations.py:492 and :536), and the routine PIT_WINDOW_OPEN advisory carries recommended_action "Pit when strategically suitable." (src/ssc_engineer/communication/phrases.py:260). Substring containment turns either into a pit command.
findings.impact: Verified by execution. guardrail.validate('Box, box, box.', tool_results=({'tool':'get_pit_execution_status','available':True,'data':{'status':'PIT ENTRY OBSERVED', ...}},)) returns allowed=True, as does 'Pit this lap.'. The same holds with get_last_engineer_call returning recommended_action 'Pit when strategically suitable.'. So after any routine pit-window advisory, or any lap on which the car has been observed entering the pit lane, an ungrounded model utterance commanding an immediate stop reaches the driver's headset as OPENAI_REALTIME audio with guardrail_outcome='PASS'. A wrongly-timed box call loses the race and can be a safety event in traffic.
findings.fix: Replace substring matching with an explicit authorisation token. Only treat an action as permitted when a deterministic field says so structurally — e.g. scenarios.recommendation.preferred_scenario == 'PIT_NOW' with automatic_call_authorized True, or an EngineerCall whose recommended_action was produced by phrases.py for a pit code. Never derive authority from an observational `status` field.

Exposure is narrower than claimed (needs a repeat/explain after a pit-window advisory rather than any observed pit entry) but an ungrounded immediate box call still reaches the driver with guardrail_outcome='PASS'. | Confirmed by execution. guardrails.py:165-167 `if action in {"box","pit"}: return "box" in evidence or "pit" in evidence`, and _permitted_actions (134-162) folds data['status'], data['exact_text'], data['recommended_action'] into that evidence string. findings.title: Action guardrail cannot distinguish an imperative from its negation
findings.why_wrong: The check is purely presence-based: if the phrase pattern matches and the evidence contains the action, the utterance is allowed. Nothing inspects polarity. "Box this lap" and "Do not box this lap" are indistinguishable to the validator, so whenever the deterministic engine authorises an action the model is simultaneously authorised to speak its exact inverse.
findings.impact: Verified by execution. With tool_results carrying scenarios.recommendation = {preferred_scenario: 'PIT_NOW', automatic_call_authorized: True}, guardrail.validate('Do not box this lap.') returns allowed=True. The deterministic engine has decided the car must pit now; the model tells the driver to stay out; the guardrail records PASS. This is the worst possible failure mode for a system whose value proposition is that the LLM can never contradict the deterministic layer.
findings.fix: Reject any utterance containing a negation token (not, don't, do not, no, never, avoid, hold off, skip) in the same clause as a matched action pattern, unless the deterministic evidence authorises that negated form specifically (e.g. STAY_OUT authorising 'do not box'). Better: forbid imperatives in the conversational path entirely and render every imperative deterministically from phrases.py.
findings.verifier_notes: Code-true. guardrails.py:394-398 is verbatim presence-only: `if pattern.search(clean) and not _action_is_permitted(action, evidence)`. No polarity handling exists anywhere in the module (grep for 'not'/'don' negation handling returns nothing; _ACTION_PATTERNS at 46-60 are bare \b word patterns). Re-executed: with scenarios.recommendation={preferred_scenario:'PIT_NOW', automatic_call_authorized:True} (which _permitted_actions:150-160 turns into evidence 'pit box'), validate('Do not box this lap.') -> allowed=True, while the deterministic fallback for the same result is 'Pit this lap, ...'. Exact inversion of the deterministic decision passes. | Confirmed by execution. guardrails.py:394-398 is purely presence-based: `pattern.search(clean) and not _action_is_permitted(action, evidence)`. Nothing inspects polarity. Repro: with get_strategy_status data {'scenarios':{'recommendation':{'preferred_scenario':'PIT_NOW','automatic_call_authorized':True}}}, validate('Do not box this lap.') -> allowed=True, while the deterministic fallback computed on the same input is 'Pit this lap, unavailable confidence.' The engine says pit now, the model is cleared to say the exact inverse, and the turn records PASS.

findings.title: Action allow-list is eleven literal phrases; equivalent imperatives pass completely unchecked
findings.why_wrong: This is a denylist of surface strings masquerading as an authority boundary. It enumerates box, pit, stay out, save fuel, save energy, push, back off, double stint, change tyres, change map, change brake bias. Any semantically identical instruction phrased differently is invisible to it, and an utterance carrying no digits also clears the numeric check trivially, so it reaches the driver as raw model audio.
findings.impact: Verified by execution against a minimal fuel tool result: 'Come in at the end of this lap.' -> allowed; 'Switch to wets now.' -> allowed; 'Do not stop, go long.' -> allowed; 'Short fill and go.' -> allowed; 'Let him by.' -> allowed; 'Double-stack behind him.' -> allowed; 'Retire the car.' -> allowed; 'Manage your fuel.' -> allowed. 'Come in at the end of this lap' is operationally identical to 'Box this lap', which the guardrail does police. The stated contract — the LLM may only render approved calls and may never invent recommendations — does not hold for any phrasing the author did not personally anticipate.
findings.fix: Invert the model: default-deny imperative mood. Classify the utterance's speech act (or require the model to return a structured {kind: 'statement'|'imperative', action_id} payload) and reject every imperative whose action_id is not in an explicit deterministic authorisation set. A phrase denylist can never be completed.
findings.verifier_notes: Code-true, not a style opinion. guardrails.py:46-60 contains exactly the eleven listed patterns and nothing else gates imperatives. Re-executed all eight of the finder's phrases against a minimal fuel result: 'Come in at the end of this lap.', 'Switch to wets now.', 'Do not stop, go long.', 'Short fill and go.', 'Let him by.', 'Double-stack behind him.', 'Retire the car.', 'Manage your fuel.' — every one allowed=True. Digit-free utterances also clear the numeric check vacuously (the loop at 378-386 iterates an empty list). The system prompt at voice/config.py:130-132 asserts the opposite contract ('Never issue box, stay out, save, push, ... instructions unless the deterministic recommended_action ... explicitly supports that exact action'); prose is the only thing enforcing it. | Confirmed by execution. _ACTION_PATTERNS (guardrails.py:46-61) is eleven surface regexes. Against a minimal {'estimated_per_lap_l':3.41} fuel result (zero action evidence), all of these returned allowed=True: 'Come in at the end of this lap.', 'Switch to wets now.', 'Do not stop, go long.', 'Short fill and go.', 'Let him by.', 'Double-stack behind him.', 'Retire the car.', 'Manage your fuel.' None contain digits, so the numeric check is also vacuous. 'Come in at the end of this lap' is operationally identical to 'Box this lap', which the same validator does reject. This is a denylist standing in for an authority boundary.

findings.title: Number regex ignores digits preceded by a letter, so "P3" position callouts are never validated
findings.quote: _DIGIT_NUMBER = re.compile(r"(?<![A-Za-z])[-+]?\d+(?:\.\d+)?")
findings.why_wrong: The negative lookbehind `(?<![A-Za-z])` was presumably meant to avoid matching version-like tokens, but it also blanks out the single most common way a race engineer states a position: P-notation. "P3" yields zero extracted numbers, so the numeric-fidelity check has nothing to compare and the utterance passes. The correctly-phrased alternative is caught, so the guardrail systematically pushes the model toward the unvalidated phrasing.
findings.impact: Verified by execution. With get_position_and_gaps returning {position: 8, gap_ahead_s: 1.2}: guardrail.validate('You are P3.') -> allowed=True (the driver is actually 8th); guardrail.validate('Currently running P1.') -> allowed=True; but guardrail.validate('You are in position 3.') -> blocked with unsupported_numbers=('3',). A driver told he is P3 when he is P8 makes wrong overtaking and fuel-saving decisions for the rest of the stint. The same hole covers car numbers ("car 51" is checked, "P51" is not) and class labels.
findings.fix: Drop the lookbehind and instead exclude only genuinely non-quantitative contexts, or add an explicit rule normalising P<n>/p<n> to the integer n before validation and checking it against the position field.
findings.verifier_notes: Code-true. guardrails.py:13 is verbatim `_DIGIT_NUMBER = re.compile(r"(?<![A-Za-z])[-+]?\d+(?:\.\d+)?")` and it is the sole digit extractor (used at line 70). Re-executed against {position:8, gap_ahead_s:1.2}: 'You are P3.' -> allowed=True, 'Currently running P1.' -> allowed=True, 'You are in position 3.' -> blocked with unsupported_numbers=('3',). The guardrail therefore validates the less idiomatic phrasing and waves through the standard one. The word-number branch does not rescue it either ('P3' tokenises as 'P' + no number word). | Confirmed by execution. guardrails.py:13 `_DIGIT_NUMBER = re.compile(r"(?<![A-Za-z])[-+]?\d+(?:\.\d+)?")`. With get_position_and_gaps {'position':8,'gap_ahead_s':1.2}: validate('You are P3.') -> allowed=True and validate('Currently running P1.') -> allowed=True (driver is actually 8th), while validate('You are in position 3.') -> allowed=False with unsupported_numbers=('3',). The lookbehind blanks out the most common engineer phrasing for position and systematically rewards the unvalidated form.

findings.title: Teammate radio text is spoken to the driver without passing any validator
findings.quote:
self._enqueue(
            text=message.text,
            priority="NORMAL",
            priority_rank=250,
            expires_utc=message.expires_utc,
            source="TEAM_SYNC",
findings.why_wrong: on_team_radio_message takes TeamRadioMessage.text straight from a WebSocket frame received by TeamSyncClient._connected_loop (src/ssc_engineer/team_sync.py:253-262) and enqueues it for TTS. The only checks applied are in TeamRadioMessage.from_payload (team_sync.py:43-55): non-empty and len <= 1200. No numeric-fidelity check, no action check, no radio-length check, and no speaker attribution is prefixed, so the driver hears it in the same engineer voice as a deterministic call. expires_utc is also attacker-supplied and used verbatim as the queue expiry.
findings.impact: A compromised or malicious team gateway, or any teammate running a modified client, can say anything into the driver's headset with full engineer authority — "Box this lap", "You have four laps of fuel left", or 1200 characters of TTS (roughly 80 seconds) that monopolises the radio queue while a real critical call expires behind it. The product's central claim that every call is deterministic or validated is false for this channel.
findings.fix: Run TeamRadioMessage.text through TranscriptGuardrail (or a stricter deterministic-only allow-list) before enqueueing, cap the length at radio-discipline limits, clamp expires_utc to a locally computed bound, and prefix the utterance with the sender identity so the driver can tell it apart from the engineer.

Confirmed additionally that queue.py:74-96 (_mode_suppression/_profile_suppression) both early-return None unless source=='AUTOMATIC', so TEAM_SYNC skips operating-mode and driver-profile suppression too, and no guardrail call exists on this path (the only guardrail.validate call site in src/ is orchestrator.py:691). | Confirmed by code path. team_sync.py:262 `self.on_message(message)` is wired to orchestrator.on_team_radio_message via runtime.py:191, and orchestrator.py:304-315 passes message.text straight to _enqueue with priority_rank=250 and attacker-supplied expires_utc. The only checks are TeamRadioMessage.from_payload (team_sync.py:43-55): type=='engineer_call', non-empty fields, len<=MAX_SYNC_TEXT (team_sync.py:25 = 1_200). TranscriptGuardrail.validate is never invoked on this path (grep confirms orchestrator.py:691 is its sole call site in src/), and no speaker attribution is prefixed, so it is rendered in the same engineer voice as a deterministic call.

findings.title: Config permits 16/44.1/48 kHz but the Realtime API is fixed at 24 kHz, breaking audio in both directions
findings.quote:
if self.sample_rate_hz not in {16000, 24000, 44100, 48000}:
            raise ConfigError("sample_rate_hz must be 16000, 24000, 44100, or 48000.")
findings.why_wrong: OpenAIRealtimeConversationBackend sends the raw capture with no resampling (realtime_backend.py:373-377, `await self._session.send_audio(block, commit=final)`) after declaring `"format": self.config.input_format` = "pcm16". The installed Agents SDK maps "pcm16" to a hard-coded 24 kHz stream (.venv/.../agents/realtime/audio_formats.py:23-24: `format = AudioPCM(type="audio/pcm", rate=24000)`). Symmetrically, _complete_collector labels the model's reply with `sample_rate_hz=self.config.sample_rate_hz` (realtime_backend.py:351) even though the API always returns 24 kHz, and playback.py:48-51 hands that wrong rate to the resampler.
findings.impact: With the supported setting sample_rate_hz=48000 (a very common headset native rate, reachable through validate_output_configuration), the driver's 48 kHz microphone PCM is interpreted by the API as 24 kHz — the model hears half-speed, octave-down speech and transcription is garbage — while the model's 24 kHz reply is resampled as if it were 48 kHz and plays back at double speed an octave high. The entire PTT conversation channel is unusable, with no error anywhere; diagnostics still reports realtime_connected=True.
findings.fix: Either reject any sample_rate_hz other than 24000 when enable_realtime is true, or resample the capture to 24 kHz before send_audio and hard-code sample_rate_hz=24000 in the ConversationResponse instead of echoing the config.

Return path confirmed: realtime_backend.py:351 `sample_rate_hz=self.config.sample_rate_hz` mislabels the always-24 kHz reply, and playback.py:47-50 forwards item.sample_rate_hz to SoundDeviceAudioOutput's resampler (output.py:227). Mitigating context: the default is 24000 (config.py:379), so this bites only a user who changes it — but the change is offered and accepted by validation (ui/settings.py:643 re-validates and passes). | Confirmed. config.py:477-478 accepts {16000,24000,44100,48000}. capture.py:89 opens RawInputStream(samplerate=self.config.sample_rate_hz) and realtime_backend.py:392-395 sends those raw bytes with no resampling after declaring `"format": self.config.input_format` = 'pcm16'. The installed SDK at .venv/lib/python3.11/site-packages/agents/realtime/audio_formats.py:24 maps that to `AudioPCM(type="audio/pcm", rate=24000)` unconditionally. findings.title: Microphone capture buffer is unbounded and has no time or size cap
findings.quote: self._frames.append(block)
findings.why_wrong: SoundDeviceAudioInput has no cap on _frames. The only bound on capture duration is PTTEdgeController.maximum_hold_s, enforced in a completely different module and only on the happy path where _read_pressed keeps succeeding (see the joystick-disconnect finding). start_capture (capture.py:75-104) and stop_capture (capture.py:106-130) impose no limit of their own, and _handle_conversation feeds the whole buffer to submit_audio with no length check.
findings.impact: If the release edge is never delivered (PTT adapter error, joystick unplug, a virtual key latched down by another application), capture runs indefinitely at 24 kHz mono 16-bit = 48 KB/s, roughly 170 MB per hour of process memory in a real-time application sharing a machine with a racing simulator, until the process is OOM-killed mid-race. If a release does eventually arrive, a multi-minute PCM blob is chunked and uploaded to the Realtime API in one turn.
findings.fix: Enforce the cap in the owner of the buffer: stop recording (or drop blocks) in _callback once accumulated audio exceeds config.ptt_max_duration_s, and have stop_capture truncate to that bound.
findings.verifier_notes: The code fact is true — capture.py:70 is verbatim `self._frames.append(block)` and neither start_capture (75-104) nor stop_capture (106-130) imposes any cap — but the impact is overstated and its stated trigger is gone. In practice PTTEdgeController bounds a held button at config.ptt_max_duration_s, default 20.0 (config.py:397, wired at ptt.py:131), which is ~960 KB at 24 kHz mono, and the joystick-disconnect latch the finding leans on does not happen (see that finding). KeyboardPTT._read_pressed (ptt.py:204-205) is a bare GetAsyncKeyState call with no realistic persistent-raise mode. What remains is a genuine defensive gap — the only bound lives in a different module and only on the path where _read_pressed keeps succeeding — not a 170 MB/hour production leak. | The missing cap at capture.py:70 is real, but no concrete path to the claimed consequence exists. All three triggers the finding names are covered by PTTEdgeController.feed's stuck-hold safety (ptt.py:65-77), which emits ('STUCK','RELEASE') at maximum_hold_s and is driven from config.py:397 `ptt_max_duration_s: float = 20.0`, and orchestrator.on_ptt_release (orchestrator.py:538-548) calls audio_input.stop_capture() on that release like any other. Joystick unplug: feed() keeps being called, as proven in the previous finding, so the release fires in ~1 s. Virtual key latched by another application: the keyboard adapter's GetAsyncKeyState poll does not raise, so feed() runs every 10 ms and the 20 s stuck release fires. That bounds a capture at 24 kHz mono 16-bit to about 960 KB, not the 170 MB/hour claimed. No OOM, and no multi-minute blob reaching submit_audio.

findings.title: Driver's own answer is silently discarded in RADIO_SILENCE, and the model can enter that mode itself
findings.quote:
if self._radio_mode == "RADIO_SILENCE":
            return item.priority_rank >= 300
findings.why_wrong: orchestrator.py:733-741 enqueues the answer to a PTT question with priority_rank=260 and source='DRIVER_RESPONSE'. 260 < 300, so _radio_allows returns False, _enqueue drops it via _drop_locked(item, 'RADIO_SUPPRESSED', ...) (queue.py:148-150) and returns False, and orchestrator.py:746-753 marks the turn DROPPED. The driver pressed the button, asked a question, the model answered and the tools ran — and nothing is ever spoken, with no tone, no state change and no error. Separately, set_radio_mode is exposed to the model as a callable tool (agent_tools.py:253-256) and its result claims {"critical_calls_suppressed": False} (tools.py:202) even though rank-290 HIGH-priority FASTER_CLASS_APPROACHING calls (arbitration.py:212-213) are also suppressed at this threshold.
findings.impact: A driver who earlier said "radio silence" — or whose model decided on its own to call set_radio_mode — gets total silence in response to every direct question for the rest of the stint, with no indication that the system heard him. He will assume the app has crashed, or worse, treat the silence as an answer. The tool simultaneously reports to the model that no critical call is suppressed, which is untrue at rank 290.
findings.fix: Treat a direct response to an explicit driver PTT turn as always allowed (it is by definition solicited): either give DRIVER_RESPONSE a rank at or above the RADIO_SILENCE threshold, or bypass _radio_allows for source=='DRIVER_RESPONSE'. Fix the critical_calls_suppressed claim to reflect the real rank-300 cut, or raise all HIGH-priority ranks above it.
findings.verifier_notes: Code-true end to end. queue.py:68-69 verbatim `if self._radio_mode == "RADIO_SILENCE": return item.priority_rank >= 300`; orchestrator.py:733-744 enqueues the answer with priority_rank=260 and source='DRIVER_RESPONSE'; _enqueue rejects it at queue.py:148-150 with _drop_locked(item,'RADIO_SUPPRESSED',...) and returns False; orchestrator.py:746-753 then marks the turn DROPPED with no tone or state change. The secondary claims also check out: set_radio_mode is model-callable at agent_tools.py:254-256, tools.py:202 is verbatim `{"radio_mode": normalized, "critical_calls_suppressed": False}`, and communication/arbitration.py:215-216 assigns FASTER_CLASS_APPROACHING rank 290, which is below the 300 threshold. (Note queue.py:66-67 does exempt priority=='IMMEDIATE' unconditionally, so genuinely IMMEDIATE calls are not suppressed; the false 'critical_calls_suppressed: False' claim is about rank-290 HIGH traffic calls, as the finding states. The path is src/ssc_engineer/communication/arbitration.py, not src/ssc_engineer/arbitration.py.) | Confirmed by code path. orchestrator.py:729-741 enqueues with priority='NORMAL', priority_rank=260, source='DRIVER_RESPONSE'; queue.py:67-69 `if self._radio_mode == "RADIO_SILENCE": return item.priority_rank >= 300`, and the IMMEDIATE bypass at queue.py:66 does not apply because the priority is NORMAL. _enqueue then hits `if not self._radio_allows(item): self._drop_locked(item, "RADIO_SUPPRESSED", ...); return False` (queue.py:148-150), and orchestrator.py:746-753 marks the turn DROPPED with no tone or state change. findings.title: Audio device failure on the model-audio path escapes the TTS fallback and leaves the turn unfinished forever
findings.quote:
if item.audio_pcm is not None:
            stream = SpeechStream(
                chunks=(item.audio_pcm,),
                sample_rate_hz=item.sample_rate_hz,
                backend="OPENAI_REALTIME",

SoundDeviceAudioOutput.play raises AudioUnavailable on device loss (output.py:306-311) and UnavailableAudioOutput.play raises it unconditionally (audio_io.py:121-123). Unlike the text branch just below it (playback.py:54-84), which catches AudioUnavailable and falls through to the next backend, this branch has no handler, so the exception unwinds past _speech_worker's per-item bookkeeping into the generic `except Exception` at playback.py:185.

findings.title: State-changing tools are exposed to the model with no deterministic confirmation gate
findings.quote: def set_lico_fuel_target(target_remaining_laps: float, reserve_l: float) -> dict[str, Any]:
findings.why_wrong: set_lico_fuel_target, clear_lico_fuel_target, set_radio_mode and acknowledge_call/acknowledge_latest_call are all registered as model-callable tools with tool_choice='auto' (realtime_backend.py:162). The only thing between a hallucinated or injected tool call and a real state change is prose in the system prompt (voice/config.py:121-125: "Only set or clear a LICO goal when explicitly requested by the driver"). The deterministic layer performs no check that the driver actually asked: tool_lico.py:205-214 forwards straight to the bridge, and the sole validation is a range check inside LicoEngineerBridge.set_fuel_target (src/ssc_engineer/lico_client.py:365: 0 < laps <= 200 and 0 <= reserve <= 200).
findings.impact: Any value inside that wide range is accepted, so a misheard "twelve" as "forty" silently reconfigures the live lift-and-coast fuel goal the driver is racing to, and acknowledge_latest_call can dismiss a safety call the driver never heard — after which arbitration.py:559-571 suppresses re-raising it under ACKNOWLEDGED_SUPPRESSED. Combined with the opponent-name prompt-injection surface, an external party can trigger these. The architecture explicitly promises the model cannot change deterministic state; these five tools break that promise.
findings.fix: Split read tools from write tools and require a deterministic confirmation for every write: match the driver's own ASR transcript against an explicit command pattern (interpret_driver_command already exists for exactly this) before the write executes, and return unavailable when no matching driver utterance is present in the current turn.
