findings.title: No test pins the production release-signing public key; every signature test injects a fresh keypair
findings.why_wrong: `grep -rn TRUSTED_RELEASE_PUBLIC_KEYS tests/` returns nothing. tests/team/test_release_manifest_v014.py:22 and tests/team/test_v08_services.py:69 both call `Ed25519PrivateKey.generate()` and pass their own `trusted_public_keys=` override, so the constant that every real installation actually trusts is never loaded, never length-checked, and never matched against a manifest produced by the real signing tooling.
findings.impact: README.md:88 states "updates are trusted only after Ed25519 manifest verification". If this constant were ever corrupted, truncated, or left pointing at a key whose private half is lost, every update would fail verification (or, worse, a wrong key would be shipped) and the suite would stay green — the signature machinery is proven, the trust anchor is not.
findings.fix: Add a test asserting the key id set and that each value decodes to exactly 32 bytes, plus a fixture manifest signed by the real release key checked into the repo that `verify_release_manifest_signature` must accept with the default `trusted_public_keys`.
findings.verifier_notes: The narrow claim is true (no test imports TRUSTED_RELEASE_PUBLIC_KEYS; test_cli_v05.py:115 only asserts _release_self_test's re-export identity), but the stated impact is already mitigated in code the finder did not read. cli.py:626-636 pins the anchor hard: `if set(TRUSTED_RELEASE_PUBLIC_KEYS) != {key_id}: raise RuntimeError("unexpected trusted release-key set")` and `if len(public_key) != 32 or fingerprint != expected_fingerprint: raise RuntimeError("embedded release trust anchor did not match")` against a hardcoded sha256 10b8dc26…. That check runs as `--release-self-test`, which scripts/validation/smoke_packaged_app.py:346-357 invokes and asserts (`self_test_payload.get("ok") is not True -> RuntimeError`), and windows-ci.yml:87 runs that smoke test. A corrupted or truncated key fails CI, so 'the suite would stay green' is false. | Confirmed. grep for TRUSTED_RELEASE_PUBLIC_KEYS across the repo hits only src/ (cli.py:626-632, v1_release.py:25/261, updater.py:17/49/137, release_manifest.py:27/63) and never tests/; tests/team/test_v08_services.py:69-71 and tests/team/test_publish_release.py:36 both do `Ed25519PrivateKey.generate()` and pass `trusted_public_keys=` overrides, so the shipped 32-byte constant at release_manifest.py:27-33 is never loaded or length-checked. Low is right: a corrupted or wrong constant fails closed (verification rejects the manifest), so the exposure is bricked updates, not a forged-update breach as the finding's 'or, worse' aside implies.

findings.title: _live_run is a 1,378-line, 301-branch god function holding the entire race loop
findings.why_wrong: This single function spans lines 385-1762 (1,378 lines) of a 1,762-line module — 78% of the file. AST analysis counts 301 branch points (If/For/While/Try/BoolOp/IfExp/ExceptHandler/comprehension), 158 distinct assigned local names, and 6 nested closures (publish_post_race_results, queue_committed_post_race_sessions, persist_lico_executions, publish_health_report, refresh_runtime_health, stop_noncritical_recording) that close over that 158-name local scope. It owns telemetry reading, the engineering pipeline, strategy, voice, LICO, persistence, health publication, post-race export, dashboard rendering and shutdown simultaneously. Nothing inside it can be unit-tested in isolation, because every seam is a local variable rather than a parameter or an object.
findings.impact: A change to, say, post-race export ordering requires reading 1,378 lines to know which of 158 locals are live at that point. Because the 6 closures capture the whole scope, an early-return path added anywhere above them can leave a closure referencing an unbound local and raise UnboundLocalError only on the rare path that triggers it — i.e. mid-race, in the process that owns the driver's radio. It is also the reason the module cannot be covered: the repo's 32k LOC of tests cannot exercise a code path inside it without standing up the whole runtime.
findings.fix: Extract the closures into methods of an explicit LiveRunSession class whose fields replace the 158 locals, then split the body along its natural phases (setup / per-frame pipeline / health publication / shutdown) into separate methods. Start with the 6 closures, which already declare their own boundaries.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified exactly. AST of src/ssc_engineer/runtime/service.py puts _live_run at lineno 385, end_lineno 1762 in a 1762-line file; my own walk counts 301 branch nodes (If/For/While/Try/BoolOp/IfExp/ExceptHandler/comprehension), 158 distinct Store-context local names, and precisely the 6 nested defs named: publish_post_race_results, queue_committed_post_race_sessions, persist_lico_executions, publish_health_report, refresh_runtime_health, stop_noncritical_recording. It is the only function in the module past line 385. No mitigation anywhere — there is no seam, no injected collaborator, and the closures do capture the full local scope. | Every metric reproduces exactly. AST over src/ssc_engineer/runtime/service.py: _live_run spans lines 385-1762 (1378 lines of a 1762-line module, and it is the last top-level def in the file), 301 branch nodes, 158 Store-context local names. The six named closures are all present (publish_post_race_results:556, queue_committed_post_race_sessions:583, persist_lico_executions:600, publish_health_report:609, refresh_runtime_health:815, stop_noncritical_recording:847). Downgraded to medium because the claimed concrete failure is prospective, not present: the UnboundLocalError scenario requires a future early-return to be added above a closure, and I could not construct one on the code as it stands today. The verified defect is maintainability and untestability, not a reproducible runtime fault.

findings.title: The limiting-resource calculation is implemented twice, and the two implementations disagree
findings.why_wrong: The identical decision — which consumable limits the stint — is computed a second time in `src/ssc_engineer/strategy_scenarios.py:57-73` (`StrategyScenarioEngine._resource_laps`) from the same two inputs (`derived.fuel_model.projected_usable_laps`, `derived.ve_model.laps_remaining`). The two disagree on tie handling: models.py:136-137 emits `limiting = "BALANCED"` when `abs(resources[0][1] - resources[1][1]) < 0.15`, while `_resource_laps` has no BALANCED branch at all and always returns a concrete resource name from `min()`. Separately, both mix incompatible units: `fuel.projected_usable_laps` is computed in engineering/fuel.py:36-38 *after* subtracting `reserve_l`, whereas `ve.laps_remaining` is computed in engineering/virtual_energy.py:38 as `snapshot.virtual_energy_pct / rate` with no reserve deduction — and `VirtualEnergyModelState` (contracts/engineering.py:158-183) has no reserve-adjusted usable-laps field at all, so the reserve-adjusted VE figure computed at virtual_energy.py:40-44 is discarded and cannot be used.
findings.impact: With fuel usable 5.00 laps and VE gross 5.05 laps, the Control Center and pit-wall render `limiting_resource = "BALANCED"` (models.py:137) while the voice engineer's strategy recommendation, driven by `_resource_laps`, reports the limit as "FUEL" — two contradictory answers to the driver from one telemetry frame. And because fuel is reserve-adjusted and VE is not, `strategy_laps_remaining` (models.py:131, rendered at dashboard.py:185 and pitwall.py:491) is optimistic by the full VE reserve whenever VE is the constraint, and VE is systematically under-reported as the limiting resource.
findings.fix: Add `projected_usable_laps` to VirtualEnergyModelState and populate it from the `usable_laps` already computed at virtual_energy.py:40-44, then delete `StrategyScenarioEngine._resource_laps` and have strategy_scenarios call one shared helper that returns (laps, resource, confidence) including the BALANCED case.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed on all three sub-claims. models.py:126-139 builds the resources list and emits "BALANCED" at the <0.15 tie branch; strategy_scenarios.py:57-73 _resource_laps builds the same list from the same two fields and returns min() with no BALANCED arm, and its output is unpacked as `resource_laps, limiting_resource, resource_confidence` at strategy_recommendations.py:30 and strategy_evaluation.py:119 — so it really does feed the spoken recommendation, not just internal scoring. Unit mismatch confirmed: engineering/fuel.py:36-38 computes usable_laps as `max(0.0, snapshot.fuel_l - (reserve_l or 0.0)) / rate`, while engineering/virtual_energy.py:85 returns `laps_remaining=gross_laps` with gross_laps computed at line 38 with no reserve. Kept at high rather than raised to critical: config.py:63 `ve_reserve_laps: float = 0.1`, so the over-report when VE limits is ~0.1 lap by default, not a gross error. One small overstatement: the reserve-adjusted VE figure is not fully discarded — it survives as projected_stint_laps/projected_completion_lap (virtual_energy.py:98-103) — but it is indeed absent from laps_remaining, which is the field both consumers read. | Fully reproducible. engineering/models.py:126-138 builds resources from fuel.projected_usable_laps and ve.laps_remaining, emits "BALANCED" when abs(delta) < 0.15; strategy_scenarios.py:57-73 _resource_laps builds the same two-element list from the same two fields and returns min() with no BALANCED arm. The contradiction reaches two live surfaces: derived.limiting_resource renders at pitwall.py:494 and dashboard.py:193 and feeds communication/context.py:270, while _resource_laps drives strategy_recommendations.py:30 whose rationale text at :40/:51 interpolates limiting_resource. Fuel 5.00 / VE 5.05 gives "BALANCED" on the pit wall and "FUEL does not support another lap" on the radio from one frame. The unit mismatch is confirmed at the source: engineering/fuel.py:108 projected_usable_laps=usable_laps (computed at :37-39 after subtracting reserve_l) versus engineering/virtual_energy.py laps_remaining=gross_laps (snapshot.virtual_energy_pct / rate, no reserve), with config.py:63 ve_reserve_laps=0.1 — i.e. the systematic bias (0.1 laps) is the same order as the 0.15-lap tie window, so it can flip the BALANCED decision itself. One sub-claim is slightly overstated: VE's reserve-adjusted usable_laps is not entirely discarded, it feeds projected_stint_laps and projected_completion_lap; it is simply not what laps_remaining carries. That does not affect the defect.

findings.title: The headless loopback API is layered on top of the Tk GUI package and imports a private name across it
findings.why_wrong: `api/server.py` is documented at line 1 as a stdlib-only loopback HTTP API, but it depends on `..ui.controller`, `..ui.presentation` (15 symbols, lines 36-51) and `..ui.privacy` (line 52). Importing `ssc_engineer.ui.controller` executes `ssc_engineer/ui/__init__.py`, which eagerly imports `.application`, `.control_center`, `.hardware` and `.settings` — the entire Tk view stack. I measured this: `import ssc_engineer.api.server` pulls in 188 `ssc_engineer` modules, versus 94 for the engineering core alone. It also reaches across the package boundary for a *private* symbol, `_voice_config`, used at server.py:554.
findings.impact: The Electron shell's host process (`python -m ssc_engineer.api`, api/__main__.py:33) loads the whole Tkinter Control Center it exists to replace. Any refactor of the private `_voice_config` silently breaks the shell, and mypy/Ruff will not flag it because a leading-underscore cross-package import is legal Python. The layering is inverted: the presentation layer is now the API's dependency rather than its consumer.
findings.fix: Move `readiness_summary`, `component_indicators`, `telemetry_values` and the other pure formatters out of `ui/presentation.py` into a GUI-free `presentation/` package that both `ui/` and `api/` import, promote `_voice_config` to a public function in `config.py`, and stop `ui/__init__.py` from eagerly importing the Tk view modules.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed. api/server.py:1-8 documents itself as "Stdlib only"; lines 31-52 import from ..ui.controller (including the private `_voice_config`), ..ui.presentation (15 symbols) and ..ui.privacy. ui/__init__.py:3-16 eagerly imports .application, .control_center, .controller, .hardware, .presentation, .settings and .theme, so the whole Tk view stack is pulled in. `_voice_config` use confirmed at server.py:554 (`current = _voice_config(self.paths)`). I could not reproduce the exact 188-vs-94 module count on this box (importing ssc_engineer.api.server dies earlier in a vendored cryptography binding), but the import edges themselves are verbatim and unguarded — no lazy import, no TYPE_CHECKING block, no try/except. | Confirmed. api/server.py:1-7 documents "Stdlib only"; :31-35 imports DesktopError, DesktopRuntimeSnapshot, _voice_config and export_support_bundle from ..ui.controller, :36-51 imports 15 symbols from ..ui.presentation, :52 imports ..ui.privacy. ui/__init__.py:3-16 eagerly imports .application, .control_center, .controller, .hardware, .presentation, .settings and .theme, so the Tk view stack loads transitively. The private cross-package symbol is genuinely used at server.py:554 (current = _voice_config(self.paths)). Downgraded to medium: on the shipped Windows target tkinter is always present, so there is no crash or user-visible failure — the confirmed harm is inverted layering, import bloat in the shell host, and a private-symbol coupling no linter will flag. That is a real architecture defect, not a production fault.

findings.title: The runtime core unconditionally imports tkinter through pitwall.py
findings.quote: from ..pitwall import PitWallClosed, PitWallDisplay, UIUnavailable
findings.why_wrong: `pitwall.py` is a 633-line Tkinter GUI (`import tkinter as tk` at pitwall.py:5) that lives at the top level of the package rather than under `ui/`. `runtime/service.py` — the module that owns the live telemetry loop and the whole engineering pipeline — imports it at module scope, so tkinter is loaded even for `--json` and `--no-ui` runs where `PitWallDisplay` is never instantiated (it is only constructed under `if args.ui` at service.py:374 and 427). I verified the hard failure: `import ssc_engineer.runtime.service` raises `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'tkinter'` at service.py:49 on any interpreter built without the Tk bindings.
findings.impact: The engineering core cannot be imported, tested, benchmarked or run headlessly without a GUI toolkit present. A CI runner, container or minimal Python build with `_tkinter` absent cannot import the race runtime at all, even to check a fuel calculation. It also means three separate UI surfaces (ui/, pitwall.py, dashboard.py) hang off the core with no shared boundary.
findings.fix: Move `pitwall.py` under `ui/`, and import `PitWallDisplay` lazily inside the two `if args.ui` branches at service.py:374 and 427 — the pattern the same file already uses for `debug_telemetry`, `iracing_reader`, `lico.adapters` and `voice.runtime` (all function-level imports).
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed and reproduced. service.py:49 is exactly `from ..pitwall import PitWallClosed, PitWallDisplay, UIUnavailable` at module scope; pitwall.py:5 is a bare `import tkinter as tk` with no guard. Running `python3 -c "import ssc_engineer.runtime.service"` from src/ on this interpreter fails with ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'tkinter', traceback terminating at service.py:49 -> pitwall.py:5. PitWallDisplay is only constructed under `if args.ui` (service.py:374, 427), so the import is genuinely unnecessary for --json/--no-ui. This is not the excluded "Windows-only API on Linux" case: tkinter is an optional stdlib module absent on plenty of Linux CI images and minimal builds, and the defect is the architectural coupling, which is platform-independent. | Confirmed with a hard repro. runtime/service.py:49 'from ..pitwall import PitWallClosed, PitWallDisplay, UIUnavailable' at module scope; pitwall.py:5 'import tkinter as tk' at module scope (633 lines, top-level of the package, not under ui/). On this interpreter 'import tkinter' raises ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'tkinter', so importing ssc_engineer.runtime.service is impossible without Tk bindings even for --json/--no-ui runs, where PitWallDisplay is only constructed inside 'if not args.no_ui and not args.json' (service.py:374 and 427). This is a genuine, reproducible barrier to headless import of the engineering core.

findings.title: No traceback is ever captured for a caught exception anywhere in the package
findings.quote:
def _record_failure(self, exc: Exception) -> None:
    with self._state_lock:
        self._failures += 1
        self._last_error = f"{type(exc).__name__}: {exc}"
        self._state = "DEGRADED"
findings.why_wrong: I grepped the whole of `src/` for `import traceback`, `format_exc`, `print_exc`, `exc_info` and `.exception(` — zero hits. There are 100 `except Exception` sites, 20 `with suppress(Exception)` blocks, and 34 places that reduce a caught exception to `type(exc).__name__` (13 of which drop even the message, e.g. runtime/model_worker.py:229 `self._last_error = type(exc).__name__[:80]`, ui/controller.py:243 `self._learning_error = type(exc).__name__`, persistence/records.py:187 and :206). The project has a full structured logger (runtime/structured_log.py) and a crash reporter that *does* walk frames (crash_reporting.py:73-86) — but the crash reporter only fires for *unhandled* exceptions. Every handled failure, which is exactly the class of failure that leaves the engineer running but degraded, is stored as a string with the stack discarded.
findings.impact: A SQLite writer that goes DEGRADED mid-race records `"OperationalError: database is locked"` and nothing else — no statement, no call site, no frame. There is no way to diagnose it from the support bundle, and the same type name can originate from a dozen call sites in persistence/writer.py's 827 lines. Field diagnosis of any degraded (non-crashing) subsystem is impossible.
findings.fix: Add an `exception(...)` method to `runtime/structured_log.StructuredLogger` that attaches `traceback.format_exception(exc)` (bounded and redacted through the existing `redact_log_value`), and call it from the ~34 sites that currently stringify `type(exc).__name__`, starting with persistence/writer.py:625, runtime/model_worker.py:229 and voice/orchestrator.py.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed by independent grep: `import traceback`, `format_exc`, `print_exc`, `exc_info`, `.exception(` return exactly 0 hits across src/. The only TracebackType use in the package is crash_reporting.py (lines 13, 66, 156, 186, 206-208), and every self.capture() call site is inside the excepthook installers — nothing in a normal except block calls it. writer.py:622-626 is verbatim as quoted, reducing the exception to `f"{type(exc).__name__}: {exc}"`. The claimed mitigation does not exist. | Confirmed. A grep of src/ for 'import traceback', 'format_exc', 'print_exc', 'exc_info' and '.exception(' returns zero non-pycache hits. Counts are close to the claim: 100 'except Exception' sites, 19 (not 20) 'with suppress(Exception)' blocks, 70 occurrences of type(exc).__name__. The cited quote is exact at persistence/writer.py:622-626, storing only f"{type(exc).__name__}: {exc}" and flipping _state to DEGRADED. The failure scenario is concrete: a DEGRADED SQLite writer records only 'OperationalError: database is locked' with no statement, call site or frame, and writer.py is 827 lines with many candidate origins. Diagnosability of any handled-but-degraded subsystem is genuinely nil.

findings.title: The voice failure recorder swallows its own failure with `except Exception: pass`
findings.quote:
except Exception:
            pass
findings.why_wrong: This is the sole `except Exception: pass` in `src/`, and it is inside `_record_failure` (orchestrator.py:465-487) — the function whose only purpose is to persist a voice-subsystem failure (component, code, message, recoverability, state, turn_id) to the voice database. If `_ensure_persistence_session()` or `store_failure()` raises, the entire failure record is discarded with no trace. It is compounded by `_set_state` at orchestrator.py:149, which wraps `self.persistence.update_state(...)` in `with suppress(Exception)` — so voice state transitions are silently dropped too.
findings.impact: If the voice SQLite file becomes unwritable (disk full, AV lock, corrupted schema) at the start of a race, every subsequent PTT error, backend disconnect and degraded-state transition is silently discarded for the whole session. The engineer keeps reporting a healthy-looking state, and the post-race evidence shows a session with zero failures — the exact opposite of the truth. `_last_error` is set at orchestrator.py:473 before the try, so the in-memory string survives, but nothing is persisted and no operator is ever told persistence stopped working.
findings.fix: Catch the narrow database errors, set a distinct `self._last_error = "Voice failure persistence unavailable"` and force `VoiceState.DEGRADED`, so the operator sees that failure recording itself has failed. Never `pass` in the failure-recording path.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed verbatim. voice/orchestrator.py:464-487: `_record_failure` sets `self._last_error = message`, then wraps `_ensure_persistence_session()` and `persistence.store_failure(...)` in try/`except Exception: pass` at lines 486-487. My grep across src/ finds exactly one `except Exception` immediately followed by `pass`, matching the finder's claim that it is the sole instance. The compounding `with suppress(Exception): self.persistence.update_state(...)` is confirmed at orchestrator.py:148-155. No logger call, no counter, no state flag records that persistence stopped working. | Confirmed verbatim. voice/orchestrator.py:465-487: _record_failure sets self._last_error = message at :473, then wraps _ensure_persistence_session() and persistence.store_failure(...) in try/except Exception: pass at :486-487. This is the only 'except Exception:' immediately followed by 'pass' in src/ (grep count: 1). The compounding claim also holds: _set_state at orchestrator.py:149 wraps persistence.update_state(...) in 'with suppress(Exception)'. Concrete scenario is constructible: an unwritable voice DB at session start means every PTT error, backend disconnect and DEGRADED transition for the whole race is discarded, and the post-race evidence shows zero failures — the exact inversion of the truth, with no operator signal.

findings.title: engineering/ is a nominal layer: 79 flat root modules (28,312 lines) sit outside it, and engineering/ imports upward into them
findings.quote: from ..strategy import PitServiceModel
findings.why_wrong: `src/ssc_engineer/` has 79 top-level `.py` files totalling 28,312 lines — 34% of the package — living beside the subpackages rather than inside them, and they are unambiguously engineering-domain modules: decision.py (582), endurance.py (648), car_health.py (632), opponents.py (737), opponent_strategy.py (715), pit_operations.py (610), track_segments.py (902), calibration.py (777), qualifying.py, weather.py, race_control.py, setup_engineering.py, fatigue.py, tracker.py, plus ten `strategy_*.py` modules. Meanwhile `engineering/` holds only 11 files, and it imports *upward* into the root: I enumerated `..config`, `..model`, `..decision`, `..endurance`, `..fatigue`, `..race_control`, `..strategy`, `..track_segments`, `..weather`, `..pit_operations`, `..setup_engineering`, `..source_capabilities`, `..car_health`. Only `contracts/` is a genuine layer (I verified it has zero `from ..` imports).
findings.impact: The package boundary conveys no information: a reader cannot tell from the tree which module owns pit strategy (strategy_pit.py at root? engineering/stint.py? strategy_scenarios.py?), and the import direction gives no dependency ordering to reason with. Any attempt to extract the engineering core as a testable unit drags in 70 root modules. This is the root cause of several other findings here — the duplicated resource calculation, the duplicated pit-window status and the duplicated fuel model all exist because there is no single place the domain lives.
findings.fix: Either move the 70 domain modules under `engineering/` and invert the imports so `engineering/` depends only on `contracts/` and `config`, or drop the `engineering/` package and admit the flat layout. The current half-move is worse than either.
findings.verifier_notes: Numbers reproduce exactly: `ls src/ssc_engineer/*.py | wc -l` = 79, `cat src/ssc_engineer/*.py | wc -l` = 28312. engineering/ contains 10 modules plus __init__. The quoted upward import is verbatim at engineering/session.py:21 (`from ..strategy import PitServiceModel`), sitting in a block with ..pit_operations, ..race_control, ..setup_engineering, ..track_segments, ..weather at lines 18-23. The contracts/ control claim also holds: zero `^from ..` lines under contracts/. | Numbers reproduce exactly: 79 .py files directly under src/ssc_engineer/ totalling 28,312 lines; engineering/ holds 11 files. The quoted upward import is exact at engineering/session.py:21 'from ..strategy import PitServiceModel', and enumerating 'from ..' across engineering/*.py yields ..config, ..model, ..decision, ..endurance, ..fatigue, ..race_control, ..strategy, ..track_segments, ..weather, ..pit_operations, ..setup_engineering, ..source_capabilities, ..car_health — all thirteen as claimed. contracts/ is indeed clean (zero 'from ..' hits). Downgraded to medium: this is an accurate structural observation with no runtime failure mode of its own — its cost is realised through the duplication findings (2, 11, 12), which are reported separately and should carry the severity.

findings.title: cli.py ships a hand-maintained 165-module / 284-symbol import manifest invisible to static analysis
findings.quote:
def _release_self_test() -> int:
    """Import frozen production entry points that are otherwise loaded lazily."""
findings.why_wrong: The `checks` dict at cli.py:235 has 165 module-name keys mapping to 284 symbol-name strings, driven through `importlib.import_module(module_name)` at cli.py:586. Every entry is a hand-typed string duplicating the module graph — `"ssc_engineer.ui.test_program": ("TestProgramPane",)`, `"ssc_engineer.strategy_scenario_support": ("_minimum_confidence", "_scenario")` — including private symbols. Because the imports are string literals, PyInstaller's static analysis cannot see them; only one module was compensated for, in `ssc_race_engineer.spec:86` (`hiddenimports = ["ssc_engineer.soak_budgets"]`). The package has 263 modules, so the manifest also covers only 63% of them, silently ignoring the rest.
findings.impact: Renaming any of those 284 symbols passes Ruff, mypy and the unit suite, then fails at release time inside the frozen exe with `AttributeError: missing symbols: ...`. Conversely, if a listed module ever becomes reachable *only* through this dict, PyInstaller omits it and `--release-self-test` fails on the packaged build only — the failure mode the single existing `hiddenimports` entry was patched around. This 448-line function also ships inside the product exe.
findings.fix: Derive the list at test time by walking `pkgutil.walk_packages(ssc_engineer.__path__)` and importing every module, rather than maintaining 165 string literals; keep the dict only for genuine third-party entry points (openai, keyring, pygame, sounddevice, pyarrow), which is maybe 10 entries.
findings.verifier_notes: Counts reproduce exactly via AST: the `checks` dict inside _release_self_test has 165 keys and 284 total symbol strings, and the function spans lines 231-678 (448 lines, as claimed). The dynamic dispatch is confirmed at cli.py:585-587 (`module = importlib.import_module(module_name)` then `missing = [symbol for symbol in symbols if not hasattr(module, symbol)]`, raising `AttributeError(f"missing symbols: ...")`). The single compensating hiddenimport is verbatim at ssc_race_engineer.spec:86 (`hiddenimports = ["ssc_engineer.soak_budgets"]`). No mitigation. | Confirmed. cli.py:231-232 is the exact quoted docstring; the checks dict opens at :235 and is driven through importlib.import_module(module_name) at :586 inside 'for module_name, symbols in checks.items()', raising AttributeError(f"missing symbols: {', '.join(missing)}") at :590 exactly as the impact describes. The PyInstaller blind spot is real and already evidenced by the single compensating entry at ssc_race_engineer.spec:86 hiddenimports = ["ssc_engineer.soak_budgets"]. The rename-breaks-only-at-release-time failure is concrete and reachable: a symbol rename passes Ruff, mypy and the unit suite because the references are string literals.

findings.title: Six incompatible `finite()` helpers with contradictory contracts — one returns a float, one a bool, one raises
findings.quote:
def finite(value: Any, default: float = 0.0) -> float:
    """Return a finite float or ``default`` for invalid telemetry values."""
findings.why_wrong: Six functions with the same name and the same apparent purpose exist, with mutually incompatible contracts: `calculations.finite(value, default=0.0) -> float` never raises and returns a default; `persistence/practice_domain.py:14 finite(value) -> bool` is a predicate; `ui/lico.py:77 _finite(value) -> float` *raises* `ValueError("Non-finite display value")`; `persistence/lico_calibration.py:30 _finite(value) -> float | None` returns None; `reporting/support.py:47 _finite(values: Iterable) -> list[float]` takes a sequence; `lico/bridge.py:26 finite_number(value) -> TypeGuard[int | float]`. Fifteen distinct `_number` helpers exist alongside them with nine different signatures (dashboard.py:19, pitwall.py:345, iracing_reader.py:112, persistence/setup.py:42, persistence/driver_capabilities.py:29, prediction_calibration.py:53, soak_budgets.py:189, race_plan_io.py:50, strategy_explanations.py:97, practice_testing.py:66, strategy_projection.py:33, lico_client.py:36, pit_operations.py:28, reporting/evidence.py:59).
findings.impact: A developer moving a line of telemetry-guard code from `ui/lico.py` to `calculations`-using code silently converts a raised ValueError into a 0.0 default, turning a rejected non-finite reading into a fabricated zero — a fuel level of 0.0 L or a gap of 0.0 s presented as measured. `from ...calculations import finite` and `from ..practice_domain import finite` both typecheck at the call site if the result is only truth-tested, but one is a float and one is a bool.
findings.fix: Keep exactly one of each in `calculations.py` with explicit distinct names (`finite_or_default`, `is_finite`, `require_finite`, `finite_or_none`), delete the five copies, and add a Ruff `flake8-tidy-imports` ban or a test that asserts no module redefines them.
findings.verifier_notes: All six signatures verified verbatim at the cited lines: calculations.py:13 returns a float with a default and catches TypeError/ValueError/OverflowError; persistence/practice_domain.py:14 returns bool; ui/lico.py:77 raises ValueError("Non-finite display value"); persistence/lico_calibration.py:30 returns float|None; reporting/support.py:47 takes an Iterable and returns list[float]; lico/bridge.py:26 is a TypeGuard. Factually airtight. Downgraded to low because the impact is a hypothetical future edit, not a defect present in the code: no call site today crosses the contracts, and the differing names (finite / _finite / finite_number) plus module-local scoping mean nothing is currently mis-binding. | All six verified by reading each definition: calculations.py:13 finite(value, default=0.0) -> float; persistence/practice_domain.py:14 finite(value) -> bool (isinstance predicate); ui/lico.py:77 _finite -> float raising ValueError('Non-finite display value'); persistence/lico_calibration.py:30 _finite -> float | None; reporting/support.py:47 _finite(values: Iterable) -> list[float]; lico/bridge.py:26 finite_number -> TypeGuard[int | float]. The name collision between a float-returning and a bool-returning 'finite' is the sharpest part and is real — both typecheck identically at a truth-tested call site. The exploit requires a developer to move code between modules rather than a runtime input, so it is a latent trap rather than a live fault; medium is the right level.

findings.title: Two byte-equivalent formatting helpers copy-pasted between the console and Tk dashboards
findings.why_wrong: `pitwall.py:345` holds the same function as a staticmethod (`return "--" if value is None else f"{format(value, pattern)}{suffix}"`), and `dashboard.py:25 _gap` / `pitwall.py:349 _gap` are logically identical to the character: both return `"--"` for None, `format_lap_time(value)` at >= 60 s and `f"{value:.3f}s"` below. Both files already import `format_lap_time` from the shared `calculations.py`, so the shared home exists and was simply not used.
findings.impact: Changing the missing-value sentinel from `"--"` (also hard-coded a third time as `UNAVAILABLE_VALUE` in ui/presentation.py:16) or the 60-second gap threshold requires finding three independent copies; miss one and the console dashboard and the pit wall disagree about the same gap on the same frame.
findings.fix: Move `_number` and `_gap` into `calculations.py` beside `format_lap_time`/`format_duration` and have dashboard.py, pitwall.py and ui/presentation.py import them.
findings.verifier_notes: The duplication is real and correctly located: dashboard.py:19-23 and pitwall.py:344-346 both define _number; dashboard.py:25-30 and pitwall.py:348-352 define _gap with identical semantics (None -> "--", >=60 -> format_lap_time, else f"{value:.3f}s"), and both modules already import format_lap_time from the shared calculations.py. UNAVAILABLE_VALUE = "--" confirmed at ui/presentation.py:16. Correction to the title, not the substance: the two _number helpers are NOT byte-equivalent — dashboard's third parameter is `missing: str = "--"`, pitwall's is `suffix: str = ""`. Only _gap is equivalent. The finder's own body text quotes the difference, so this is a title overstatement rather than a misread. | The duplication is real but the title overstates it. dashboard.py:25-30 _gap and pitwall.py:349-353 _gap are logically identical (None -> '--', >= 60 -> format_lap_time, else f'{value:.3f}s'); the third sentinel copy is confirmed at ui/presentation.py:16 UNAVAILABLE_VALUE = '--'. However the two _number helpers are NOT byte-equivalent: dashboard.py:17 takes (value, pattern, missing='--') while pitwall.py:345 is a staticmethod taking (value, pattern, suffix='') — different signatures and different behaviour. Both files do already import format_lap_time from calculations.py, so the shared home exists. Finding stands at low with that correction.

findings.title: `_pit_window_status` is implemented twice with different return vocabularies for the same state
findings.why_wrong: `strategy_scenario_support.py:39` defines the same function over the same two fields (`fuel_model.pit_window_open_lap` / `pit_window_close_lap`) and the same `snapshot.completed_laps + (snapshot.lap_progress or 0.0)` comparison, but returns a *different* string set: `"UNAVAILABLE" / "BEFORE" / "OPEN" / "CLOSED"` versus this one's `"UNKNOWN" / "NOT OPEN" / "OPEN" / "CLOSED"`. Both are public enough to matter — the communication one is re-exported from `communication/__init__.py:26` as `_pit_window_status as _pit_window_status`, and the strategy one is re-exported through `strategy_scenarios.py:23` and `strategy.py:22`.
findings.impact: The same pit window produces the token `"BEFORE"` in the strategy scenario state and `"NOT OPEN"` in the engineer context that feeds the radio call and the team-mobile payload. Any consumer matching on one vocabulary silently falls through on the other — e.g. a UI or gateway consumer testing `status == "NOT OPEN"` will never match the strategy path, and no type checker can catch it because both are bare `str`.
findings.fix: Delete one implementation, make the survivor return a `StrEnum` rather than a bare `str`, and have both `communication/context.py` and `strategy_scenario_support.py` import it.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed verbatim on both sides. communication/context.py:105-113 returns UNKNOWN / NOT OPEN / OPEN / CLOSED; strategy_scenario_support.py:39-49 computes the identical `current = snapshot.completed_laps + (snapshot.lap_progress or 0.0)` comparison over the same fuel_model.pit_window_open_lap / pit_window_close_lap and returns UNAVAILABLE / BEFORE / OPEN / CLOSED. Both re-exports confirmed: communication/__init__.py:26 `_pit_window_status as _pit_window_status` and strategy_scenarios.py:23 `_pit_window_status = _support._pit_window_status`. Both are bare `str`, so no type checker can catch a consumer matching the wrong vocabulary. | Confirmed exactly. communication/context.py:105-113 returns UNKNOWN / NOT OPEN / OPEN / CLOSED; strategy_scenario_support.py:39-49 computes the identical comparison over the identical two fields (fuel_model.pit_window_open_lap/close_lap, snapshot.completed_laps + (snapshot.lap_progress or 0.0)) and returns UNAVAILABLE / BEFORE / OPEN / CLOSED. Both are re-exported and reachable: communication/__init__.py:26 '_pit_window_status as _pit_window_status', strategy_scenarios.py:23 '_pit_window_status = _support._pit_window_status', strategy.py:22 '_pit_window_status = _scenarios._pit_window_status'. Two divergent bare-str vocabularies for one state, with no type checker able to catch a mismatched consumer.

findings.title: A second, independent fuel-consumption model lives in lico/ with different reserve and saving semantics
findings.quote:
class FuelEstimator:
    def __init__(self, target_laps: float = 0, reserve_l: float = 1) -> None:
findings.why_wrong: `engineering/fuel.py:24 FuelModelMixin._fuel_model` and `lico/fuel.py:42 FuelEstimator.update` are two entirely separate fuel models for the same car in the same session. They disagree on every component: consumption is `_rate_estimate(...)` (a robust average over two deques) in engineering vs `statistics.median(x[0] for x in self.samples)` over a 12-deep deque in lico (lico/fuel.py:93); the reserve is `rate * fuel_reserve_laps + 2.0 * deviation` (engineering/fuel.py:33-35, widening with observed variance) vs a flat constructor argument `reserve_l` (lico/fuel.py:29); required saving is `max(0.0, -margin / max(target, 0.01))` in litres-per-lap (engineering/fuel.py:74-78) vs `max(0.0, consumption - usable / remaining_laps)` (lico/fuel.py:96). Neither reads the other's output.
findings.impact: During a fuel-save phase the Control Center's fuel panel (engineering model) and the Traffic LICO overlay's lift-and-coast budget (lico model) can instruct the driver differently from the same telemetry — one saying the stint is safe while the other holds a save budget open, or vice versa. There is no reconciliation point and no test that asserts the two agree.
findings.fix: Either have `FuelEstimator` consume `FuelModelState` from the engineering model instead of re-deriving consumption from raw frames, or document explicitly (in code, not a handoff doc) that LICO's is a short-horizon lift-and-coast controller and make it read the engineering model's `reserve_l` rather than a constructor default of 1.0 L.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed, and I checked specifically for the reconciliation point that would refute it — there is none. lico/fuel.py:26-29 has the flat `reserve_l: float = 1` constructor arg; line 93 `consumption = statistics.median(x[0] for x in self.samples)` over a `deque(maxlen=12)` (line 31); line 96 `saving = max(0.0, consumption - usable / remaining_laps)`. Against engineering/fuel.py:24 `_rate_estimate(...)`, :33-35 `rate * self.policy.fuel_reserve_laps + 2.0 * deviation`, :74-78 `max(0.0, -margin / max(target, 0.01))`. FuelEstimator is constructed only at lico/engine.py:56 from Engine.target_laps/reserve_l, which trace back to CLI args (lico/__main__.py:37, 113) and manual bridge overrides (lico/bridge.py:80-85, 175-176) — never from DerivedMetrics.fuel_model. The two models never exchange a value. | Confirmed by reading both. lico/fuel.py:26-29 FuelEstimator(target_laps=0, reserve_l=1) with a flat constructor reserve and a 12-deep deque; consumption at lico/fuel.py:93 is statistics.median(x[0] for x in self.samples); saving at :96 is max(0.0, consumption - usable / remaining_laps). Against engineering/fuel.py: rate from _rate_estimate over two deques (:29), reserve_l = rate * policy.fuel_reserve_laps + 2.0 * deviation (:33-35, variance-widening), saving = max(0.0, -margin / max(target, 0.01)) (:73-77). Different consumption estimator, different reserve semantics, different saving units, and neither reads the other. Both are simultaneously shipped (installer/SSC_Race_Engineer.iss installs the frozen Tk app and the shell/LICO side), so a divergent lift-and-coast instruction versus Control Center fuel status is constructible from one telemetry stream.

findings.title: handle_driver_command branches on command_type three separate times, with three types repeated across chains
findings.quote:
mapping = {
        DriverCommandType.OPERATING_MODE: "get_operating_mode",
findings.why_wrong: This 375-line function has the highest branch density in the codebase (138 branch points). It dispatches on `command.command_type` in four places: the `mapping` dict at line 216 (32 entries -> tool names), a single `if` at line 250 (STATUS), an argument-building chain at lines 257-276, and a 33-arm response chain at lines 277-580. `STRATEGY_EXPLANATION` is tested at line 261 *and* line 301; `TEST_PROGRAM` at line 263 *and* line 307; `RADIO_SILENCE` at line 257 *and* line 577. The response chain terminates in a catch-all `else: response = "Calls resumed."` at line 580.
findings.impact: Adding a 36th driver command means editing four separate structures in one function. I verified the current set is exhaustive by exactly one member (only RESUME_CALLS legitimately reaches the `else`), which means the safety margin is zero: add a `DriverCommandType` with a `mapping` entry and forget the response arm, and the engineer speaks "Calls resumed." over the radio in reply to, say, a fuel question — a wrong answer to the driver mid-race, with no exception, no log line and no test failure, because the `else` absorbs it.
findings.fix: Replace the four parallel structures with one table keyed on `DriverCommandType` holding `(tool_name, argument_builder, response_builder)`, and make the lookup raise on an unregistered member instead of falling through to a default sentence.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed by AST: handle_driver_command spans lines 212-586 (375 lines) with 138 branch nodes; the `mapping` dict literal spans lines 216-249 with exactly 32 entries. findings.title: Three release/dev scripts still bootstrap sys.path with the pre-src-layout repo root

Eleven sibling scripts were correctly updated to insert both `parents[2] / "src"` and `parents[2] / "third_party"` (e.g. scripts/release/validate_windows_artifacts.py:10-12, scripts/validation/run_fault_campaign.py). findings.title: ControlCenterView.__init__ takes 27 parameters, 26 of them typed `Any`
findings.quote:
def __init__(
        self,
        *,
        tk: Any,
        ttk: Any,
        root: Any,
findings.why_wrong: The constructor spans lines 78-197 and takes 27 keyword parameters — the highest arity in the codebase by a wide margin (the runner-up is prediction_calibration.create_prediction at 23). Twenty-six of the 27 are annotated `Any` (`runtime_text: Any`, `credential_text: Any`, `key_entry: Any`, `startup_value: Any`, `sync_text: Any`, `update_text: Any`, `race_files_text: Any`, `privacy_text: Any`, `storage_text: Any`, `team_operations_text: Any`, `race_mode_value: Any`, `race_plan_text: Any`, ...); only `actions: ControlCenterActions` is typed. Since `pyproject.toml:101-106` enables `check_untyped_defs` and `disallow_incomplete_defs`, this is a deliberate opt-out: the signature satisfies the strict-mypy gate while conveying nothing.
findings.impact: Mypy cannot detect a swapped pair of `Any` StringVars at any of the call sites — passing `privacy_text` where `storage_text` belongs typechecks cleanly and only surfaces as the wrong text in the wrong panel at runtime. The widest boundary in the application is also its least type-safe, and adding a 28th panel means threading another parameter through every constructor call.
findings.fix: Replace the 26 `Any` parameters with a frozen dataclass of typed `tkinter.StringVar` / `BooleanVar` fields (one per panel group), so mypy checks the wiring and new panels extend the dataclass rather than the signature.
findings.verifier_notes: The defect is real but the finder's numbers are materially wrong, so I am correcting rather than confirming as written. AST at control_center.py:78-197 gives 26 keyword-only parameters plus self (27 including self, not 27 params). Of the 26, 20 are `Any`; six are concretely typed: version: str, app_data_root: str, auth_mode: str, frozen: bool, actions: ControlCenterActions, database_path: Callable[[], Any] | None. The claim "only actions: ControlCenterActions is typed" is false. The surviving substance — 20 same-typed `Any` StringVar-ish parameters at the application's widest boundary, so a swapped pair typechecks cleanly under the pyproject.toml:105-106 strict flags — holds. Downgraded to low: it is a typing-discipline observation with no demonstrated live defect, and the inaccurate arithmetic weakens the case as stated. | The defect class is real but the finding materially misstates its own evidence, so I am downgrading it to low. AST over ui/control_center.py: __init__ at line 78 has 27 arg slots INCLUDING self, i.e. 26 actual parameters, of which 20 (not 26) are annotated exactly Any. The claim that 'only actions: ControlCenterActions is typed' is false — version: str, app_data_root: str, auth_mode: str, frozen: bool and database_path: Callable[[], Any] | None are all typed as well, six typed parameters in total. The stated exploit is also weakened: every parameter is keyword-only (the '*' at line 80), so a positional 'swapped pair' is impossible; producing the wrong-text-in-the-wrong-panel outcome requires a caller to deliberately write the wrong keyword name. What survives verification is that 20 widget parameters carry no type information across the widest boundary in the app while pyproject.toml:104-105 enables check_untyped_defs and disallow_incomplete_defs — a real but narrow gap.

findings.title: The SSE stream thread never observes shutdown and outlives LocalApiServer.close()
findings.why_wrong: The `while True` loop at server.py:644-650 has no stop condition; it only exits when a write raises `BrokenPipeError/ConnectionError/OSError`. `LocalApiServer.close()` (server.py:511-513) calls `self._server.shutdown()` and `server_close()`, which stop the accept loop and close the listening socket but do not touch in-flight handler threads, and `daemon_threads = True` (server.py:502) means they are never joined. Worse, `api/__main__.py:43-44` calls `controller.shutdown()` *before* `server.close()`, so a live stream thread keeps calling `api.state()` -> `self.host.ensure_learning()` and `host.desktop_snapshot()` against an already-shut-down controller every 0.5 s.
findings.impact: Every SSE client leaks one thread per connection for the life of the process, each holding a strong reference to the RuntimeController and polling it twice a second. In `tests/api/test_shell_api.py` and `scripts/validation/shell_api_scenarios.py`, which create and close `LocalApiServer` repeatedly in one process, those threads accumulate and keep hitting torn-down state. In the shipped host the process exits immediately after, which is the only reason this is not user-visible today.
findings.fix: Add a `threading.Event` to `LocalApiServer`, set it in `close()`, and make `_stream` loop on `while not api._closing.wait(STATE_INTERVAL_S)` instead of `while True` + `time.sleep`. Also swap the order in api/__main__.py:43-44 so the server closes before the controller shuts down.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed line by line, including the ordering claim I specifically went looking to refute. server.py:637-651: `while True:` with the only exit being `except (BrokenPipeError, ConnectionError, OSError): return` — no stop event, no server-state check, no generation counter. close() at server.py:511-513 is only `self._server.shutdown()` + `self._server.server_close()`, neither of which touches in-flight handler threads, and `self._server.daemon_threads = True` at server.py:502 means they are never joined. api/__main__.py:42-44 does call `controller.shutdown()` before `server.close()` in the finally block, so a live stream thread keeps calling api.state() -> host.ensure_learning() / host.desktop_snapshot() (server.py:517-520) against a torn-down controller at the 0.5 s STATE_INTERVAL_S cadence. | The code reads as described but the claimed consequence does not hold, so I cannot construct the failure. (a) 'Every SSE client leaks one thread per connection for the life of the process' is false: the thread lives for the life of the CONNECTION, exiting on the next write once the client disconnects — at most STATE_INTERVAL_S = 0.5 s later, via the 'except (BrokenPipeError, ConnectionError, OSError): return' at server.py:651-652. Thread-per-connection with daemon_threads = True is the standard ThreadingHTTPServer contract, not a leak. (b) The test accumulation claim does not reproduce: tests/api/test_shell_api.py:317-321 opens /api/stream inside a with-block on the urllib response, and scripts/validation/shell_api_scenarios.py:316 calls host.stream(2.2) with a bounded read — both close their sockets, retiring the thread within one tick. (c) The __main__ ordering at api/__main__.py:43-44 (controller.shutdown() then server.close()) is real, but RuntimeController.shutdown() at ui/controller.py:283-287 only sets _closing/_learning_enabled and calls stop(); a stray api.state() in that window reads status, it does not corrupt or crash, and main() returns immediately afterwards so daemon threads are torn down by interpreter exit. The finding itself concedes the shipped host is unaffected. Ordering the two close calls the other way is a fair cleanup, but there is no reachable bad outcome.

findings.title: Critical persistence records are dropped silently after two retry attempts
findings.why_wrong: `_retry_batch` discards a command flagged `critical=True` after two failed attempts by incrementing a counter and hitting `continue` (writer.py:640). No logger call, no exception, no state transition at that point — the only trace is the integer. The same silent-drop pattern appears three more times in the same file (writer.py:329 on queue exhaustion, :656 when the re-queue is rejected). `_record_failure` at writer.py:622 sets `_state = "DEGRADED"` but stores only `f"{type(exc).__name__}: {exc}"` with no stack (see the traceback finding above).
findings.impact: Race-critical persisted evidence — completed laps, stints, pit service, engineer calls — can be permanently lost mid-session with the only signal being a counter that surfaces two layers away in reporting/evidence.py:195 and runtime/supervision.py:172, i.e. in the post-race report rather than at the moment of loss. The driver and engineer get no indication during the race that the session's data is now incomplete.
findings.fix: Emit a structured ERROR log at the drop site (writer.py:635) naming the command type and the originating exception, and raise the writer state to DEGRADED there rather than relying on a counter read downstream.

findings.title: Proprietary EULA forbids the modification and reverse engineering that LGPL-2.1/LGPL-3.0 require for pygame-ce and pystray
findings.quote:
- modify, translate, decompile or create derivative works of the Software,
    except to the extent that applicable law expressly permits;
findings.why_wrong: The "Software" is defined at LICENSE:4-6 as the whole product including its documentation, and THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md:142-147 confirms the packaged application embeds pygame-ce (LGPL-2.1) compiled modules and pystray (LGPL-3.0) "as bytecode in the application archive". LGPL-2.1 section 6 requires the distributor to permit modification of the work for the customer's own use and reverse engineering for debugging such modifications; LGPL-3.0 sections 4(d)/4(e) require conveying the work in a form that permits the user to recombine or relink a modified library. The EULA grants the opposite: it forbids modification, decompilation and derivative works outright, and forbids redistribution of "any part of" the Software (LICENSE:13-14), which also blocks the LGPL's own redistribution grant. The carve-out at LICENSE:19-22 ("those terms take precedence for those components") does not cure it, because the LGPL obligation is on the terms under which the combined executable is conveyed, not only the library files. Offering upstream PyPI source (THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md:145-147) satisfies neither section 6 nor section 4(d)(0), which are about relinking the shipped binary.
findings.impact: Squadra Svizzera Corse distributes an installer to team members and "evaluators" under terms that withhold rights the LGPL requires it to pass on. Under LGPL-3.0 section 8 the licence terminates on violation, so continued distribution of the installer is unlicensed copying of pystray and pygame-ce. A single complaint from either upstream forces a takedown of every installer already handed out.
findings.fix: Either (a) add an explicit carve-out to LICENSE stating that, for pygame-ce and pystray, the recipient may modify the components and reverse engineer the Software as needed to debug such modifications, and ship the LGPL Minimal Corresponding Source plus a relink kit alongside the installer, or (b) unbundle both: load pystray/pygame-ce as separate replaceable DLL/PYD files outside the PyInstaller archive with a documented relink procedure, or (c) replace them with permissively licensed equivalents.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified LICENSE:13-17 verbatim: "copy, publish, sublicense, sell or otherwise redistribute the Software or / any part of it" and "modify, translate, decompile or create derivative works of the Software, / except to the extent that applicable law expressly permits". "Software" is defined at LICENSE:4-6 as software plus documentation, with no carve-out for bundled components in the prohibition itself. THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md:142-145 confirms pystray ships "as bytecode in the application archive" and pygame-ce compiled modules under _internal\pygame, and the spec excludes list (ssc_race_engineer.spec:97-112) only drops pystray's non-Windows backends, so both are in the shipped binary. The only mitigation is LICENSE:19-22 ("those terms take precedence for those components"), which the finder already addressed: it scopes third-party terms to the component files, not to the terms under which the combined executable is conveyed, which is what LGPL-2.1 s6 / LGPL-3.0 s4(d) govern. Nothing else in the tree cures it. | Confirmed by reading LICENSE:1-22. "Software" is defined at LICENSE:4-6 as the product and its documentation, and the prohibitions at LICENSE:13-17 are unqualified: "copy, publish, sublicense, sell or otherwise redistribute the Software or any part of it" and "modify, translate, decompile or create derivative works of the Software". THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.txt line 7702 carries `pygame-ce 2.5.8  [LGPL v2.1]` and line 9410 `pystray 0.19.5  [LGPLv3]`, and THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md:142-147 confirms pystray ships "as bytecode in the application archive" inside the frozen app. Neither is in the PyInstaller excludes (ssc_race_engineer.spec:97-112 lists pathspec, numpy, mypy, ruff and pystray backend modules, not pystray or pygame themselves). Concrete sequence: SSC builds SSC_Race_Engineer_v1.0.4_Setup.exe, hands it to an evaluator under LICENSE (installer/SSC_Race_Engineer.iss:36 `LicenseFile=..\LICENSE`), and that recipient is contractually barred from the modification-for-own-use and debugging reverse engineering LGPL-2.1 s6 and LGPL-3.0 s4(d)/(e) require the conveyor to permit. The carve-out at LICENSE:19-22 says third-party terms "take precedence for those components" - it does not relax the terms on the combined executable, which is what s6 and s4 govern. The finding's reasoning survives.

findings.title: THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.txt claims to cover "every bundled distribution" and that React is not embedded; both false since the Electron shell ships
findings.quote:

findings.why_wrong: On this branch installer/SSC_Race_Engineer.iss:68 installs the packaged Electron shell to {app}\shell and line 74 adds a Start-menu entry for it. That shell bundles React 19, react-dom, scheduler, @stylexjs/stylex, styleq, lucide-react, the Geist fonts, the @astryxdesign packages, the @formatjs/intl-messageformat chain, invariant, js-tokens, loose-envify, css-mediaquery and the Electron/Chromium/Node runtime - 18 production packages plus Electron, none of which appear in the root THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.txt (I extracted all 71 section headers: PyPI distributions plus CPython and Tcl/Tk only). The same file states at line 17 "The React packages are not embedded in the Engineer runtime", contradicted by apps/shell/src/App.tsx:1-12 and apps/shell/src/main.tsx:1-6 importing @astryxdesign/core React components that Vite bundles into the shipped renderer. The later section at lines 130-138 partially walks this back, but the opening sentence and line 17 are what an auditor reads first.
findings.impact: The legal notice installed at the application root affirmatively misstates what the product bundles. An audit or upstream query is answered with a document saying React is not embedded while react-dom ships inside {app}\shell\resources\app.asar, undermining the credibility of the entire notice set and of the OFL-1.1 attribution the Geist fonts require.
findings.fix: Rewrite THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md:3-7 to say the root file covers the Python runtime only and that apps/shell/THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.txt (installed at {app}\shell\resources) covers the desktop shell; delete or correct line 17 to note that the Electron shell does bundle the React packages.
findings.verifier_notes: Half of this is a misread. THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md:17 reads "The React packages are not embedded in the Engineer runtime." and sits inside the section headed "## Astryx native theme adaptation" (line 13), whose subject is the native Tk/ttk theme (line 15: "The Engineer's native Tk/ttk theme adapts design tokens from"). React is indeed not embedded in the Python/Tk Engineer runtime; it is in the separate Electron shell process, which the same document discloses explicitly at lines 130-138 ("The Electron shell has its own production dependency graph (React, the Astryx design system, StyleX, the Geist fonts under the SIL Open Font License 1.1, and the Electron runtime)" ... "generated by apps/shell/scripts/licenses.mjs into apps/shell/THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.txt"), and apps/shell/scripts/package.mjs:37 does ship that file as an extraResource. So the statement is not false and the shell's licences are not missing, only held in a second file. What survives is the narrow imprecision of line 3's "every bundled distribution and runtime are in THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.txt" when a second notice file exists alongside. That is a wording nit in a document that self-corrects 127 lines later, not a compliance breach. | The two quoted sentences are scoped statements the finding reads out of context. THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md:17 sits under the heading `## Astryx native theme adaptation` (line 13), whose subject is "The Engineer's native Tk/ttk theme adapts design tokens from @astryxdesign/theme-neutral"; "The React packages are not embedded in the Engineer runtime" is true of the Tk runtime and is not a claim about the shell.
